en: *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll One.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty. 1.
The First Section on Expedient Means: Chapter One, the Nature of the Lineage (*Gotra*). The first section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* contains eighteen chapters.
Homage to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, the future, and the present.
There are ten dharmas that fully comprise the Bodhisattva path and are subsumed within the Mahāyāna.
What are the ten? First is upholding;
second is characteristics.
Third is assistance;
fourth is purity of mind;
fifth is abiding.
Sixth is arising;
seventh is inclusion;
eighth is the stage.
Ninth is practice;
tenth is establishment.
What is meant by "sustaining"?

The bodhisattva’s own lineage (*gotra*), the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), and all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are called "sustenance" (*dhāra*). Why is this?
Because by relying on the lineage, the bodhisattva is necessarily capable of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, the lineage is called "the sustenance of certainty."

Based on their initial resolve for enlightenment, Bodhisattvas practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).

By cultivating these six pāramitās—the discipline of merit, the discipline of wisdom, and the factors of enlightenment—one is therefore called a bodhisattva who, having first resolved upon awakening, maintains the practice of skillful means.
The Bodhisattva relies on the skillful means of practice to fulfill *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, the practice of skillful means is called the "upholding of great bodhi."

Those who lack the spiritual lineage, because they possess no such lineage, will certainly not reach the ultimate realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even if they resolve their minds upon it and apply themselves with diligent vigor.
Therefore, you should know that although one may not have generated the aspiration for enlightenment nor practiced the skillful means, they can still be said to possess the "upholding of the lineage.
However, if a bodhisattva possesses the lineage yet does not generate the aspiration nor practice the skillful means, they will be unable to swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there are those with the bodhisattva lineage who resolve their minds on enlightenment and practice with diligent vigor, they will be able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the lineage (gotra) is called "sustenance," "nourishment," "cause," "basis," "ladder," "guide," and "shelter."
Just as with the lineage and the generation of the resolve, so too are the practices and skillful means.
What is meant by "lineage"?
Briefly stated, there are two types:
First is the nature-lineage (prakṛti-gotra);
second is the cultivated-lineage (samudānīta-gotra).

As for the nature-lineage: it refers to the excellence of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) of a bodhisattva, which has been transmitted in succession from beginningless time as the natural law of phenomena; this is called the nature-lineage.
Regarding the nature of the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣāgotra*): if it is obtained through the cultivation of virtue from previous times, it is called the nature of the lineage of cultivation.
Furthermore, "lineage" (*gotra*) is termed "seed" (*bīja*), termed "element" (*dhātu*), and termed "nature" (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, for one who does not practice, the fruit is subtle and distant;
for one who practices, the fruit is coarse and near.
A Bodhisattva who has perfected their spiritual lineage (gotra) surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? There are two kinds of purity: first, the purity of the afflictive hindrances;
[and second, the purity of the cognitive hindrances].
Second is the purification of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Those of the two vehicles’ lineage purify the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not the cognitive hindrance;
those of the bodhisattva lineage possess both purifications, and for this reason, they are the most excellent and supreme of all.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one excels all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
first, excellence of faculties; second, excellence of the path; [third, excellence of wisdom; fourth, excellence of liberation].
Third is the excellence of skillful means;
fourth is the excellence of the fruit.
Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties by nature, pratyekabuddhas possess middling faculties, and śrāvakas possess dull faculties; this is called the excellence of faculties.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas seek only their own deliverance, whereas the Bodhisattvas are not like this; they deliver themselves and others as well, which is called "superiority in the path.

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are only able to understand the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), sense bases (āyatanas), the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), and the four noble truths;
the Bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), are able to fully understand all phenomena (dharmas), which is called "superiority in skillful means."

Śrāvakas attain the enlightenment of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas attain the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the excellence of the fruit.
There are six pāramitās, which are the marks of the bodhisattva lineage that enable all sentient beings to recognize them as bodhisattvas.
What are these six?
They are the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā.

Regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of the *dānapāramitā*: this bodhisattva’s nature is one that naturally delights in giving; they bestow the objects of their charity equally upon recipients without weariness. Whether the material wealth is much or little, they give with an impartial mind, rejoicing and without regret. If there is nothing to give, their mind is always filled with shame and remorse.
They constantly praise the merit of giving to others and exhort them to practice it; seeing those who give, their heart always rejoices in accordance with them.
Toward those who are venerable, elders, fields of merit, and those worthy of offerings, they relinquish their own seats and respectfully offer them up.
If someone asks about matters concerning this life and future lives in accordance with the Dharma, he explains them all;
if there is fear of kings, thieves, water, fire, or evil associates, he bestows fearlessness according to his ability;
he never fails to return items entrusted to him by others, and if he owes a debt to someone, he never evades it.
When brothers divide their wealth, they do so with equality and without partiality.
As for those who are deeply attached to various precious treasures, he teaches them to abandon greed;
if he even teaches others to abandon it, how much more so himself? How could he be personally attached to greed?
By nature, he is able to renounce and enjoy wealth; he delights in cultivating superior deeds, the rewards and benefits of which are vast and manifold.
Regarding all matters of intoxication, sensual beauty, song, dance, performers, and various displays of entertainment, he always feels shame and is able to distance himself from them quickly.
Even when obtaining great wealth and treasures, one does not become attached to them, let alone small profits.
Such instances as these are called the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of *dānapāramitā*.

Regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of the *śīlapāramitā*: the nature of this bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind is inherently supple; they do not increase in unwholesome conduct and take no pleasure in killing;
even if they should commit an evil deed, their mind gives rise to shame and remorse.
They are able to swiftly repent and eliminate [faults] so that they do not increase;
they do not terrify sentient beings with weapons or staffs, for their nature is benevolent and virtuous, and they always harbor loving-kindness and compassion;
they respect and honor their elders, welcoming and making offerings to them, and they skillfully understand the appropriate timing and employ clever expedient means in all they do.
He follows the inclinations of others' minds, always speaking with a smile, maintaining a relaxed countenance and a steady gaze, and inquiring after their welfare before they have spoken.
He recognizes kindness and repays it;
his aspirations are upright, being neither hypocritical nor crooked.
He receives wealth in accordance with the Dharma and not through unrighteous means.
By nature he always delights in cultivating all manner of merit; seeing others cultivate merit, he would even assist them with his own person, let alone doing so himself.

If there are sentient beings who harm one another, beating, binding, cutting, mutilating, reviling, or reproaching, and who endure such immeasurable sufferings, whether seeing or hearing of them, my mind is always filled with compassion.

Valuing the goodness of this life and the happiness of future lives, he is constantly filled with dread regarding even minor offenses; how much more so would he be wary and cautious of other grave evils?

If he sees others engaged in farming, commerce, herding, writing, arithmetic, accounting, mediating disputes, seeking or guarding wealth, lending at interest, giving alms, marriage, or social gatherings, he joins them in all such lawful activities.

Engaging in strife, discord, and litigation, and mutually instilling fear—whether toward oneself or others—is neither righteous nor beneficial; all such things he does not share in, being well able to restrain the ten unwholesome paths of action.
If one is commissioned by others and must follow their instructions, one should consult with the wise regarding what is appropriate for one's own conduct.

In all undertakings, one should set aside one’s own interests to accomplish theirs; always harboring compassion and never giving rise to anger or malice, should such emotions briefly arise, they must be immediately extinguished.

He constantly cultivates truthful speech and does not deceive sentient beings; he does not alienate others from their kin nor engage in meaningless talk. His words are always gentle and never coarse or harsh.
He does not even speak roughly to his own servants, much less to others.
One who always delights in all meritorious qualities with the mind, and who rejoices in and praises those who practice them when seeing others do so—
such as these are called the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of śīlapāramitā.

Regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): this bodhisattva is naturally gentle and mild by nature; even when encountering harmful actions from others, they do not give rise to anger, malice, or a desire for retaliation. If the other person repents and apologizes, they immediately accept the apology, harboring no lingering resentment and having no further thoughts of grievance.
Such as these are called the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage regarding the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

As for the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage regarding the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*): by their very nature, such bodhisattvas are inherently diligent; they rise at dawn and retire at night, taking no pleasure in indulging in sleep or reclining.
In all undertakings, one should be diligent and never abandon them; one must be able to reflect skillfully to ensure they reach completion.
When first initiating an action, one must be resolute and firm; if the task is not yet accomplished, one shall never cease midway.
In the ultimate sense, his mind does not retreat or sink; he does not disparage himself by saying he cannot accomplish what must be done, but is capable and courageous in all his undertakings.
He enters into great assemblies to subdue heterodox arguments and is skillfully able to respond to all difficult questions.
One is able to endure all other forms of suffering; through the power of great skillful means, one never feels sorrow or regret, let alone regarding minor matters.
Such characteristics as these are called the signs of the bodhisattva lineage of *vīryapāramitā*.

Regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage of the dhyāna-pāramitā: this bodhisattva, with respect to both phenomena and their meanings, possesses a nature that excels in reflection and is free from all distracted thoughts.
Whether seeing or hearing of mountain crags, forests, or thickets, they find them free from all clamor and conducive to silence, and immediately give rise to this thought:
"This place is peaceful and blissful; this place is secluded."
He then went to that place and applied himself diligently to study and practice.

This bodhisattva, by nature having few afflictions and light, subtle hindrances, went to a secluded place to contemplate his own welfare; he was not disturbed by unwholesome thoughts, and even if they should occasionally arise briefly, he immediately eliminated them.
One should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward those who are hostile and hateful, let alone toward others.

Upon seeing or hearing sentient beings undergoing suffering, one should immediately give rise to a mind of compassion and, according to one's strength and skillful means, deliver them so that they may be freed from suffering.

By nature, they delight in benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings; whether faced with hardships such as the loss of relatives, wealth, or being subjected to execution, imprisonment, or exile, they are able to endure them all with patience.

They are able to swiftly grasp the profound meaning of all dharmas; having perfected their power of mindfulness, they maintain what they have received with single-minded devotion. They are able to remember everything practiced over a long period of time, and they also cause others to remember it so that it is not forgotten.
Such as these are called the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage regarding the dhyāna-pāramitā.

As for the characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage regarding the prajñā-pāramitā: it is that this bodhisattva gives rise to the accomplishment of wisdom in all fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) and all bases of omniscience (*sarvajña-pada*); they are neither dull-witted nor deficient, nor are they foolish, and they are able to deliberate upon all objects of negligence.
This is called the characteristic of the bodhisattva lineage in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
I have briefly explained these coarse characteristics of the bodhisattva lineage; as for all other ultimate meanings, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know them with certainty.

A Bodhisattva of the lineage who is fully endowed with such inherent qualities of virtue accomplishes the truly pure and white dharmas; for this reason, they are called "difficult to obtain," "extraordinary," "inconceivable," "immovable," "unsurpassed," and "corresponding to the true cause of the Tathāgata’s dwelling."
A bodhisattva of the lineage who has accomplished pure and white dharmas is not defiled by the four kinds of afflictions.
If they were defiled, the pure and white dharmas would not manifest before them, or they would be reborn in the evil realms.

Bodhisattvas of the lineage dwell for a long time in saṃsāra or may fall into the evil destinies; yet those who fall into the evil destinies quickly attain liberation, and even while remaining in those evil destinies, they do not undergo great suffering.

Just as other sentient beings who enter hell are able to feel revulsion and detachment when suffering touches their bodies, and are able to give rise to compassion upon seeing others suffer, such a spiritual lineage serves as the cause for great compassion.
Therefore, although a bodhisattva may fall into the evil realms, they surpass all other sentient beings in those evil realms.
What are the four kinds of afflictions?
First, the frequent and sharp affliction of long-practiced negligence;
second, the practice of associating with evil associates out of ignorance.
Third, being oppressed by a sovereign lord, kings, thieves, or enemies, one lacks autonomy and the mind becomes confused;
fourth, lacking sufficient provisions, one is constantly anxious for one's life and body.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva of the lineage fails to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. What are these four?
First, they originally lack virtuous friends—Buddhas and bodhisattvas who skillfully expound the Dharma.
Second, although one encounters virtuous friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who skillfully expound the Dharma—one mistakenly receives and studies it.

Third, although one encounters virtuous friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who skillfully expound the Dharma—and does not mistakenly receive and study it, one does not apply oneself diligently to skillful means nor exert fervent vigor.

Fourth, although they may encounter virtuous friends—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who skillfully expound the Dharma—and diligently practice skillful means, their roots of goodness have not yet matured and their adornments are incomplete, for their minds have remained unsubdued since time immemorial.
Although a bodhisattva possesses the bodhisattva lineage, if the necessary conditions are not fulfilled, they cannot achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
By being free from these four dharmas, one will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one lacks the bodhisattva lineage, although one may possess all various skillful means, one will ultimately never attain unsurpassed enlightenment.

Chapter Two: The Chapter on Generating the Bodhicitta, within the Section on Skillful Means of the Bodhisattvabhūmi. When a bodhisattva first generates the mind [set on enlightenment], it is the beginning of all correct vows; it is capable of encompassing all correct vows. Therefore, this initial correct vow constitutes the essential nature of the vow.
The Bodhisattva resolves the mind and speaks these words:
"I shall seek unsurpassed bodhi and establish all sentient beings, causing them to attain ultimate nirvana without remainder and the great wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Thus, one who resolves to seek the bodhisattva path is therefore called a "bodhisattva seeking practice" at the first moment of resolve.

Because this resolve is made by taking both awakening (*bodhi*) and sentient beings as its objects, the initial resolve encompasses all roots of goodness conducive to awakening; it serves as the supreme guide, the ultimate skillful means, the perfection of merit, the most virtuous, and the most authentic. One should know that it causes all sentient beings to completely abandon evil conduct, and that among all mundane and supramundane right aspirations, it is the highest and unsurpassed. Thus should it be understood.
The initial arousal of the mind has five aspects:
first, its intrinsic nature;
second, its practice.
Third is the object-condition;
fourth is the quality;
fifth is the excellence.

A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is said to have entered the ranks of those bodhisattvas who transcend the Great Vehicle; therefore, the first resolution of the mind is subsumed within that which transcends.
Having generated this mind, one gradually attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, the first resolution of the mind is the root-wood of enlightenment (*bodhi*).

Having generated this mind, one perceives all sentient beings undergoing immeasurable suffering and gives rise to a heart of compassion, desiring to deliver and liberate them; therefore, the initial generation of the mind is the basis for great compassion.

Based on the initial aspiration, one establishes the bodhisattva factors of enlightenment and is able to cultivate all that is to be studied by a bodhisattva in relation to sentient beings; therefore, the initial aspiration is the basis for the bodhisattva’s training.
Thus, the initial arousal of the mind of awakening is called "gathering," it is called the "root," and it is called the "basis.
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas who have first aroused this mind:
the first are those who have emerged;
Second is non-emergence.
As for emergence, it refers to not regressing from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation.
Non-emergence, on the other hand, involves regression.
There are two kinds of regression:
first, ultimate regression;
second, non-ultimate regression.
Regarding those who regress ultimately, once they have regressed, they never again give rise to the bodhisattva vow.
Those who do not regress ultimately, having regressed, give rise to it once more.
A bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind possesses four conditions, four causes, and four powers.
What are the four conditions?

First, if a son or daughter of good family sees or hears that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess inconceivable supernatural transformations, and having seen or heard this, they immediately give rise to this thought:
"This is a great matter, truly inconceivable; they are able to perform such various transformative deeds."
Because these sights and sounds serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they take pleasure in the Buddha’s great wisdom and resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Second, although they do not see or hear such supernatural transformations as described above, when they hear a teacher of the Dharma praising *bodhi* and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they rejoice, feel gladness, and develop faith and delight upon hearing it.
Because this hearing of the Dharma serves as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they delight in the Buddha’s great wisdom and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Third, although they do not hear the Dharma, seeing the signs of the Dharma's extinction, they reflect:
"Immeasurable sentient beings will surely encounter great suffering; if a Bodhisattva remains in the world, he can eliminate it."
I shall now cultivate the path to enlightenment, uphold the True Dharma, and extinguish the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings.
Taking the protection of the Dharma as my predominant condition, I delight in the great wisdom of the Buddha and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Fourth, they do not see the extinction of the Dharma, but rather see the sentient beings of this degenerate age being afflicted and disturbed by the ten afflictions:
first, ignorance; second, lack of shame and remorse; [and so forth].
Third is stinginess and envy;
fourth is suffering and affliction;
fifth is defilement.
Sixth, afflictions;
seventh, unwholesome conduct;
eighth, negligence.
Ninth, laziness; tenth, lack of faith.
Having seen this, he thinks thus:
When this great age of turbidity arises, in such an evil world one cannot even give rise to the aspiration for the Two Vehicles, much less resolve to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
I shall now arouse the mind [for enlightenment] and cause others to do so as well.

Because the arousal of the resolve [for enlightenment] is difficult to attain within this defiled world, one takes this as a predominant condition and delights in the Great Wisdom of the Buddha by generating the bodhicitta.
What are the four causes?
First, the full possession of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second, being sustained by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends;
third, giving rise to great compassion;
and fourth, having no fear in one's heart toward these manifold sufferings—the suffering of birth and death, the suffering of difficult practices, and such long-lasting, immeasurable sufferings.
One who is endowed with the spiritual lineage (gotra) is so by virtue of the beginningless, natural order of phenomena (dharmatā).
One who is embraced by a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) possesses four qualities:
first, the virtuous friend is neither foolish nor dull-witted, but is wise and not perverse.
Second, one does not teach others to be heedless, nor does one provide others with the requisites for heedlessness.
Third, one does not teach others to engage in unwholesome conduct, nor does one provide others with the requisites for unwholesome conduct.

Fourth, one never causes others to fall away from superior faith, superior aspiration, superior receptivity, superior diligence, superior skillful means, or superior merit; nor does one bestow upon others inferior faith, inferior aspiration, inferior receptivity, inferior diligence, inferior skillful means, or inferior merit. This refers to severing them from the unsurpassed Mahāyāna and causing them to study the two vehicles (Hīnayāna); severing their wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) and giving them the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); severing their wisdom of reflection and giving them the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); severing their wisdom of hearing and giving them meritorious deeds; severing their ethical discipline and giving them mere generosity. In such ways, one severs superior merits and causes them to fall away, then bestows inferior merits upon them and causes them to practice.
There are four matters regarding the arousal of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

there may be worlds where there is suffering and affliction, or there may be worlds where there is no suffering and affliction. A bodhisattva is born in a world where there is suffering and affliction; seeing others undergoing suffering, or experiencing suffering oneself, or seeing both together, or seeing that one undergoes uninterrupted suffering for a long duration within saṃsāra—the bodhisattva, relying on their own spiritual lineage (*gotra*) which is inherently virtuous and noble, arouses inferior, middling, and superior degrees of compassion toward these four objects.
There are four things by which one does not fear the intense suffering of the uninterrupted cycle of infinite birth and death:
first, a nature that is inherently peaceful and courageous;
second, wisdom dedicated to the cultivation of contemplation.
Third, they give rise to superior joy toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
fourth, they give rise to superior compassion for all sentient beings.
What are the four powers?
First, the power of self;
second, the power of others;
third, the power of causes.
Fourth is the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).
When a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) through their own strength, this is called "self-power.
When they generate the mind of enlightenment due to another, this is called "other-power."

Having previously cultivated roots of goodness associated with the Mahāyāna, one now sees a Buddha or various bodhisattvas, or hears even a brief praise or teaching, and immediately resolves the mind [for awakening]; this is called the power of causes.
In this present life, one draws near to virtuous friends and, upon hearing their teachings, is able to cultivate various forms of goodness; this is called the power of skillful means.

When a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment through the four conditions, the four causes, personal effort, and the power of past causes, that resolve becomes firm, unshakable, and certain to reach its ultimate fulfillment.
Those who resolve their minds through the power of others' expedient means do so without firmness; their resolve wavers and is unstable.
There are four matters by which a bodhisattva regresses from the bodhicitta. What are these four?
First, the lack of complete spiritual predisposition (*gotra*);
second, being under the influence of evil associates (*pāpamitra*);
third, having a meager sense of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Fourth, one gives rise to a mind of fear toward the suffering of birth and death.
There are two matters by which the initial resolve becomes firm and steadfast, surpassing the world as a supreme, extraordinary, and unprecedented phenomenon:
first, one conceives of all sentient beings as one's own kin.
Second is the absence of the fault of gathering kinsmen.
As for the fault of gathering kinsmen, because one takes in relatives, the mind gives rise to attachment and aversion.
There are two matters by which the initial resolve remains firm and steadfast: giving rise to a truly pure mind toward all sentient beings.
First is the mind of peace and security;
second is the mind of happiness.
As for the mind of peace and security, it removes sentient beings from unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome states.
Regarding the joyful mind: for destitute sentient beings who have no one to rely upon, one can benefit them through a mind that embraces them with the Dharma and so forth.
There are two skillful means for making the initial resolve firm and enduring: first, the skillful means of purifying the mind; [and second, the skillful means of accumulating merit].
Second is the skillful means of the path.
Regarding the skillful means of purifying the mind, one’s mind of peace and mind of happiness increase day by day.

Regarding the skillful means of the path, one personally matures the Buddha-dharma day and night; according to one's own capacity, relying on the skillful means of purifying the mind, one brings peace, happiness, and benefit to all sentient beings.
There are two gates through which the firmness of the initial resolve enters into wholesome dharmas:
first, the skillful means for one's own benefit, which is the generation of the bodhicitta;
second, the skillful means for the benefit of others, which is the eradication of all sufferings.

There are two matters regarding the firmness and stability of the initial resolve: the wholesome dharmas encompassed by the resolve to attain enlightenment surpass all other encompassed wholesome qualities;
first, superiority of cause;
second, superiority of result.
The wholesome dharmas cultivated as the causes for that bodhi are called "superiority of cause.
Unsurpassed bodhi is called "superiority of fruit.
Because it surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the cause and fruit of the bodhisattva are thus exceptionally superior.
The firm and steadfast initial resolve to attain enlightenment brings two kinds of benefit:
first, once this mind has been generated, one immediately becomes a field of merit worthy of respect, providing pure offerings for all immeasurable sentient beings.
Second is the acquisition of purely pure merit.

One who has accomplished pure merit is protected by the merit of two wheel-turning kings; whether lying down or awake, they are not afflicted or harmed by wild beasts, malevolent spirits, ghosts, or demons, and in whatever place they are born, they have little illness or none at all.
When preaching the Dharma, his body does not grow weary and his mind does not forget.

For a Bodhisattva of the nature-lineage (*gotra*), the evil tendencies of body, speech, and mind are naturally subtle and thin; once he has resolved his mind [on enlightenment], they become even more attenuated.
If there are incantations used by others that lack efficacy, when the Bodhisattva employs them, they all become divinely effective.
Having already achieved compliance with the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), he is able to endure the afflictions of others and does not afflict others;
seeing people harming one another, he gives rise to a heart of compassion.
All higher afflictions such as anger, envy, concealment, deceit, hypocrisy, and crookedness will become extremely attenuated; even if they should arise, they will be swiftly extinguished.
In whatever place one dwells, there will be no terrors, strife, famine, or harassment by non-human beings.
Thus, these various difficulties do not arise where they have not yet arisen; even if they do arise, they are swiftly extinguished.
A bodhisattva who has resolved their mind may be born in the evil realms, yet they quickly attain liberation; the suffering they undergo is slight, and they swiftly develop weary detachment from it.
Because they are protected by pure merit, they are able to give rise to compassion toward other sentient beings.
They thus accomplish such immeasurable pure merits.
Chapter Three: Benefit for Oneself and Others, from the Section on Skillful Means in the Bodhisattvabhūmi. What is the practice of a bodhisattva?
To speak briefly of what Bodhisattvas train in: they train by training as they should;
this is collectively called the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
In what do Bodhisattvas train?
There are seven bases of training. What are the seven?
The first is self-benefit.
Second is benefiting others;
third is the true meaning;
fourth is power.
Fifth, maturing sentient beings;
sixth, maturing the Buddha-dharma for oneself;
seventh, unsurpassed bodhi.
What is self-benefit and benefit for others?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of self-benefit and benefit for others:
first, purity;
Second is commonality;
third is tranquility;
fourth is bliss.
Fifth, inclusion by cause;
sixth, inclusion by fruit;
seventh, this world;
Eighth, the future life;
ninth, the ultimate;
tenth, the non-ultimate.
Regarding those that exclusively benefit both oneself and others, there are two types:
first, those that exclusively benefit oneself;
second, those that exclusively benefit others.
One should know and abandon that which contravenes the Bodhisattva path, and one should practice and study that which accords with the Bodhisattva path.

Seeking wealth for one's own pleasure; seeking out and guarding the Buddha’s sutras and teachings for the sake of secret doctrines; upholding the prohibitive precepts, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and other dharmas for the sake of rebirth in heaven; making offerings at Buddhist stupas out of greed for worldly fruits; putting on the appearance of seeking profit for the sake of personal gain; speaking of various merits without cause in order to deceive others; being greedy for others' attachment and improperly gathering them in; and remaining in the bliss of one's own meditation while abandoning the welfare of sentient beings—these are called purely self-benefiting acts, and they should be known and abandoned.

With generosity, patience, and compassion as the foremost, dedicating these toward awakening and the desire to be born in the heavens—this is called self-benefit shared with others, which one should practice and study.
Excluding what has been described above, any other form of self-benefit that contradicts [the welfare of others] is called "self-benefit shared with others.

Pure benefit for others (*parārtha*) consists of: giving while holding wrong views that there is neither cause nor effect; preaching the Dharma to others while violating precepts and deviating from the Path; attaining purification on a lower stage and then bestowing those lower-stage pure dharmas upon others; a Bodhisattva relinquishing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to vow birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); a sovereign Bodhisattva manifesting various transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings; and the Tathāgata’s ultimate powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) that benefit all immeasurable sentient beings—this is called pure benefit for others.
The two types of purely altruistic [actions] previously mentioned should be understood and abandoned;
the remaining purely altruistic [actions] should be diligently studied.
Apart from what has been thus described, those that are contrary to purely altruistic [action] are termed "altruistic [action] shared with one's own."
The establishment of the welfare of oneself and others is briefly explained as fivefold:
first, the characteristic of being blameless;
second, the characteristic of inclusion.
Third is this world;
fourth is the other world;
fifth is cessation.

Whatever roots of goodness are embraced by a bodhisattva—whether many or few—that they cultivate and bring to fulfillment, and by which they likewise bring sentient beings to fulfillment, discipline, and establishment, is called the characteristic of being blameless.

The Bodhisattva who brings peace to self and others, through the joy of being free from defilement and the joy of various requisites, abides in the bliss of dhyāna to benefit both self and others; this is called the characteristic of gathering and sustaining.

For a bodhisattva who brings benefit to both self and others, there are four types of peace: that which pertains to this world but not the next, that which pertains to the next world but not this one, that which pertains to both this world and the next, and that which pertains to neither this world nor the next. These four kinds of experience and four kinds of phenomena follow their respective order as appropriate.

What are the four? There are phenomena that bring happiness in the present life but suffering in future lives; there are phenomena that bring suffering in the present life but happiness in future lives; there are phenomena that bring happiness in the present life and happiness in future lives; and there are phenomena that bring suffering in the present life and suffering in future lives. These are called the benefits for oneself and others, and peace in this world and the next.
Nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, the factors conducive to nirvāṇa, and mundane and supramundane dharmas—these are called the tranquility that brings peace to oneself and others.
For those who delight in the welfare of both self and others, there are briefly five kinds of joy:
first, the joy of the cause;...
Second is the pleasure of sensation;
third is the pleasure that counteracts suffering;
fourth is the pleasure of the cessation of sensation.
Fifth is the bliss of being free from fault.
Regarding the causes of bliss, there are two kinds:
first, the arising of pleasant sensation due to the causal conditions of the contact between the sense faculties and their objects.
Second is the karma that results in desirable fruits in this life and future lives;
this is called the pleasure of the cause.
Once all sufferings have ceased, one contemplates these three kinds of causal pleasure, giving rise to mental and physical sensations; this is called the pleasure of sensation.
There are two kinds of feeling pleasure:
with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
That which is without outflows belongs to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding "with outflows" (*sāsrava*):

they are bound to the three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. All these [factors] of the three realms are distinguished according to their respective six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Arising through the causal conditions of eye-contact, up to the causal conditions of mind-contact, those associated with the five consciousnesses are called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*), while those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are called "mental feeling" (*caitasikī vedanā*).

Regarding the various afflictions of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth, one employs remedies for those already arisen and those yet to arise to cause them to cease; once they have ceased, the arising of the knowledge of bliss occurs—this is called the bliss of the remedy for suffering.
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is called the severance of the pleasure of sensation.
As for blameless pleasures, there are four kinds:
first, the pleasure of renunciation;
Second is the joy of detachment;
third is the joy of tranquility;
fourth is the joy of enlightenment.

To have faith that the household life is not a home and to leave it behind to study the Way, thereby liberating oneself from the various difficulties of domestic life—this is called the happiness of renunciation (*pravrajyā-sukha*).
To sever desire and unwholesome, evil states, and to attain the joy and happiness born of seclusion in the first dhyāna—this is called the happiness of solitude (*viveka-sukha*).
Taking the second dhyāna as the foremost, the cessation of vitarka and vicāra is called the bliss of tranquility (śānti-sukha).
The ultimate extinction of all afflictions and the bliss of awakening to all phenomena as they truly are is called the bliss of bodhi.
Pleasure as a cause is a cause of pleasure, not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Pleasure as experience is not a cause of pleasure, but is its intrinsic nature.
Pleasure as an antidote is neither a cause of pleasure nor its intrinsic nature; rather, it is the cessation of suffering and the removal of suffering.

Regarding the abandonment of pleasant feeling: it is not caused by pleasure, nor is it its intrinsic nature, nor is it the removal of suffering; rather, all feeling is truly suffering. When one abides in meditative concentration, that feeling ceases, and it is subsumed under faultless bliss.
The bliss of ultimate enlightenment is the final cessation of all past, future, and present afflictions; the various other blameless pleasures that accord with it are called "blameless bliss."

This bodhisattva benefits sentient beings with peace and happiness; knowing as it truly is what constitutes peace and happiness, he teaches and instructs them according to his power and skillful means to eliminate and sever [what is not].

If something is painful at first but leads to peace later, although it may cause distress and affliction, it must ultimately be beneficial; this is the Bodhisattva’s reliance on skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

If something is pleasant at first but leads to unrest later, although one may not wish to abandon it due to its initial suffering, one must nonetheless eliminate and sever it through the power of skillful means.
Why is this? Because they will certainly obtain happiness in the future.
This bodhisattva, desiring that sentient beings be at peace, wishes for them to obtain happiness; and to those who are already at peace, he likewise wishes to grant happiness.
"Peace" refers to the causal state; "happiness" refers to the resultant state.
Therefore, one should know that those who wish to bring happiness to sentient beings must first establish them in peace.

The karma that seeks such results is encompassed by the causes of happiness in both this life and future lives—namely, the happiness that counteracts suffering, the happiness of the cessation of sensation, and the happiness free from fault. It is certainly through these that one benefits sentient beings; this is also called "gathering" (*saṃgraha*), and it is also called the happiness of receiving what is blameless and the happiness caused by the contact of the sense faculties with their objects.
That which is defiled, culpable, and insecure, he does not teach for the sake of benefiting others, but rather instructs them to eliminate and sever it.
That which is non-defiled, blameless, and secure, he uses to benefit all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva also constantly practices according to his own capacity; this is called the Bodhisattva’s inclusion of the causes for the benefit and happiness of both self and others.
Regarding the inclusion of the fruits of the benefit of self and others, briefly stated, there are three kinds of causes and three kinds of fruits.
The cause of retribution and its fruit of retribution; the cause of merit and its fruit of merit; the cause of wisdom and its fruit of wisdom.
What is meant by "retribution"?
There are eight kinds of retribution:
First, the perfection of longevity;
second, the perfection of physical form;
third, the perfection of lineage.
Fourth, the perfection of mastery;
fifth, the perfection of authoritative speech;
sixth, the perfection of great power.
Seventh is the perfection of human form;
eighth is the perfection of power.
Longevity that endures for a long time is called the perfection of life span.
Having a countenance that is upright and dignified is called the perfection of form.
Being born into a noble lineage is called the perfection of lineage.
Attaining great wealth, a large retinue, and many followers is called the perfection of sovereignty.

In adjudicating matters and hearing lawsuits, he establishes laws and regulations; in receiving, bestowing, and entrusting, he always acts with integrity. All his words are trusted and respected by others; this is called being endowed with trustworthy speech.

Possessing great renown, great skillful means, and great wisdom, he is esteemed by others for his various arts and crafts; the great assembly reveres, honors, and praises him—this is called being fully endowed with great power.
To accomplish the qualities of a great man is called being endowed with human excellence.
To have little illness and little affliction, and to possess capability, is called being endowed with strength.
What is the cause of retribution?
Not harming sentient beings and having no intent to injure them is called the cause of longevity.
Giving lamps, pure objects, and bright things is called the cause of physical form.
Abandoning arrogance is called the cause of noble lineage.
Generously bestowing all necessary provisions is called the cause of mastery.
Refraining from the four verbal transgressions is called the cause of trustworthy speech.
Gathering all merits and establishing great vows, while making offerings to the Triple Gem and one's elders and superiors, is called the cause of great power.

Delighting in the qualities of a man and feeling aversion toward the qualities of a woman, one speaks of the qualities of a man for the benefit of others and teaches them to feel weary of and detached from the qualities of a woman; this is called the human cause.
In whatever righteous deeds sentient beings undertake, one goes to assist them according to one's own ability; this is called the cause of power (*bala-hetu*).
These eight kinds are called the causes of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of excellence in the causes of retribution that cause the retribution to become predominant:
first, purity of mind;
second, purity of skillful means.
Third is the purity of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

With a pure mind, one aspires for unsurpassed *bodhi* and dedicates these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), causing them to gradually increase. One takes joy in practicing what is supreme, wondrous, and purely wholesome; upon seeing others who practice, one gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Day and night, in every thought-moment, one accords with the True Dharma, following it through constant awareness and contemplation. This is called purity of mind.

To practice diligently and without interruption throughout the long night, and furthermore to transmit this Dharma to others; to rejoice and praise those who receive it, and to provide instruction in accordance with their practice and realization; and likewise to establish oneself in this Dharma as well—this is called purity through skillful means.
Briefly stated, the skillful means and the arising of the fruit of skillful means are called the purity of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
What is the fruit of retribution?

Because the Bodhisattva is endowed with a full lifespan, he long cultivates wholesome dharmas so that all sentient beings may achieve roots of goodness; this is called the fruit of the endowment with a full lifespan.
Because the Bodhisattva is endowed with excellence of form, the great assembly loves and delights in him;
because they love and delight in him, they all together revere and respect him and joyfully listen to what he says. This is called the fruit of excellence of form.

Because the bodhisattva is fully endowed with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they are respected, honored, and praised by all; whatever they say is necessarily accepted and practiced without violation. This is called the fruit of being fully endowed with the spiritual lineage.
Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with mastery, he universally gathers and brings sentient beings to fulfillment through giving; this is called the fruit of being fully endowed with mastery.

Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with authoritative speech, he constantly benefits others through loving words and acting in concert with them, gathering them in and transforming them until they achieve fulfillment; this is called the fruit of being fully endowed with authoritative speech.

Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with great power, he is able to assist in all that sentient beings undertake; sentient beings, recognizing his kindness, all come to seek refuge in and look up to him, and whenever he issues instructions, they all receive and implement them—this is called the fruit of being fully endowed with great power.

Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the human state, he achieves the male form and is a fit vessel for all meritorious qualities. He attains fearlessness regarding all skillful means and all knowledge and vision; he dwells with sovereign ease at all times; and he engages in coming and going and shared activities with all sentient beings, moving freely and without hindrance through human realms and wildernesses. This is called the fruit of being fully endowed with the human state.

Because the Bodhisattva is fully endowed with power, he practices diligence, firmness, and swiftness as skillful means; he cultivates goodness without weariness and gathers in others without fatigue—this is called the fruit of being fully endowed with power.

By means of these eight kinds of retributive fruits, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings and personally matures the qualities that accord with the Buddha-dharma. Abiding in these retributive fruits, the bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to perform what they ought to do; following his instructions, each sentient being cultivates their respective aspirations.
If a bodhisattva possesses personal power yet the other does not comply, this is not called benefiting others.
If one lacks personal power yet those to be transformed follow accordingly, this likewise is not called benefiting others.
If one possesses personal strength and those to be transformed are compliant—if these two conditions are fulfilled—one can benefit both oneself and others.

When a bodhisattva is endowed with these two dharmas, they are able to practice the Buddha-dharma for themselves and bring sentient beings to maturity through the Three Vehicles; thus, they can personally realize unsurpassed bodhi and cause those among sentient beings who are ripe for it to attain liberation.

Therefore, by abiding in these eight kinds of retributive fruits, a bodhisattva is able to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings. All sentient beings have undergone boundless birth and death since time immemorial, which has been empty and devoid of benefit; [the bodhisattva] causes them all to become non-empty and to obtain great fruits.
What is merit? What is wisdom?
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)—these are called merit.
The Prajñāpāramitā is called wisdom (jñāna).
The Dhyānapāramitā and the Vīryapāramitā each have two parts:
the first is the part of merit (puṇya).
The second is the division of wisdom (*jñāna-bhāga*).
Cultivating the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth based on dhyāna is called the division of merit (*puṇya-bhāga*).

Cultivating skillful means regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana-kauśalya*), skillful means regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*), and being able to discern and observe as they truly are—suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path; wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; blameworthy and blameless phenomena; inferior and superior phenomena; defiled and pure phenomena; and all dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) based on dhyāna, is called the division of wisdom.
Based on diligence, one practices giving, morality, the four immeasurables, and so forth; this is called the "merit portion.

Based on diligence, one cultivates the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the skillful means regarding the aggregates and so forth, as previously explained; this is called the "wisdom portion."
Thus, merit and wisdom are briefly explained as being of six kinds; if explained extensively, they are immeasurable.
What are the causes of merit and the causes of wisdom?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of causes of merit and causes of wisdom:
First, there is the aspiration for the means of cultivating merit and wisdom;
second, there is compliance with proximate conditions;
third, regarding those who have cultivated merit and wisdom as their proximate conditions, they do not abide in perverted conditions, but abide in non-perverted conditions.
Associating with evil associates and explaining merit and wisdom erroneously, or conceiving and receiving them erroneously, is called abiding in the conditions of perversion.
That which is contrary to this, the pure portion, is called abiding in the conditions of non-perversion.
When one is free from the obstacles of desire regarding the means for cultivating merit and wisdom, these do not arise; this is called "proximity.
If these three causes are not complete, merit and wisdom will not be produced.
What are the fruits of merit and the fruits of wisdom?

By relying on merit, the bodhisattva endures all manner of sufferings throughout the infinite cycle of birth and death for the sake of all sentient beings, gathering them in according to their respective inclinations.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on wisdom, they gather various skillful means of right merit for the sake of all sentient beings until the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi.
Thus, it is briefly said that there are four kinds of fruits of merit and wisdom; if explained extensively, they are immeasurable.

Whether it be retribution, the cause of retribution, or the fruit of retribution, all arise based on merit; merit arises based on wisdom. When these two are fully possessed, they are most excellent and supreme, leading to the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi;
if merit and wisdom are not possessed, one will ultimately never attain it.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others through the inclusion of causes and the inclusion of results.
What is the benefit for self and others in this life and in future lives?

Practicing meritorious deeds in the present to obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma; receiving the fruit of retribution now due to the causal conditions of past goodness; being well able to turn away from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to dwell in the happiness of this life; relying on this life to benefit sentient beings; and relying on the various meditative absorptions to attain *nirvāṇa* in the present life—such as the mundane and supramundane aspects of reality regarding conditioned phenomena directed toward *nirvāṇa* in the present life—this is called the benefit for oneself in this life.
To transform sentient beings by means of this very dharma is called benefiting others in this life.

To desire the body and wealth of the desire realm in future lives, up to birth in the realms of meditative concentration and the formless realm, and to contemplate and cultivate the causes for such births—which result in the sorrow and suffering of this life—is called benefiting oneself and others in future lives.

The joy and happiness of this world, the cultivation of the causes for body and wealth through reflection, and even the meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) and formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) belonging to the stage of decline in this world—these are called the benefit of self and others in this world and the next.
What is meant by ultimate and non-ultimate benefit for oneself and others?
The body and wealth of the desire realm have causes and fruits; the mundane purity of ordinary beings has causes and fruits—this is called non-ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
The ultimate extinction of all afflictions, the Eightfold Noble Path, and the mundane wholesome dharmas arising in dependence upon them—these are called the ultimate benefit for oneself and others.
There are three types of the ultimate and the non-ultimate:
first, intrinsic nature; [second, cultivation; third, fruit].
Second is retrogression;
third is the exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruit.
As for their intrinsic nature: nirvāṇa is ultimate, whereas all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are not ultimate.
The Eightfold Noble Path is non-retrogressive; its enjoyment of the fruit is inexhaustible and ultimate.
Other wholesome, outflowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas are subject to retrogression; their enjoyment of the fruit is exhaustible and not ultimate.
These are called the ten kinds of benefit for oneself and others, thus briefly explained, and can be further elaborated upon.

A bodhisattva should practice and study according to their capacity—having studied in the past and shall study in the future—all ten types of benefit for oneself and others; these are called ultimate and non-ultimate benefits for oneself and others.
Chapter Four: The Meaning of Reality, Part One. Regarding the Bodhisattvabhūmi, the Section on Skillful Means, Chapter Four: The Meaning of Reality. What is the meaning of reality?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Second is the dharmatā of all phenomena.
These two types of dharmatā, when distinguished by their categories, further comprise four kinds:
the first is that which is known through worldly cognition;
Second, the objects of knowledge for those in training;
third, the dharmas that are the domain of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obstructions;
and fourth, the dharmas that are the domain of the wisdom purified of the cognitive obstructions.
What is the meaning of reality as known by the world?

Regarding the various phenomena of the world, they all agree in their conventional understanding and perception: that earth is simply earth, and is not water, nor anything else such as fire, water, or wind.

Regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and even suffering and pleasure—in brief, these things are simply themselves and not other things. All such objects that are the domain of definitive mental understanding are, from the very beginning of the world, known through innate conceptualization and do not arise from cultivation; this is called the "truth of what is known by the world."
What is the true meaning of what is known through learning?

It is as follows: based on worldly wisdom—namely, direct cognition, inferential cognition, and that which is derived from hearing and reflecting upon the teachings of a teacher—one compiles and establishes the objects within the sphere of certain knowledge; this is called the true meaning of what is known through learning.
What is the reality of the objects of knowledge accessible to the wisdom purified of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddha-jñāna-gocara-dharma-tattva*)?

It refers to the realm of practice for the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as their untainted skillful means (*anāsrava-upāya*) or the mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) that arises in accordance with them. Within the objective conditions of that wisdom, the afflictive hindrances are purified, and hindrances in future lives will never again arise; this is called the reality of the objects of knowledge accessible to the wisdom purified of the afflictive hindrances.

These are the so-called Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. By contemplating these four truths, one enters into immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) and the wisdom arising from that immediate realization. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive that within the aggregates (*skandha*) and apart from the aggregates, no self can be found; they see that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise through dependent origination and are subject to birth and extinction in combination. Thus, they cultivate the knowledge and vision that there is no self or personal identity within the aggregates or apart from them.
What is the true meaning of the dharmas that constitute the sphere of activity for the wisdom purified of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaradharma*)?

That which obstructs what is to be known by wisdom is called an obstruction. The sphere of activity for the practice of the wisdom that is liberated from those cognitive obstructions is called the true meaning of the dharmas that constitute the sphere of activity for the wisdom purified of cognitive obstructions.

This refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas entering the dharma of non-self; having entered it, they become purified. Regarding all dharmas, they abide in the realm of the practice of great wisdom—equanimous and free from all conceptual constructions—which is beyond the nature of verbal expression and the nature of provisional names. It is the foremost, suchness, unsurpassed, and boundless, wherein the discernment of all dharmas brings about their eternal cessation and non-arising.
Furthermore, the establishment of the true characteristic is twofold:
first, existence-nature;
second, non-existence-nature.
Regarding "existence" (*sat*), it is the establishment and designation of a conventional name for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since time immemorial, the world has been attached to all the roots of conceptualization and delusion, namely: "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness"; "eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind"; "earth, water, fire, and wind"; "form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena," up to and including "nirvāṇa. Such dharmas that possess an intrinsic nature through worldly conventional designations are called "existence."

Regarding "absence of nature" (*abhāva*): from the conventional designation of form (*rūpa*) up to the conventional designation of nirvāṇa, there is no objective entity and no basis for such designations; since all that is depended upon is entirely non-existent, this is called "absence."
As explained above, existence and non-existence—these two—are both devoid of the characteristics of dharmas.
The two dharmas thus subsumed are non-dual; this non-duality is called the Middle Way, and being free from the two extremes is called the Unsurpassed.
Such is the reality, which is the sphere of the pure wisdom of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and that which all bodhisattvas should cultivate and study.
Those who so cultivate and study are called bodhisattvas of great wisdom and skillful means; they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva is endowed with the liberation of emptiness; while remaining within birth and death, he knows birth and death as they truly are, yet does not give rise to revulsion toward the impermanence and other characteristics of birth and death, and is thus able to accomplish the Buddha-dharma to benefit sentient beings.
If one does not know birth and death as they truly are, one cannot abandon all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

If these are not abandoned, one undergoes various births and deaths with a defiled mind; and one who undergoes births and deaths with a defiled mind cannot accomplish the Buddha-dharma to benefit sentient beings.
If one gives rise to revulsion and detachment toward the conditioned phenomena of birth and death, such as impermanence and so forth, that bodhisattva will quickly attain nirvana.
One who quickly attains nirvana, moreover, will be unable to accomplish the Buddha-dharma for the benefit of sentient beings.
How can one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If a bodhisattva is in accord with the liberation of emptiness, then they neither fear nirvāṇa nor seek nirvāṇa.

If a bodhisattva fears nirvāṇa, they will be unable to fulfill the path to nirvāṇa; because they fear nirvāṇa, they do not perceive its merits and benefits, and failing to perceive its merits and benefits, they become entirely alienated from pure faith and aspiration.
If a bodhisattva seeks nirvana and practices it excessively, they will quickly enter parinirvāṇa.
One who quickly enters parinirvāṇa is unable to accomplish the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings.
If one does not know birth and death as they truly are, then one will undergo birth and death for a long time;
if one is weary of birth and death, then one will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa.
If one fears nirvāṇa, one will be unable to fulfill the path to nirvāṇa.
If one who seeks nirvana practices it extensively, they will quickly attain parinirvāṇa; it should be known that such a bodhisattva lacks great skillful means regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If one attains knowledge of birth and death as it truly is, then the mind will not be stained by or attached to birth and death. If one does not feel weary of or seek to escape from the conditioned phenomena of impermanence and so forth within birth and death, one will not enter nirvana hastily; yet, if one does not fear nirvana, one will be able to fulfill the path to nirvana and deeply perceive its merits and benefits.

If one does not diligently seek swift nirvāṇa, it should be known that this bodhisattva possesses great skillful means regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this great skillful means relies upon the liberation of the foremost emptiness. Therefore, it is called the supreme skillful means of a bodhisattva cultivating the liberation of the foremost emptiness, because it is directed toward the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata.
