If he conceals such an evil deed even when it is committed by another to deceive them, how much more so when it concerns himself?
Wishing to fulfill their aspirations, he gives them wealth according to their desires; having received it, they feel no shame or remorse, but depart with joy, free from fear and full of delight.

Even if the Bodhisattva is deceived by those merchants—having not been aware of the deception beforehand but realizing it only after it has occurred—he does not reproach them nor cause them to remember it; desiring that they do not commit the taking of what is not given, he gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
The relinquishing of such objects of giving is called the bodhisattva’s wisdom-giving (*prajñā-dāna*).

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva has no material wealth to give, he employs the worldly crafts previously practiced by him; through the manifestation of those skills and with minimal effort, he acquires great wealth and profit, which he then uses to bestow upon sentient beings.

Furthermore, if one preaches the Dharma for others with adornment, with beauty and excellence, and with a compassionate heart, those who are poor and suffering will hear the Dharma and joyfully make offerings; how much more so those who are wealthy and happy?
One who is stingy has no sense of renunciation, much less one who constantly delights in giving.

If there is a faithful elder or householder who habitually practices generosity, possessing immeasurable wealth, they will bring seekers to them, thereby benefiting those recipients through the gifts they bestow.
Regarding the meritorious deeds performed, one should personally go to assist them, being capable of fulfilling their practice through pure actions of body, speech, and mind.
According to one's own strength and ability, one should aid them in their management so that they may proceed without hindrance and satisfy those who seek their help.

If one lacks material resources, the act of giving is difficult to accomplish; this may occur if one follows factions, acts contrary to the Dharma, or loses right mindfulness. In such cases, even if a bodhisattva possesses no wealth, they practice the gift of wisdom, continuing until they attain a pure mind.
A Bodhisattva with a pure mind does not fall into the evil realms, and in every birth they constantly obtain inexhaustible wealth.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva recognizes those who hold wrong views and seek the Dharma with ulterior motives, they do not transmit the Dharma to them nor provide them with scriptural scrolls.
If one is by nature greedy for wealth and sells sutra scrolls, one should not give them to such a person.
If one obtains sutra scrolls and conceals them rather than making them manifest, one should likewise not give them to such a person.
If the meaning is not something that the person understands, one should also not give it to them.

If the meaning of this scripture is already known to that person, the Bodhisattva, having already understood its meaning from this scroll, shall then uphold the scripture and give it to them according to their wish.
If he does not yet know the meaning and must study it himself, and furthermore knows that another possesses such a scripture, he shall point out its location or provide a copy for them.

If there is no place to show it and it cannot be written down, the bodhisattva should further examine his own mind: "Is it that my mind is entangled by stinginess regarding these dharmas such that I am unable to give?
Or is there something else for which I do not give to others?"
Having thus observed oneself, if one possesses even a slight amount of Dharma that is held with stinginess, one should give this sutra for the sake of the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

I would rather give the gift of Dharma, even if it results in being foolish or mute in the present life; since one should still give it to eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*), how much more so when it serves as the wisdom and skillful means for the future?

When observing in this way and finding not even the slightest trace of stinginess toward any phenomenon, that bodhisattva should train themselves thus: "I practice the gift of Dharma for the sake of eliminating afflictions; I practice the gift of Dharma for the sake of fulfilling wisdom and skillful means; I practice the gift of Dharma out of love and compassion for sentient beings."

The Bodhisattva perceives within himself that he is free from afflictions; seeing that he does not bestow [gifts] upon others, he realizes that wisdom is attained in the present and will increase immeasurably in future lives.
It is not because of giving to others that he attains this merit.
One who practices the Dharma-giving of the sutras will obtain a small measure of Dharma-benefit in future lives, yet this does not equal the awakening of wisdom attained through one's own study.
Although one may not give now, one will surely bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings by bestowing upon them wisdom.
It would be better to not give it to anyone at all now than to give this scripture to only one person.
Having known this as it truly is, there is no fault or regret in not giving it to him, nor does he transgress the prohibitions undertaken by a bodhisattva.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful means of not giving?

It is when one does not endure speaking bluntly that "I certainly will not give," but instead uses gentle words to explain, resolve, and dismiss [the petitioner]; employing such skillful means, one does not give despite having the means to do so.

Having already offered all the requisites and articles for giving that a bodhisattva has previously maintained, with a pure mind, as a pure gift to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.
For example, suppose a bhikṣu were to relinquish his own robes to his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) as a pure gift (śuddha-dāna).

By virtue of such an act of pure giving, he is permitted to possess various and immeasurable goods; therefore, he is called a bodhisattva who dwells in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa). Furthermore, he attains immeasurable merit, and by constantly recollecting such merit at all times, it ever increases.

Whatever items have been held as pure gifts (viśuddha-dāna) are entrusted to and protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. When one sees someone come seeking them, if one observes that the person possesses the signs of accomplishment, one may take back those previously relinquished items that were designated as pure gifts and give them to that person; for there is nothing that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will not relinquish for the sake of sentient beings.
Having formed this understanding, one fulfills the aspirations of the seeker.
Observing that the person lacks the signs of accomplishment, one instructs and liberates them through the Dharma of pure giving, addressing them as: "O Noble One!"
"This item was previously given away and already belongs to another.
With gentle words, he dismisses them so as not to cause resentment, and if possible, he gives other items two or three times the value.
By employing such skillful means, he makes it known that the Bodhisattva does not refuse to give out of stinginess, but rather because the object is not his own to bestow upon him.
Such sutras and dharmas are not given away [to those who do not seek them].
When a bodhisattva practices such giving of the Dharma, it is called the gift of wisdom.
Furthermore, all giving by a bodhisattva consists of what are known as the gift of Dharma, the gift of material wealth, and the gift of fearlessness.

Having analyzed the resemblances of appearances, whether in terms of names or meanings, and having understood cause and effect as they truly are, one practices giving; this is called the Bodhisattva’s giving through wisdom.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind of loving-kindness toward those who do not benefit them, with a mind of compassion toward those who suffer, with a mind of sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit, and with a mind of equanimity toward those who benefit them, as well as toward spiritual friends and kinsmen—this is called the bodhisattva’s giving of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are obstructions to giving for a bodhisattva; he knows them as they truly are as the remedies for these obstructions to giving.
There are four kinds of obstructions to giving:
first, not having previously cultivated [the habit of giving].
Second, the objects given in charity are few;
third, although material wealth is abundant, craving increases;
fourth, seeing the fruits of abundant wealth in future lives, one gives rise to greedy attachment.

Regarding "one who has not previously practiced giving": when a bodhisattva sees a rightful seeker and possesses abundant wealth yet does not give rise to the thought of giving, they should recognize this as being due to their own lack of practice in giving. They should swiftly exercise wisdom and reflect thus:

"In the past, I must certainly have failed to practice the mind of giving, which has resulted in my present state where, although I possess wealth, the thought of giving does not arise when I see a seeker coming."
"If I do not practice giving now, there will again be this obstacle to giving in future lives.
Having understood this, one practices giving by applying the remedies for obstacles to giving; thus, one can abandon and cease the habituation to such obstacles.
When the objects to be given are few, a bodhisattva sees a petitioner in need and does not wish to practice giving because of this obstacle to generosity.
Swiftly applying wisdom, they reflect:
"I would rather endure poverty and suffering than fail to practice giving."
Having reflected thus, he gave with a heart of compassion and further thought:

"From time immemorial, due to the transgressions of my past karma and because others have held power over me, I have been subjected to hunger, cold, and suffering, such that I have been unable to benefit all sentient beings."
"Rather than let me lose my life and suffer in this present existence because of this, I must practice giving to gather in sentient beings, so that the recipients' hearts are not left unsatisfied."
"How much more so today, when I sustain my life with fruits and vegetables; I must endure this hardship and practice giving.

Even if one possesses abundant wealth, if their craving is predominant, then upon seeing a legitimate seeker, because that object is so highly esteemed and supreme to them, they do not give rise to the intention to give it away.
Because that bodhisattva understands the fault of hoarding and accumulating, he swiftly applies his wisdom, thinking:
"I have conceived the notion of pleasure within suffering; in future lives, I shall undergo great suffering."
Having thus reflected on how such perversions are to be known and abandoned, one is able to practice giving.

As for those who, seeing the arising of future wealth as a fruit, develop craving and attachment: although such Bodhisattvas have practiced giving, they perceive the great wealth resulting from that gift as a source of personal benefit and merit, and are thus unable to aspire toward unexcelled enlightenment.

Once the Bodhisattva has recognized that the perception of results as real is a fault, he swiftly applies wisdom to contemplate reality as it is: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) lack solidity and perish moment by moment; the enjoyment of their karmic fruits is likewise entirely subject to dispersion and extinction.
When observing in this manner, the perception of results is severed, and all that is given is dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment.

This should be known as the bodhisattva’s fourfold wisdom that serves as the remedy for obstacles to giving: namely, the patience to distinguish [the nature of suffering], knowing how to subdue perversions, and observing that conditioned formations are not solid.
The first three types of remedial wisdom constitute right giving, while the latter type of remedial wisdom encompasses the attainment of the correct fruit.
This is called the bodhisattva’s giving of wisdom.

Furthermore, with an inner mind that is solitary, pure, profound, and characterized by pure faith and sublime perception, the bodhisattva mentally resolves to bestow immeasurable objects of generosity upon all sentient beings.
By means of slight expedient means, this bodhisattva generates immeasurable merit; this is the gift of great wisdom by the wise bodhisattva.
This is called a brief explanation of the dharmas subsumed under the bodhisattva’s giving of both material wealth and non-material wealth.

Such giving as the gift of Dharma, analytical giving, giving with a pure mind, the wisdom-giving that counteracts obstacles to giving, and the giving through the mental resolve of a purified mind—this is called the uncommon giving of a bodhisattva.

One should know that this is called the detailed classification of all internal and external objects given by a bodhisattva; regarding the aforementioned classification of all giving, one should know that it is classified as "difficult giving" and so forth.
What is the bodhisattva’s difficult giving?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds.
When a bodhisattva possesses only a small amount of wealth and, enduring the suffering of poverty himself, gives it to others, this is called the bodhisattva’s first difficult giving.

If a bodhisattva takes an object that is dear to them—something for which they have a deep-seated attachment due to long-standing habituation—and yet, surpassing even their most intense craving for it, can awaken themselves and give it away to another, this is called the second difficult gift.
If a bodhisattva gives wealth to others after obtaining it through diligent toil, this is called the bodhisattva’s third difficult giving.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving through all doors?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds.

If a bodhisattva gives away their own possessions, or things obtained by encouraging others to give, or things gathered through their own accumulation of giving, or the persons of their parents, wife, children, slaves, servants, as well as virtuous friends, ministers, and relatives—whenever these are required by others—all such acts are called the bodhisattva’s fourfold universal-gate giving, as briefly described.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving as a virtuous person?
Briefly stated, there are five kinds:
first, the bodhisattva gives with faith.
Second, giving with reverence;
third, giving with one's own hands;
fourth, giving at the proper time.
Fifth is giving without encroaching upon others.
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of a virtuous person.
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of giving in all ways?
Briefly stated, there are thirteen kinds:
first, giving without dependence;
second, extensive giving; [and so forth].
Third is giving with joy;
fourth is constant giving;
fifth is giving from a vessel.
Sixth, giving everything;
seventh, giving everywhere;
eighth, giving at all times.
Ninth is giving without fault;
tenth is giving all things;
eleventh is giving the products of a region.
Twelfth is the gift of material wealth;
thirteenth is the gift of grain.
These thirteen kinds are called the "vessels for all the practices of giving" by a bodhisattva; that is to say, the vessels of the pure field of merit consisting of the four paths.
What is the bodhisattva’s giving that removes affliction?
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds:
first, when a bodhisattva sees one who requires food and drink, he gives them food and drink.
Second, one who needs a vehicle shall be given a vehicle;
third, one who needs clothing shall be given clothing;
fourth, one who needs ornaments shall be given ornaments.
Fifth, one must give all manner of utensils;
sixth, one must provide flower garlands and ointments according to their desires;
seventh, one must give dwellings to those who require dwellings.
Eighth, to those who require light, one gives light.
These eight kinds are called the bodhisattva’s giving that removes affliction.
What is giving that brings happiness in this world and the next?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds, namely: the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), and the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).
As for the gift of material wealth, it is superior, excellent, and pure, because it rightly subdues the defilement of stinginess and the defilement of hoarding.
One who practices the perfection of giving and subdues the stain of stinginess abandons the mind of attachment.
One who subdues the stain of hoarding abandons attachment to possessions.
As for the gift of fearlessness, it refers to rescuing and delivering others from various terrors, such as those caused by lions, tigers, wolves, kings, thieves, water, fire, and so forth.
The gift of Dharma consists of teaching the Dharma without error, teaching it in its full completeness, and bestowing the prohibitive precepts upon others.
Thus, in brief, these are the nine kinds of giving of a bodhisattva, which cause all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness in both this life and future lives.
That gift of material wealth and the gift of fearlessness distinguish happiness in this world.
The gift of Dharma distinguishes happiness in both this life and future lives.
What is the pure gift of a bodhisattva?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds. What are the ten?
First, being without hindrance;
Second, not viewing [things] as different;
third, not accumulating;
fourth, not having a haughty mind.
Fifth, being without dependence;
sixth, not being discouraged;
seventh, having no dejected mind.
Eighth, not turning one's back;
ninth, not seeking favor;
tenth, not seeking recompense.

Regarding "giving without delay": when a petitioner comes to the Bodhisattva, he bestows gifts swiftly without creating obstacles; he fulfills their wishes in full, exceeding even their expectations of speed.

Regarding "not holding divergent views," it means that a bodhisattva does not give rise to divergent views concerning giving by claiming there is no karmic retribution; they do not consider the harming of living beings for the sake of giving to be the Dharma; and they do not seek mundane or supramundane purity through such giving.
Regarding "giving without accumulation": a bodhisattva does not amass wealth for a long time and then give it all at once.

Why is this? It is not that a bodhisattva possesses objects to give and, upon seeing a seeker, is capable of giving yet refuses to do so out of an improper view; rather, it is not that they fail to bestow gifts. How, then, could they wait until after accumulation before giving?
Nor is it the case that the merit of giving increases through accumulation.
Since the objects given and the recipients are equal, by what causes and conditions is a difference in merit observed between gradual giving and instantaneous giving?
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva perceives the fault in hoarding for the sake of giving, but does not perceive a fault in giving according to circumstances. Why is this?

It is because regarding the act of hoarding for the sake of giving, if there are hundreds who have come seeking in the past and he does not bestow anything upon them, it causes them to harbor resentment and give rise to a heart of intolerance.
Later, as supplicants accumulated, they offered their gifts all at once.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not accumulate his gifts.

Regarding "giving without a haughty mind," the Bodhisattva gives with a humble mind toward those who seek; he does not give with a competitive mind seeking to surpass others, nor does he praise himself on account of his giving.
"I am the donor; others cannot. Regarding giving without reliance on reputation, the bodhisattva does not practice generosity for the sake of fame; they regard false names and renown as mere dust.

Regarding the giving that is free from weakness: when a bodhisattva intends to give, the mind is joyful; while giving, there is delight; and after having given, there is no regret. Thus, their wealth and possessions increase and expand, becoming foremost, supreme, and sublime.
When a bodhisattva hears of another’s extensive and superior giving, they do not disparage themselves nor give rise to a regressive or weak mind.
As for "giving with an undepressed mind," it means that the bodhisattva reflects upon giving the most excellent, supreme, and wondrous things; this is called giving with an undepressed mind.

Regarding "giving without partiality": the Bodhisattva maintains an impartial mind and practices compassionate giving equally toward friends, enemies, and neutral persons, without following the bias of factions.

Regarding "not seeking gratitude for the gift": the Bodhisattva practices giving out of compassion and pity, not calculating the recipient's sense of indebtedness; rather, they observe that sentient beings who crave pleasure are ablaze with the fire of attachment and lack any power [to repay such kindness].

Regarding those who do not seek a reward for their giving: after the Bodhisattva has given, he does not fear the future; his wealth and body will be fully provided, as he contemplates that all conditioned phenomena are subject to total decay and extinction, and perceives the true benefit and merit of unsurpassed bodhi.
These ten kinds are called the pure and joyful giving of a bodhisattva.
By relying on these nine kinds of giving, a bodhisattva fulfills the dānapāramitā and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Chapter Ten: The Chapter on Ethics, Part One of the Section on Skillful Means in the Bodhisattvabhūmi. What is the bodhisattva’s śīlapāramitā?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, the morality of essential nature (svabhāva-śīla); [and so forth].
Second is the precept of all [virtues];
third is the difficult precept;
fourth is the precept of all gateways.
Fifth, the precept of the virtuous person;
sixth, the precept of all-encompassing conduct;
seventh, the precept of eliminating affliction.
Eighth is the precept of happiness in this world and other worlds;
ninth is the pure precept.
What is the precept of intrinsic nature?
Briefly stated, the accomplishment of four virtues is called the morality of essential nature (*svabhāva-śīla*). What are these four?
First, receiving [the precepts] correctly from another.
Second, receiving [the precepts] with a thoroughly pure mind;
third, immediately repenting after having committed an offense;
fourth, single-mindedly applying oneself to mindfulness and abiding in it so as to firmly maintain them without transgression.
One who receives [the precepts] from another looks outward to others; thus, a sense of shame (*hrī*) arises regarding transgressions.
One who receives them with a pure mind looks inward at oneself; thus, a sense of self-respect (*apatrāpya*) arises regarding transgressions, and one immediately repents upon committing an offense.
Being single-mindedly diligent and non-transgressing—this is how one does not violate the precepts.

A bodhisattva is free from regret due to two causes and conditions: this bodhisattva relies upon the reception of the precepts, whereby the pure mind gives rise to the precepts and the mind of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) arises;
because of the mind of shame and remorse, they are well able to protect the precepts, and by protecting the precepts, they have no regret.
Whether receiving [the precepts] from another or receiving them with a pure mind—these two are the Dharma.
Whether repenting after having committed an offense or being diligent and not committing one—these two follow the Dharma.

Whether receiving [the precepts] from another, receiving them with a pure mind, or practicing with single-minded diligence without transgression—these three dharmas constitute the indestructible morality of a bodhisattva.
If one should transgress, immediately repenting constitutes restoring what was damaged.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four virtues, this is called the morality of intrinsic nature and the true morality; it brings peace to oneself and peace to others, providing much security and much happiness, out of compassion for the world to benefit and bring peace to devas and humans.
One who receives and follows the precepts should know that they encompass immeasurable benefits.

The immeasurable pure precepts of a bodhisattva gather in all sentient beings and bring them peace and happiness; they produce great fruits of retribution and secure great welfare and benefit, leading swiftly to the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The second is the category of renunciation; this is called all-encompassing precepts.
These all-encompassing precepts further comprise three types:
first, the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*);
The second is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas;
the third is the precept of gathering sentient beings.

Regarding the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), it refers to the precepts received by the seven classes of followers: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Whether for laypeople or monastics, according to their respective circumstances, this is called the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).

Regarding the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), it refers to the bodhisattva’s practice of the physical, verbal, and mental actions of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) based upon the morality of restraint they have received; this is the brief explanation.
What is the precept of gathering all wholesome dharmas?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, relying on and abiding in the precepts, cultivates the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of cultivation consisting of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; dwelling in seclusion and silence; respectfully honoring, serving, and making offerings to teachers and elders; giving rise to a heart of compassion and providing care for those who are ill; exclaiming "Excellent! upon hearing those who preach the Dharma; praising and extolling those with genuine merit; mentally reflecting upon and verbally rejoicing in all the merits performed by all sentient beings; being able to endure all offenses; and dedicating all physical, verbal, and mental actions—whether already performed or yet to be done—toward unexcelled enlightenment.

At all times, one should cultivate various sublime vows, constantly and diligently making offerings to the Triple Gem, and remain heedful regarding all wholesome dharmas. One should maintain the pure precepts of body and speech through mindfulness and wisdom, guard the sense faculties, and know moderation in eating. During the first and last watches of the night, one should never sleep; one should associate with virtuous people and rely upon spiritual friends. One should examine one’s own faults and, recognizing them, refrain from transgressing; should a transgression occur, one should repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma before Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and fellow practitioners.
The precepts for upholding, cultivating, and nurturing such wholesome dharmas as these are called the "precept of gathering wholesome dharmas" (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Briefly stated, the "precept of gathering sentient beings" (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) consists of eleven kinds:
first, acting as a companion to all sentient beings in whatever beneficial tasks they undertake.
Second, they act as companions to all sentient beings who are afflicted by various sufferings such as illnesses—whether already arisen or not yet arisen—as well as to those who tend to the sick.
Third, they expound upon mundane and supramundane dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, or employ skillful means to enable them to attain wisdom.
Fourth, they recognize kindness and repay it.
Fifth, when sentient beings face various terrors—such as lions, tigers, wolves, kings, thieves, water, or fire—they are able to provide protection and rescue for all.

If there are sentient beings who have suffered the loss of relatives, wealth, or other calamities, he is able to provide them with consolation and liberation, enabling them to leave behind their grief and distress.
Sixth, seeing sentient beings who are impoverished and destitute, he is able to provide them with gifts according to whatever they require.
Seventh, he is fully endowed with virtuous conduct and relies upon meditative absorption (*samādhi*), maintaining a community of disciples in accordance with the Dharma.

Eighth, he is the first to speak words of comfort, visiting them at appropriate times; he provides food and drink and speaks wholesome worldly discourse, yet his coming and going is not for his own sake, but follows the needs of others.
Regarding such matters as these, they accord with all that brings peace and security to sentient beings;
they distance themselves from all that does not bring peace and security.
Ninth, they praise and rejoice in those who possess genuine virtue.
Tenth, those who have transgressions and evils he shall reprimand with a mind of loving-kindness, subdue them, and penalize or expel them, causing them to repent and reform.

Eleventh, by means of his supernormal powers, he manifests the miserable realms of existence to cause those sentient beings to fear and loathe all evils, so that they may reverently practice the Buddha-dharma, and with joy, faith, and delight, give rise to a sense of rare wonder.

How does a bodhisattva abide in the morality of restraint, abide in the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and abide in the morality of gathering sentient beings; how do they well-guard and uphold the morality of restraint, well-gather the morality of virtuous dharmas, and encompass all practices within the morality of gathering sentient beings?

The Bodhisattva, abiding in the *pratimokṣa* precepts, renounces the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) to leave the household life and study the Path. He regards his noble position as no more than grass or soil, and he abandons the five desires as if discarding mucus or spittle; even toward the Māra-heavens of future lives, he has no longing or delight, and he will never practice the holy life for their sake.

Their minds are constantly apprehensive as they perceive things according to reality; they renounce present pleasures as if fearing wind and hail, observing with right view and remaining free from attachment.

Their nature is tranquil and they delight in solitude; whether in a group or alone, their minds are always settled in peace. Without being restricted by mere observance of precepts, they conceive the thought of contentment, relying on the precepts and abiding in them to cultivate the immeasurable merit born of the bodhisattva’s right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

If one stays near the fourfold assembly, one does not preach what is contrary to the Dharma; in secluded places, one does not dwell in evil thoughts; even if such thoughts should briefly arise, one immediately reproaches oneself and deeply perceives their fault; having recognized these afflictions, one returns to the original state of mind.

If, upon hearing of all the bodhisattva precepts—the subtle, immeasurable, inconceivable, and long-enduring difficult practices of the great earth bodhisattvas—one’s mind feels no terror nor does it falter or retreat, but instead thinks:
"They too were men who were able to maintain the inconceivable pure precepts of body and speech of a bodhisattva."
"I too am a man of integrity; I shall certainly be like him, without any doubt.
A Bodhisattva who abides in the moral discipline constantly examines his own faults and does not look at the deficiencies of others.

If one encounters those who are violent or of evil character, one should not harbor resentment in the mind, but should instead give rise to the thought of the Dharma and a heart of compassion, employing skillful means out of pity to bring them to liberation.
A bodhisattva established in ethical discipline does not even conceive a thought of fear toward sentient beings, much less inflict harm upon them.

A bodhisattva abiding in the vows accomplishes five kinds of heedful practices: those associated with the past, those associated with the future, those associated with the present, those already performed, and those yet to be performed.
That a bodhisattva repents according to the Dharma for transgressions committed in the past is called non-negligence regarding the past.
That they shall repent according to the Dharma for transgressions yet to be committed in the future is called non-negligence regarding the future.
To repent according to the Dharma for what has been transgressed in the present is called the practice of non-negligence in the present.
To protect and maintain with single-minded devotion that which has been practiced and that in which one abides is called the practice of non-negligence regarding what has already been done.

Relying on the practice of heedfulness already performed, acting as one acts and dwelling as one dwells, one does not give rise to transgressions of the precepts; this is called the practice of heedfulness yet to be performed.

A bodhisattva abiding in ethical discipline conceals their virtues, discloses their faults, has few desires and is content, endures all sufferings without giving rise to grief or distress, is steady and composed in movement and stillness, maintains dignified deportment, and remains free from all deceit while purely cultivating right livelihood.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are said to abide in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).

They skillfully guard and uphold the precepts: that is, they do not look back with longing at the five desires of the past, do not give rise to thoughts of delight regarding the five desires of the future, and do not harbor thoughts of greedy attachment toward the five desires of the present. They take pleasure in dwelling in seclusion without conceiving thoughts of self-satisfaction; they remain free from evil speech and evil reflections, do not disparage themselves, dwell in peace and happiness, are well able to endure hardships, and are not negligent in their majestic deportment or pure livelihood.

When a bodhisattva dwells in the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, if even a slight attachment arises toward body, life, or wealth, they immediately eliminate it so that it does not increase; likewise, all afflictions and conditions that lead to the violation of the precepts arise and are immediately eliminated.

If thoughts of anger, malice, or enmity toward sentient beings arise, they are immediately extinguished; if laziness arises, it is immediately extinguished; if meditative absorption associated with worldly attachment arises, it is immediately extinguished.

One knows the five points as they truly are—namely, the wholesome fruit, the wholesome cause, the wholesome cause-and-effect, the inverted, and the non-inverted—and thus knows, as they truly are, all obstacles to the gathering of wholesome dharmas.
When a bodhisattva perceives the benefits and rewards of wholesome fruits and seeks their wholesome causes, they understand as it truly is the perversion of grasping at wholesome dharmas.

Having attained these roots of goodness, the bodhisattva does not give rise to the view of the impermanent as permanent, the suffering as pleasant, the impure as pure, or the non-self as self; thus, they understand as it truly is the obstacles to grasping wholesome dharmas and remain free from those dharmas that do not grasp the wholesome.

When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten practices, they are said to abide in the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). They swiftly gather all virtuous dharmas and all practices, namely: relying on generosity, relying on ethical discipline, relying on patience, relying on diligence, and relying on meditative concentration—thus accomplishing wisdom through these five practices.
When a bodhisattva abides in the precept of gathering sentient beings, there are eleven types, and in each type they accomplish all practices.

First, they share the same purpose with sentient beings in everything they do: whether it be initial deliberation and what is undertaken, traveling to and fro, professional activities and skillful means, guarding wealth and property, reconciling disputes, worldly auspicious gatherings, or various meritorious deeds—in all these they share the same purpose.

Second, he acts as a companion in all matters of suffering: if he sees one who is ill, he attends to and provides for them; he guides the blind, leads those who have lost their way, points out the path to the deaf, and carries those who are lame. To those afflicted by the suffering of sensual craving, he teaches how to distance themselves from it; likewise, he causes them to abandon the hindrances of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, as well as other such forms of suffering.

He teaches them to completely distance themselves from thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, thoughts of kin, thoughts of country, thoughts of immortality, thoughts of contempt, and thoughts of lineage.
For those sentient beings who engage in disputes and do not recognize suffering, they are able to provide resolution.
To those exhausted by travel, they grant all that brings peace and comfort.

Third, for the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma in its fullness; to those of evil conduct, they teach the words, flavors, and meanings of goodness that eliminate evil conduct, thereby enabling them to accord with, penetrate, and increase the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).

As for teaching through skillful means: it is for the sake of evil sentient beings to teach the removal of evil conduct, to teach the dharma for removing stinginess so as to obtain present retributions, and to show how one may obtain great wealth through minor and correct skillful means, and having obtained it, protect it.

Regarding those who harbor hatred and envy toward the Dharma, one causes them to give rise to faith and joy, to see the truths with purity, to leave behind all evil destinies, and to bring about the eternal exhaustion of afflictions and the cessation of all suffering.
Fourth is knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.

To benefit others, one speaks with a virtuous mind, greeting them with inquiries and consolation; one welcomes them with words of praise, provides a seat, and settles them comfortably. One repays them with equality or more, never less; in all their activities, one engages as a fellow practitioner. One attends to their suffering from illness, teaches the Dharma in accordance with their needs, eliminates their fears, and frees them from all grief and regret.
If there are those who lack anything, one provides them with all necessary requisites; one relies upon them in accordance with the Dharma and accords with their minds.

Those who possess genuine virtue are praised and gladdened; those who have faults or evils are reprimanded with a compassionate heart, subdued, and penalized or expelled, so as to cause them to reform and repent.
Fifth, they manifest supernatural powers as appropriate to the occasion;

they provide protection and refuge for sentient beings who are terrified—namely, from all fears such as those caused by water, fire, kings, thieves, ghosts, spirits, evil beasts, humans, and non-humans—and ensure that they attain peace and security.

If they see sentient beings afflicted by the anxieties and distress of difficulties concerning their relatives or wealth; or if they see them lose their relatives, virtuous friends, spiritual teachers, or those whom their masters revere; or if their wealth has been seized by kings or thieves, lost to fire or water, or squandered from their treasuries; or if their undertakings fail and their private property is forcibly divided; or if they have evil kinsmen who dissipate their assets—they resolve all such matters for them, causing them to be free from sorrow and distress.
Sixth, seeing sentient beings who lack the necessities of life, one provides them with what they require:

food and drink, clothing, medicinal decoctions, various utensils, incense, flowers, lamps, ornaments, carriages, servants, wealth, and dwellings; all such deficiencies are fully provided and bestowed.

Seventh, he should receive the community in accordance with the Dharma and first grant them reliance; he should preach the Dharma to them with a mind free from greed and out of compassion, providing for their necessities.
If he lacks these himself, he should seek them from faithful householders or elders and give them to the community.
Whatever robes, food, medicine, and dwellings are obtained in accordance with the Dharma, they shall be used collectively by all without being stored or accumulated.
They shall provide instruction and admonition at the appropriate times through five methods, as explained in the *Balagotrapaṭala* (Chapter on the Lineage of Powers).
Eighth is the precept of conforming to the minds of others.

First, one must discern the individual natures and dispositions of sentient beings; those with whom it is appropriate to dwell, one should cohabit with, and engage in activities alongside them as is suitable for each.
Furthermore, regarding "acting in accordance with the mind," one observes their conduct:
if such physical actions or such verbal actions would cause others distress and lack wholesome benefit, the Bodhisattva does not perform them;
however, even if they cause distress, if they result in wholesome benefit, the Bodhisattva performs them.

If a bodhisattva’s own physical or verbal actions are not encompassed by the precepts, nor are they accompanied by merit, wisdom, or skillful means, and if they cause others distress or lack wholesome benefit, the bodhisattva does not perform them;
conversely, if they are the opposite of the above, the bodhisattva performs them.
Just as it is with the arising of sorrow and suffering, so it is with joy and pleasure; these should be explained in detail according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, regarding "conforming to the mind": if one sees sentient beings with an expression of anger and resentment, one should not even praise their virtues, much less speak of their faults, nor should one offer an apology.

Furthermore, as for following the mind: even if others do not come to inquire after one’s welfare or offer consolation, one still goes of one's own accord to inquire and console them; how much more so when they come to inquire, yet one fails to respond in kind? This applies except in the case of providing instruction and admonition.
Furthermore, "acting in accordance with the mind" means not troubling others; except when, out of a heart of compassion, one quiets the senses and rebukes disciples to bring them under discipline.
Furthermore, "acting in accordance with the mind" means not mocking or ridiculing them, thereby causing them shame and the arising of doubt or regret.
Although he was not as good as the other,
he did not say, "You have now fallen into defeat.
Seeing that the other person was humble, he likewise did not exalt himself.
Furthermore, "acting in accordance with the mind" means not failing to associate with others, not associating excessively, and not associating at improper times.

Furthermore, "acting in accordance with the mind" means not speaking of the faults of those who are dear and close to others, not praising the virtues of those who are enemies to others, and not agreeing with those who are not one's own friends.
One should not seek many desires; if one takes anything, one should know the measure and be content.
If there is someone who invites one, one should not oppose their intention; if there is anyone who reproaches one, one should repent and apologize in accordance with the Dharma.

Ninth, those who possess actual merit are praised with joy; those who are endowed with faith are commended for their virtuous faith, and the same applies to their morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Tenth, those who deserve censure are rebuked and disciplined: those with minor faults or minor transgressions are rebuked with gentle words out of a heart of compassion; those with middling faults or middling transgressions are rebuked with middling words; and those with superior faults or superior transgressions are rebuked with superior words.

As it is with reprimand, so too it is with subduing, punishment, and expulsion; for those who have committed minor or middling offenses, they are driven out at the appropriate time and then permitted to live together again. For the sake of transforming those who violate the precepts as well as others, one expels them from the assembly with a heart of loving benefit.

Regarding those who have committed superior or superlative offenses: they shall not dwell together nor eat together, and even upon repentance, they shall still not dwell together. This is done out of a heart of compassion, so as not to allow such persons to give rise to further transgressions within the Buddha-dharma, and also for the sake of instructing other sentient beings.

Eleventh, for the sake of benefiting others, the Bodhisattva manifests supernormal powers, sometimes to cause terror and sometimes to cause joy. To those who practice evil deeds, he shows the retribution of evil, namely the various states of miserable rebirth such as the Cold Ice Hells and the Bordering Hells, saying to them:
"You should observe this: having committed evil in the human world, you shall be born therein and undergo immeasurable suffering."
Seeing this, they were struck with terror and gave rise to revulsion and fear, thereby abandoning all unwholesome conduct.

When the Bodhisattva saw those among the great assembly who did not believe him and failed to answer when questioned, he immediately manifested as Vajrapāṇi and various powerful devas and spirits to terrify them. Because of this terror, they cast aside their arrogance and respectfully answered correctly; the rest of the great assembly, hearing that correct answer, were likewise tamed.
Furthermore, by means of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he manifests one as many and many as one; he passes through stone walls as if they were open space, and water and fire issue from his body.

Or again, he may manifest supernormal powers in common with the śrāvakas to cause them joy: those who have no faith gain faith, those who have broken the precepts become pure, those of little learning become widely learned, the stingy become able to give, and the deluded attain wisdom.

In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the morality of benefiting sentient beings through all practices; this is called the bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of morality, an immeasurable aggregate of merit.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty at Guzang.

The remainder of the "Chapter on Precepts" within the "Section on Expedient Means" of the *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*. If a bodhisattva wishes to study the bodhisattva’s *vinaya*—namely, the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*)—whether they be a householder or one who has gone forth, after having generated the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi, they should first prostrate at the feet of a fellow-practitioner bodhisattva who has already made that vow, who possesses wisdom and power, who is skilled in speech and meaning, and who is able to recite and uphold [the teachings], and then speak as follows:
"I beg the Virtuous One to grant me the reception of the Bodhisattva precepts.
If the Virtuous One does not find it a hardship, I pray that you will compassionately grant your permission.

Having made this request, he bared his right shoulder and, before the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, paid respectful homage and recollected their merits, giving rise to a mild, middling, or superior state of pure and sincere mind.
Before the wise one, he should prostrate himself with humility and reverence, kneeling and bowing his body,
and speak these words before the image of the Buddha:
"I only pray that the Virtuous One will confer upon me the Bodhisattva precepts."
Having spoken these words, he focused his mind with single-minded attention to cultivate a pure heart, thinking:
"Before long, I shall attain an inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed mass of great merit."
Having reflected thus, he remained silent.
At that time, the wise one did not give rise to a distracted mind toward that recipient; whether sitting or standing, he spoke these words:
"O you, son of good family [Name]!..."
Listen attentively,
brother in the Dharma! Are you a bodhisattva?
He replied, "Yes. [The Buddha asked:
"Have you yet made the vow for bodhicitta?"
He replied, "I have already set out.
Having been thus questioned, he spoke again as follows:
“O son of good family!
You wish to receive from me all the bodhisattva precepts:
the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*).”

These precepts are the precepts in which all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present abide; they have been studied by all bodhisattvas of the past, shall be studied by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are being studied now by all bodhisattvas of the present.
"Can you accept this? He replied, "I can."
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.
After the wise one had spoken three times and conferred the precepts upon him, the recipient did not rise.
At that time, the wise one paid homage before the image of the Buddha to the assembly of bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and addressed them thus:
"Such-and-such a bodhisattva has before me, such-and-such a person, thrice received the bodhisattva precepts;
I act as their witness.

First, one should likewise announce this to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, the supreme and unsurpassed Great Teachers who possess present knowledge, vision, and awakening, who possess present knowledge, vision, and awakening regarding all sentient beings and all phenomena:
"Such-and-such a bodhisattva has received the bodhisattva precepts from me, such-and-such a person, three times.
I act as their witness.
A second and third time, he should announce this in the same manner.
Having thus completed the reception of the bodhisattva precepts,
thereupon, before all the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions and the bodhisattvas dwelling on the great stages, signs of the Dharma appeared.
At that time, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, mindful of this bodhisattva, give rise to knowledge and vision in accordance with reality:
"In such-and-such a world, such-and-such a bodhisattva has received the bodhisattva precepts from such-and-such a bodhisattva."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva conceives of them as a son and a younger brother, cherishing them with a heart of loving-kindness.
Because he cherishes them with a heart of loving-kindness, this Bodhisattva’s wholesome dharmas increase and never decline.

Having thus made the formal declaration, thus attained awareness, and thus received the Bodhisattva precepts, the wise recipient bows respectfully toward the Buddhas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and withdraws.

Thus, the ethical discipline of restraint received by a bodhisattva is the most excellent and supreme among all other forms of ethical discipline of restraint, encompassing immeasurable and boundless merit.

Compared to the prātimokṣa precepts—which arise from the first unsurpassed mind of truth as an antidote to all kinds of evil conduct of all sentient beings—the [previously mentioned] restraint of discipline does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor one part in a hundred thousand million, nor even any part reachable by calculation or analogy, because these [prātimokṣa precepts] encompass all merits.
One who abides in the bodhisattva precepts should reflect thus:
"That which is in accordance with the Dharma is practiced, and that which is not in accordance with the Dharma is not practiced; thus, one's merit increases further.
A bodhisattva training in the precepts, having heard what is taught in the Sūtra-piṭaka and what is taught in the Bodhisattva-mātṛkā-piṭaka, should diligently protect and uphold them.
A wise Bodhisattva does not receive the Bodhisattva precepts from every Bodhisattva.

If one lacks faith, they shall not receive them from such a person—namely, one who, upon first hearing the Bodhisattva precepts, does not believe, does not comply, and is unable to contemplate them; or one who is stingy, greedy, full of desire, insatiable, a breaker of precepts, lax, one who does not guard the precepts, angry, resentful, intolerant, indolent, lazy, addicted to sleep, or delights in discussing worldly affairs. From such persons as these, one must by all means not receive them.

If there is a bodhisattva who cultivates a virtuous mind for even as long as it takes to milk a cow once, who does not drink alcohol, who is not foolish, who is not cowardly, who is not of little learning, and who does not slander the sūtras of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka—from such a person as this, one should receive the bodhisattva precepts.
When a bodhisattva has received the bodhisattva precepts, they should neither explain them to nor instruct those who slander and oppose the Bodhisattvapitaka. Why is this?
Having heard this, they do not believe; because their ignorance obscures them, they give rise to slander.

For one who slanders in this way, the retribution for their sin is equal to the immeasurable mass of merit gained by receiving the bodhisattva precepts. As long as they do not abandon their evil speech, evil views, and evil thoughts, they will never be able to cast off such sinful karma.

When a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, a wise person should first explain the Bodhisattvapiṭaka for them, teaching the bodhisattva precepts and the characteristics of their transgressions, so that the recipient may observe with their own mind and contemplate through wisdom, thinking: "I am capable of receiving these precepts; I do not receive them merely to imitate others."
This is called a steadfast bodhisattva.
Such a person as this should receive the bodhisattva precepts.
For a bodhisattva who abides in the code of discipline (vinaya-śīla), there are four dharmas constituting grounds for defeat (pārājika-sthānīya-dharma).
What are the four?
When a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and profit, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called the first *pārājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva possesses personal wealth but, due to a nature of stinginess and attachment, fails to give rise to a heart of compassion to provide what is sought by poor and suffering sentient beings who come seeking refuge; and if, when there are those who wish to hear the Dharma, they are parsimonious and refuse to speak it—this is called the second *pārājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva, out of anger, utters harsh and evil words and yet their intent does not cease, further striking with the hand or inflicting blows with sticks or stones, causing injury and terror while their malice increases; and if the offender seeks repentance but they do not accept the apology, harboring resentment and refusing to let it go—this is called the third *pārājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, expounds counterfeit teachings with great zeal, and—whether through personal understanding or having received them from another—adheres to those counterfeit teachings, this is called the fourth *pārājika* offense.
These are called the four *pārājika* rules for bodhisattvas.
If a bodhisattva commits even one of these four *pārājika* rules, it is called a *pārājika* offense; how much more so if they commit all four?

One who cannot expand and broaden the present life, nor adorn awakening, and furthermore does not increase the purity of mind in the present, is called a semblance bodhisattva, not a real bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva commits the four transgressions through weak or middling afflictions, it is not called abandoning the vows of discipline;
however, if committed through superior afflictions, it is called abandoning them.

If one repeatedly transgresses against these four dharmas and, instead of feeling shame or remorse, feels joy and delight, claiming them to be virtues, this is called an offense of superior affliction (*adhimātra-kleśa*).

A bodhisattva does not suddenly commit an offense equivalent to the four *pārājika* rules that would cause him to relinquish the bodhisattva vows and ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), as a bhikṣu relinquishes his vows and ethical discipline.

Once a bodhisattva has lost the vows of discipline (saṃvara-śīla), they are capable of receiving them again; this is not like a bhikṣu who, having violated the prātimokṣa precepts, may not receive them again.
There are two causes and conditions for losing the bodhisattva’s discipline:
first, abandoning the vow for unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Second, there is the transgression arising from predominant afflictions.
In this case, there is no loss of the bodhisattva precepts upon discarding one body and taking up another; even throughout successive births in the ten directions, they are never lost.

If a bodhisattva does not abandon their great vow and has not committed an offense through superior afflictions, then although they do not remember it when changing bodies after death, they receive it again and again from spiritual friends; this remains their original precept and is not called newly acquired.

It should be known that a bodhisattva who abides in the morality of restraint must distinguish between what is an offense and what is not, what is defiled and what is not, and the degrees of light, medium, and heavy.

If a bodhisattva abiding in the morality of restraint, within a single day and night, whether the Buddha is present in the world, or at his stūpas and temples, or toward the Dharma, or the sūtras, or the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka, or the Bodhisattva Mātṛkā-piṭaka, or the community of bhikṣus, or the assembly of great bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions—fails to make even a small amount of offerings, or fails to perform even a single prostration, or fails to praise the merits of the Triple Gem with even a single verse, or fails to cultivate a pure mind for even a single thought-moment, this is called committing many offenses.
If one commits an offense out of disrespect, laziness, or indolence, it is an offense arising from affliction (*kliṣṭa*).
If one commits an offense through forgetfulness or error, it does not arise from affliction.

There is no offense for a Bodhisattva who has entered the stage of the pure mind (*śuddhacitta*), who, like a monk who has attained the fourfold unshakable faith (*aveccappasāda*), constantly makes offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
However, if a Bodhisattva is full of desire, lacks contentment, and is greedily attached to wealth and goods, this is called a "multitudinous offense," and it is an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense if, for the sake of severing those [afflictions], one has generated the desire and skillful means to adopt the antidote, yet by nature one’s afflictions are sharp and arise repeatedly.

If a bodhisattva, seeing a senior who is virtuous, worthy of respect, and a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, fails to give rise to reverence due to pride or resentment, does not yield his seat, and neither greets nor answers when asked about the Dharma, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one commits an offense out of laziness or indolence, with a neutral state of mind, or through forgetfulness, it does not arise from affliction.
There is no offense if one is insane, suffering from a serious illness, or mentally deranged.
If one is asleep and perceives oneself as awake, and does not respond to greetings or requests for the Dharma, this is called no offense.

If the senior elder is preaching the Dharma or engaging in definitive discussion, or if one is oneself preaching the Dharma or listening to the Dharma, or if one is oneself engaging in definitive discussion; or if one is in the midst of an assembly preaching the Dharma or in the midst of an assembly engaging in definitive discussion—failing to pay homage in these cases constitutes no offense.

If one protects the mind of the speaker; or if, through skillful means, one causes them to be disciplined, to abandon unwholesome states, and to cultivate wholesome dharmas; or if one protects the regulations of the Sangha or the intentions of the majority.

If a bodhisattva, when invited by a donor—whether to their own home, to a monastery, or to another's house—refuses to accept or go because the donor offers clothing, food, or various requisites out of anger or pride, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill or lacks physical strength; if one is insane or in a remote location; if there are dangers or difficulties on the road; if one knows that by not accepting the invitation, the person will be disciplined, abandon evil, and abide in goodness; if one has previously accepted another invitation; if one is practicing wholesome dharmas and does not wish to interrupt them even for a moment; if one desires to hear unprecedented teachings, beneficial meanings, or definitive discourses; if one knows that the requester acts out of deceit or malice; if one wishes to protect the feelings of many people who might harbor resentment; or if one is upholding the regulations of the Saṃgha.

If a bodhisattva has a donor who offers various precious objects such as gold, silver, pearls, mani-jewels, and lapis lazuli, and the bodhisattva, out of a mind of anger or pride, rejects and does not accept them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a defiled offense because it arises from abandoning sentient beings.
If one commits an offense out of laziness or indolence, it is not an afflictive transgression (*kliṣṭa*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is insane; if one knows that after receiving [the gift] one will certainly give rise to craving and attachment; if one knows that after receiving it the donor will feel regret; if one knows that after receiving it the donor will fall into confusion; if one knows that after receiving it the donor will suffer poverty and distress; if one knows that the object belongs to the Three Jewels; if one knows that the object was obtained through robbery; or if one knows that after receiving it one will undergo much suffering and affliction, namely: being killed, bound, punished, deprived of wealth, or rebuked.

If a bodhisattva, when sentient beings come to him desiring to hear the Dharma, out of anger, resentment, stinginess, or envy fails to preach it for them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.

If one commits an offense through laziness or indolence, it does not arise from defilement. There is no offense in the following cases: if a non-Buddhist seeks to find fault; if one is gravely ill or insane;

if one knows that by not speaking [the truth] one can bring that person to discipline; if the Dharma being practiced has not yet been mastered; if one knows the person before one will be unable to show respect or comply with properly regulated decorum; if that person has dull faculties and would develop fear upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma; if one knows that upon hearing it, they will increase their wrong views; if one knows that upon hearing it, they will disparage and fall away from the path; or if one knows that upon hearing it, they will speak of it to evil people and thereby destroy the True Dharma.

If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment toward fierce and precept-breaking sentient beings, either abandons them himself or prevents others from helping them, failing to provide instruction and transformation, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If one fails due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, or intentionally obstructing another, the transgression arises from non-afflictive causes. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva’s cultivation of compassion toward those who are evil is deeper than that toward those who are virtuous.

There is no offense if one is insane; or if one knows that by not speaking, the other person will be subdued, as previously stated; or if one protects the mind of another; or if one observes the regulations of the Sangha.

If a bodhisattva, within the prātimokṣa-vinaya established by the Tathāgata, observes prohibitive offenses for the sake of protecting sentient beings—causing those without faith to gain faith and those with faith to increase it—they train in the same manner as the śrāvakas.

Why is this? Because the śrāvaka aims at nothing less than his own liberation, and does not even refrain from protecting others by causing those without faith to believe and those who already believe to further increase their training in the precepts; how much more so for the bodhisattva, whose liberation is that of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), yet who abides in the prohibition of offenses while possessing little benefit, little activity, and few skillful means.
The precepts established by the World-Honored One for śrāvakas are not those in which bodhisattvas train.
Why is this? Śrāvakas seek their own liberation, abandoning others; they should abide in few benefits, few activities, and few skillful means.
It is not for a bodhisattva to dwell in self-deliverance, nor to deliver others with little benefit, little effort, or little skillful means.
For the sake of sentient beings, a bodhisattva may seek hundreds of thousands of robes from Brahmins or householders who are not their relatives.
Furthermore, when receiving offerings during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one should observe whether the donor is capable or incapable of giving, and accept according to what is offered.
As it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls.

Just as with robes and bowls, so too may one, for the sake of sentient beings, request thread and have a weaver who is not a relative weave it; one should possess silk (*kauśeya*) bedding and sitting mats even up to hundreds of thousands, and one should likewise accept gold and silver even up to hundreds of thousands.

In such dwellings as these, where there is little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means, these are offenses by prohibition for Śrāvakas, but they are not shared trainings for Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), if one dwells with a mind of resentment toward sentient beings characterized by little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction (*kliṣṭa*).
If one commits an offense due to indolence, laziness, or remaining in a state of little benefit, little effort, and little skillful means, it is not an offense arising from affliction.

However, if a bodhisattva is deceitful or crooked in body or speech—whether by manifesting signs, disparaging others, or seeking profit through profit—and dwells in a life of wrong livelihood without a sense of shame or remorse, unable to abandon such conduct, this is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction.
There is no offense if, in order to sever those [defilements], one applies the means of desire, yet the afflictions increase and arise repeatedly.

If a bodhisattva’s mind is restless and finds no joy in tranquility, and for this reason makes loud noises and plays for the amusement of others, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one commits an offense through forgetfulness or error, it does not arise from defilement.
There is no offense if, for the purpose of abandoning that [fault], one applies the desire and means as previously described.

Furthermore, there is no offense if: another has given rise to resentment and one acts to cause it to cease; if another is distressed and one acts to cause it to subside; or if another is by nature fond of play, and one acts to win them over, to sever that habit, or to protect them.
If others suspect a bodhisattva, harboring resentment or opposition, [the bodhisattva] displays a smiling countenance and playful laughter because his mind is pure.
If a bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus:
"A bodhisattva should not delight in nirvāṇa, but should turn away from nirvāṇa; he should not fear the afflictions (kleśa), nor should he be exclusively weary of them."
Why is this? A bodhisattva should undergo birth and death for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas in pursuit of great enlightenment.
One who speaks thus is said to commit a multitude of offenses; this is an offense arising from defilement.

Why is this? Because the śrāvakas’ deep delight in nirvāṇa and their dread and weariness of afflictions do not equal those of the bodhisattvas’ deep delight in nirvāṇa and their dread and weariness of afflictions by even a hundred-thousand-millionfold margin.

That is to say, while the śrāvakas act solely for their own benefit, the bodhisattvas do not; they act universally for the sake of all sentient beings. Their practice does not defile the mind, and they surpass the arhats who, though accomplished, possess outflows (*sāsrava*) despite being free from afflictions (*kleśa*).

If a bodhisattva does not guard against words of lack of faith, nor guards against slander and defamation, nor eliminates them—and if there are actual faults and evils that he does not eliminate—this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
There is no actual fault or transgression that has not been eliminated, nor does it arise from defilement.

As for those who do not commit an offense: if it is an outsider who slanders, or other wicked persons; or if, due to the causes and conditions of practicing virtue while living as a mendicant monk, one incurs the censure of others; or if the person before one is angry or insane when they utter such censure.

If a bodhisattva, observing sentient beings, perceives that they should be benefited through skillful means by means of harsh and urgent words, yet fails to do so out of fear that it will cause them distress and anxiety, this is called a transgression of many offenses; this transgression arises from non-afflictive causes.
There is no offense if one perceives that [responding] would bring little benefit to the other in the present and cause much distress and vexation.

If a bodhisattva, when reviled, reviles in return; when provoked to anger, returns anger; when struck, strikes back; or when slandered, slanders in return, this is called a transgression of many offenses, and it is an offense arising from defilement.
If a bodhisattva offends another, or even if they do not offend but cause another to suspect them, they should immediately offer an apology.
To harbor resentment or contempt and fail to apologize according to the Dharma is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement.
If an offense is committed through laziness or indolence, it does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one employs skillful means to subdue the other; if the other person desires to perform an impure act before accepting an apology; if one knows that the person’s nature is prone to quarreling and litigation, and that an apology would only increase their anger; or if one knows that the person is naturally harmonious and patient, free from resentment, and fears that an apology would cause them shame. In these instances, there is no offense for not apologizing.

If a bodhisattva, when another person comes to them having committed an offense and offers a formal apology and confession according to the Dharma, refuses to accept that confession out of a mind of resentment and with the intent to cause them distress, this is called a transgression of the many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If one does not feel resentment or aversion, yet by nature refuses to accept an apology, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-affliction.
There is no offense if one employs skillful means to subdue the other person, as previously described.
If the other person does not repent according to the Dharma or their mind is not impartial, and one does not accept their confession, there is no offense.

However, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of resentment toward another and clings to it without relinquishing it, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction.
There is no offense if, for the sake of severing that [affliction], one generates the desire and employs the skillful means as previously described.
If a bodhisattva, out of greed for service and honor, maintains a retinue of followers, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
There is no offense if one keeps [possessions] without a mind of greed.

However, if a bodhisattva is indolent, lazy, or addicted to pleasure and sleep; or if they do not know the proper time or moderation, this is called a transgression of many offenses, and it is an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense if one is ill, lacks strength, is exhausted from traveling a long distance, or has applied the skillful means of generating the desire to abandon that [fault] as previously described.
If a bodhisattva, with a defiled mind, engages in worldly talk for an extended period, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one forgets or errs for a period of time, the offense is non-afflicted.
There is no offense if, seeing others engaged in conversation, one listens for a brief moment out of consideration for their feelings;
or if one briefly answers another's question regarding something they have not previously heard.

If a bodhisattva, desiring to seek a concentrated mind, harbors resentment and pride and refuses to accept the teacher’s instruction, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one commits an offense through indolence or laziness, it does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense if one is ill, lacks strength, knows that the other person is speaking erroneously, possesses great learning and capability oneself, or has already received the teaching previously.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to the five hindrances and does not awaken to them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
There is no offense if, for the sake of abandoning those hindrances, one generates the desire and applies the skillful means as previously described.
If a bodhisattva perceives the savoring of meditative absorption as a merit, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
There is no offense if, for the sake of abandoning that [savoring], one generates the desire and applies the skillful means as previously described.
If a bodhisattva views things in this way and speaks thus:
"A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas; they should not accept them, nor should they study them."
"What use has a bodhisattva for the dharmas of the śrāvakas?
This is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva even listens to the heterodox doctrines of outsiders, how much more so the words of the Buddha?
There is no offense if he is exclusively studying the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and has not yet been able to master it entirely.

However, if a bodhisattva, without employing skillful means, abandons the study of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and devotes himself solely to practicing and collecting the sūtras and dharmas of the Śrāvakas, this is called a "multitudinous offense" (prabhūta-āpatti); it is an offense that arises from non-afflictive causes.

If a bodhisattva, having been taught by the Buddha, abandons that teaching and fails to train in it, instead practicing the heterodox treatises of non-Buddhists or worldly scriptures, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense if one is exceptionally intelligent and able to learn quickly; or if one has studied for a long time and does not forget; or if one understands the meaning through reflection; or if one attains unshakable wisdom by fully investigating the Buddha-dharma.
If one studies Buddhist scriptures for two parts of each day and one part of non-Buddhist texts, this is called non-offense.

If a bodhisattva is skilled in worldly classics and the heterodox treatises of outsiders, yet delights in them, does not abandon them, and does not regard them as poison, this is called an offense of many transgressions; it is an offense arising from defilement.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the profound meaning and the true meaning of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as well as the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, slanders and refuses to accept them, saying, "These are not beneficial and were not spoken by the Tathāgata," then they will likewise be unable to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings. This is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.

Whether they slander out of improper reflection within their own minds or because they follow others, such bodhisattvas do not give rise to a mind of understanding when hearing this foremost, most profound meaning. These bodhisattvas should give rise to a mind of faith and a mind free from deceit, training themselves in this way:
"I am greatly at fault; I am blind and lack the eye of wisdom."
"The Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom speaks thus in accordance with reality.
Since the Tathāgata has made this further explanation, how could one give rise to slander?

This Bodhisattva, while remaining in a state of non-knowing, [recognizes that] the Tathāgata thus manifests the knowledge and vision of dharmas, observing correctly and proceeding rightly, without transgression; it is not due to a lack of understanding that he slanders.
If a bodhisattva, with a mind of greed or anger, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement.
