There is no offense if one disparages non-Buddhists in order to extol the Buddha-dharma, or if one employs skillful means to subdue them as previously described.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one causes those without faith to have faith, or causes those who already have faith to increase and expand it.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing that there is a place where the Dharma is being taught or a place for definitive discussion, does not go to listen due to a mind of pride or a mind of resentment, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If one fails to go due to indolence or laziness, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-affliction.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one does not understand; if one is ill or lacks physical strength; if the other person teaches the Dharma erroneously; if one protects the mind of the speaker; if one has already heard it repeatedly, mastered it, and understood its meaning; if one is widely learned; if one is one who hears and retains; if one practices according to what has been taught; if one is practicing meditative concentration and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment; or if one has dull faculties and finds it difficult to realize, difficult to receive, or difficult to retain [the teaching]. In these cases, not going does not constitute an offense.
If a bodhisattva treats those who preach the Dharma with contempt, failing to give rise to reverence and instead deriding and disparaging them, saying:
"They merely cling to the words and do not rely on the true meaning," this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.

If a bodhisattva abiding in the morality of restraint sees sentient beings engaged in various activities and, out of a mind of malice and resentment, does not join them in those shared tasks—namely, deliberating on matters such as traveling, engaging in lawful business, farming, herding cattle, mediating disputes, auspicious gatherings, or performing meritorious deeds—and fails to participate with them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If the offense is committed through laziness or indolence, it does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense if one is ill or lacks strength; or if the other person is capable of accomplishing it themselves; or if they already have many companions; or if the task to be performed is contrary to the Dharma or not beneficial; or if one employs skillful means to subdue them as previously described.

There is no offense if one has previously consented to another; or if that person harbors enmity toward them; or if one is personally cultivating wholesome karma and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment; or if one is by nature dull-witted; or if one protects the feelings of many people; or if one upholds the regulations of the Saṃgha—provided that one does not associate with such a person.

If a bodhisattva, upon seeing a person who is weak and ill, fails to go and attend to them out of a mind of resentment and hatred, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.

If one commits an offense out of indolence or laziness, it is not an unwholesome transgression (*kliṣṭa*). There is no offense in the following cases: if one is personally ill; if one lacks physical strength;

if one instructs another who has the strength to attend to the sick person in accordance with their needs; if one knows that the person already has their own relatives; if that person has the strength to manage their own affairs; if the illness recurs frequently; if it is a chronic illness; if one is cultivating a superior practice and does not wish to interrupt it even briefly; if one is dull-witted and finds it difficult to understand, receive, retain, or remain focused upon the object of meditation; or if one was previously attending to another patient.
As it is with illness, so it is with poverty and suffering.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings committing unwholesome karma in this life and future lives, yet fails to provide correct instruction due to a mind of resentment, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.

There is no offense if one lacks wisdom oneself, or lacks the power [to speak], or causes someone who has power to speak; or if the other person already possesses power themselves, or already possesses good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); or if one employs skillful means to bring them to discipline, as previously described.

If one explains the teaching correctly, yet the person harbors increased resentment toward me, utters harsh words, misapprehends the meaning, lacks affection and respect, or is by nature stubborn and perverse.

If a bodhisattva, having received a kindness from another, out of a mind of resentment does not repay that person with an equivalent or greater benefit, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If the offense is committed through laziness or indolence, it does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense if one employs skillful means but lacks the power; or if one employs skillful means to subdue the other as previously described; or if one desires to repay a kindness but the other person does not accept it.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings facing difficulties regarding their relatives or their wealth, yet out of a mind of resentment fails to provide relief and resolve their distress, this is called committing a multitude of offenses.
This constitutes an offense arising from defilement; however, if it is committed through indolence or laziness, it does not arise from defilement.
Those who do not commit the offense are as previously explained in the section on different matters.

If a bodhisattva, when requested for food, drink, or clothing, fails to give them due to a mind of resentment and hatred, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If the offense is committed through laziness or indolence, it does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense if one lacks the item oneself; or if one seeks an improper object; or if the object would not benefit the recipient; or if one employs skillful means to discipline the person as previously described; or if the person has violated the king’s law and one acts to protect the king’s mind; or if one acts to uphold the regulations of the Saṃgha.

If a bodhisattva gathers a following and, out of a mind of resentment and ill will, fails to provide instruction in accordance with the Dharma, or fails to provide at the appropriate times robes, food, bedding, medicine, and dwellings as requested from brahmins and householders, this is called an offense of many transgressions; it is an offense arising from affliction.
If one commits an offense due to laziness, indolence, or negligence, it is not an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one employs skillful means to subdue the person as previously described; if protecting the regulations of the Sangha; if one is ill; if one lacks the strength; if one causes someone who has the strength to speak on their behalf; if the person concerned has the power and many acquaintances, being a person of great virtue (*mahāpuṇya*) who seeks out the necessary requisites themselves; if they have already received instruction and know the Dharma for themselves; or if they are an outsider who has stolen the Dharma and cannot be subdued.
If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment or malice, does not comply with others, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction.
If the violation occurs due to indolence or laziness, it is not an offense arising from affliction.
There is no offense if the other person intends to perform an improper act; or if one is ill, lacks strength, or is observing a monastic regulation;
or if, although the act is lawful, it would cause many people to engage in unlawful acts.
If, for the sake of subduing non-Buddhists, or by means of skillful means to bring them under control;

or if a bodhisattva knows that other sentient beings possess genuine merit, yet out of a heart of resentment neither speaks of it to others nor praises it, and does not exclaim "Excellent! when someone else praises them—this is called a transgression of many offenses, and it is a transgression arising from affliction.
If one commits an offense due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it is not an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense if one knows that the other person has few desires and acts thus to protect their feelings; or if one is ill or lacks physical strength; or if one employs skillful means to subdue them; or if one is observing the regulations of the Sangha.
It is for the purpose of removing those afflictions that might cause such a person to give rise to defilements, excessive joy, pride, or what is unwholesome;

or when actual merit appears as if it were not real merit, or when a true well-spoken teaching appears as if it were not well-spoken; or for the sake of subduing the false views of non-Buddhists; or while waiting for the discourse to be completed.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who ought to be reproached, ought to be subdued, or ought to be punished and expelled, yet—due to a defiled mind—does not reproach them, or reproaches them but does not subdue them, or subdues them but does not punish and expel them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement.
If one commits an offense due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it does not arise from defilement.
There is no offense in cases where the person is incurable, cannot be spoken with, is difficult to instruct, or frequently gives rise to resentment.

If, when observing him, one fears that because of him there will arise strife, opposition, mutual litigation, disputes within the Saṃgha, or a schism in the Saṃgha—and if that person is not deceitful, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, and gradually reforms himself—[then one should not report it].

If a bodhisattva accomplishes various supernormal powers, they should terrify those who ought to be terrified and attract those who ought to be attracted, in order to cause sentient beings to consume their offerings of faith.
If one does not use supernormal powers to terrify and lead them [to the truth], this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.

There is no offense if those sentient beings further give rise to defiled attachment, or if they are non-Buddhists who revile the noble ones and have established wrong views; in all such cases, there is no offense.
If one becomes insane or if intense painful sensations arise, these circumstances constitute the arising of the bodhisattva precepts.

The Buddha has taught throughout various sūtras that there are the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*); [in such cases], it is subsumed under the precept of restraint.

This is the compendium (*mātṛkā*) of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, spoken in its entirety; bodhisattvas should diligently uphold it, giving rise to supreme reverence and training with a focused mind. Having correctly received it from another, they should possess a mind of utterly pure desire to learn, a mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and a mind that benefits sentient beings, and from the moment of first receiving the precepts, they should guard and maintain them with single-minded diligence.
If one commits any transgression, one should immediately perform repentance according to the Dharma.

All such offenses committed by Bodhisattvas should be understood as being subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); one should perform repentance according to the Dharma before those capable of understanding the language and accepting the confession, whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.
If a bodhisattva commits an offense involving a *pārājika* matter due to intense afflictions (*adhimātra-kleśa*), they lose the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and should receive them again.

If they commit an offense involving a *pārājika* matter due to middling afflictions (*madhya-kleśa*), they should approach three or more persons, kneel with palms joined, and perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense, stating the name of the previously committed offense and speaking as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind!"
"I, [Name], relinquish the Bodhisattva Vinaya.
Regarding the matter as previously described, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The remainder is as explained in the method for repenting a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *bhikṣu*.
If one commits an offense involving a *pārājika* matter or other transgressions due to secondary afflictions, one should confess them before a single person.
If there is no such person present, one should arouse a pure mind and think:
"I shall never again commit this offense; in all future lives, I will always maintain the restraint of the precepts."
If one can do so, the offense is immediately removed.

If there is no person endowed with such complete merit from whom one may receive the Bodhisattva precepts, that Bodhisattva should receive them before an image of the Buddha; they should be received in this manner.
Adjusting one's robes and baring the right shoulder, with the right knee touching the ground and the body bent in prostration with palms joined, one speaks these words:

"I, [Name], inform all Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the Great Stages: I now, before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, receive the vows of all Bodhisattvas—the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*)."
These precepts are those which all bodhisattvas of the past have already studied, all bodhisattvas of the future shall study, and all bodhisattvas of the present are now studying.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
Having finished speaking, one should rise; the rest is as previously stated.

Regarding the offenses committed by a bodhisattva, there is no offense that leaves no remainder. As the Blessed One has said, when a bodhisattva gives rise to the affliction of anger and commits an offense, it must be re-undertaken; this does not apply to what is committed through the arising of desire.
One should understand this intention:

when a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings as the predominant motive, whatever they undertake, they are capable of accomplishing it all. What the bodhisattva performs is not merely what is to be done; even if they should transgress, they must undergo renewed commitment.
If a bodhisattva harbors anger toward sentient beings, they will be unable to deliver themselves or others, nor will they be able to perform the deeds of a bodhisattva.
Failing to perform such deeds constitutes a transgression that must be confessed and undertaken anew.
It should be understood that the minor, medium, and major transgressions of a bodhisattva are as explained in the "Chapter on the Four Means of Integration.
If a bodhisattva fully accomplishes three correct dharmas within these rules of discipline, they will abide in peace and happiness:
first, the fullness of skillful means; [the second and third are as follows].
Second is the fulfillment of a pure mind;
third is the fulfillment of the original cause.

When a bodhisattva is without breach or leakage regarding the precepts, purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind without repeated transgressions, and discloses all evils, this is called the fulfillment of skillful means.

A bodhisattva leaves the household life for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of body or life; they seek the meaning and meditative concentration, not wealth or profit; they seek the state of a śramaṇa and nirvāṇa, not what is unrighteous or indolence. With diligence and without regression, they remain unmixed with various evil and unwholesome dharmas, afflictions, or the burning retribution of existence, as well as birth, aging, sickness, and death in future lives. This is called the perfection of pure mind.

When a bodhisattva extensively cultivated various virtues in previous lives, they now lack nothing in terms of clothing, food, bedding, medicine, and other necessities, enabling them to practice generous giving; this is called the perfection of the primary cause.
A bodhisattva dwelling in the precepts of restraint who is endowed with the three right dharmas is said to dwell in peace and happiness;
the opposite of this is said to be being endowed with the precepts of the three wrong dharmas, which should be known as dwelling in suffering.
This is a brief explanation.
A detailed exposition of all the precepts for both householders and renunciants should be understood as being categorized into the "difficult precepts" and so forth.
Briefly stated, there are three types of difficult precepts.
That a bodhisattva, possessing great wealth and great power, is able to renounce it all to leave the household life and receive the bodhisattva precepts—this is called the first difficult precept.

If a bodhisattva encounters urgent peril even to the point of losing their life, they do not allow the precepts they have received to be deficient, much less commit a full violation; this is called the second difficult precept.

In all practices, all meditative attainments, and all recollections, the bodhisattva’s mind dwells without distraction, and even unto the end of their life, they never fail or diminish in even the most subtle precepts, let alone the more serious ones; this is called the third difficult precept.
The precepts of all gates are of four kinds:
first, the precepts received through formal undertaking;
second, the precepts of intrinsic nature.
Third is the cultivation of precepts;
fourth is the fulfillment of precepts through skillful means.

Regarding the formal reception of precepts, a bodhisattva has already received the three types of disciplinary vows (*saṃvara-śīla*), namely: the vow of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*).
Regarding natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*): the Bodhisattva is naturally virtuous by nature, with body, speech, and mind being pure.

Regarding cultivated precepts (*abhyāsa-śīla*): in previous lives, the Bodhisattva has already practiced the three kinds of precepts as previously described; because of these original causes, they take no pleasure in committing any evil, their minds are constantly weary of it, and they delight in cultivating wholesome conduct.

Regarding the precepts accomplished through skillful means: a bodhisattva, relying on the four bases of sympathetic appeal (*saṃgrahavastu*), performs wholesome physical and vocal actions toward all sentient beings.
There are five kinds of the precepts of virtuous persons:
first, maintaining pure precepts oneself;
Second, bestowing [the precepts] upon others;
third, praising pure ethical discipline;
fourth, feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing those who share the same Dharma.
Fifth, even if there is transgression, it is rectified through repentance in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the "precepts of all practices," those six and seven types are collectively summarized as thirteen types dedicated toward great enlightenment; because they extensively encompass the precepts, this is called "extensive."
Because it is free from these two extremes—attachment to sensual pleasures and self-mortification—it is called the place of faultless joy.

Because throughout one’s entire life one never returns the precepts, and because all forms of gain, the practices of non-Buddhists, heterodox arguments, and the various entanglements of afflictions cannot deceive or violate them, nor can they take them away, this is called firm precept; it is so named because it is adorned with accomplishment.

One should know that the adornment of ethical discipline (*śīla-alaṃkāra*) refers to the restraint of ethical discipline—namely, the precepts of abstaining from killing and so forth on the stage of the Śrāvaka—as well as the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*); it includes ethical discipline that is compliant and that which is non-compliant, primary and secondary protective ethical discipline, the retribution of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the retribution of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), the retribution of rebirth in happy realms (*sugati*), and the retribution of benefiting sentient beings.
The precept for removing affliction has eight aspects. A bodhisattva first reflects:

"Just as I do not desire others to kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, use divisive speech, harsh words, or idle chatter, nor do I desire to be touched or afflicted by hands, stones, staves, and the like; just as I find these undesirable and unpleasant, so it is for them. How could I inflict such things upon others?"
For this reason, one does not cause distress to others, nor does one apply such things as hands, stones, or staffs to them.
Having formed this reflection, one does not afflict sentient beings with the eight matters; this is called the bodhisattva’s precept of removing distress.
Regarding the precepts for happiness in this world and the next, there are nine types:
the Bodhisattva prohibits what should be prohibited, permits what should be permitted, gathers what should be gathered, and subdues those who should be subdued.
For a bodhisattva, these four types of precepts pertain to the karma of body and speech.
Furthermore, there are five types of precepts: those concurrent with the *dāna-pāramitā*, and those concurrent with the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Thus, these nine kinds of ethical discipline have been briefly explained.

Because they bring about a pleasant dwelling in the present life and happiness in future lives for both oneself and others, they are called the "ethical discipline that brings happiness in this world and the next."
There are ten kinds of pure precepts:
first, initially receiving the precepts with excellence, for the sake of being a śramaṇa and for the sake of bodhi, not for the sake of body or life;
second, never regressing or diminishing, nor giving rise to doubt or regret.
Third, not transgressing the precepts and avoiding the arising of groundless doubt and regret.
Fourth, remaining free from all indolence and taking no pleasure in sleep, one applies oneself with diligence day and night to accomplish wholesome dharmas.
Fifth, one should collect the mind and not allow it to become negligent, as previously explained regarding non-negligence.
Sixth, one should cultivate right aspirations, not aspiring for wealth, profit, or rebirth in the heavens, but constantly practicing the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

Seventh, he maintains dignified deportment and is skilled in all matters pertaining to such conduct; through skillful means, he cultivates goodness, his physical and verbal actions are in accordance with the Dharma, and he is fully endowed with right livelihood, remaining far removed from all forms of deceit, crookedness, wrong livelihood, and various faults and evils.
Eighth, it is free from the two extremes, because it avoids both the pursuit of sensual pleasures and various ascetic practices.
Ninth, it cultivates the path of liberation, remaining entirely detached from the various views of heterodox schools.
Tenth, one does not violate or diminish the precepts one has received.
These ten kinds are called the pure precepts; this is termed the bodhisattva’s great aggregate of precepts, which attains the fruit of bodhi.
Relying upon these precepts, the Bodhisattva fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) and attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, until they have realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they obtain five kinds of benefits:
first, they are constantly kept in mind by all Buddhas;
Second, at the time of death, their mind is filled with joy;
third, upon relinquishing the body, they will always have pure-precepted bodhisattvas as their spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in whatever place they are reborn;
fourth, they achieve the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), which is a mass of immeasurable merit.
Fifth, there is the accomplishment of natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*) in both this life and future lives.

As previously explained, the nine kinds of morality, such as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), should be understood as being subsumed within three types of morality: namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*).
Furthermore, these three types, briefly stated, can perform three functions for a bodhisattva:
first, the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), which enables the mind to abide [in stability];
second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), by which one personally accomplishes the Buddha-dharmas.
Third is the precept of gathering in sentient beings, which brings sentient beings to maturity.
This is called all the activities of a bodhisattva.

That is to say, in this present life, the mind attains a state of joyful dwelling and body and mind do not grow weary; one is able to fulfill the Buddha-dharma and bring sentient beings to maturity. This is called the bodhisattva’s precept, and this is called the merit of the precept.

The deeds performed by this bodhisattva are complete and unsurpassed; all bodhisattvas of the past who sought great enlightenment studied therein, those of the future shall study therein, and those of the present are currently studying therein.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Dharmakṣema translated [this] at Guzang. Chapter Eleven:
The Chapter on Forbearance (*Kṣānti-paṭala*) in the Section on Skillful Means (*Upāya-sthāna*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of forbearance (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, patience by nature;
second, all-encompassing patience.
Third, patience that is difficult to endure;
fourth, patience in all circumstances;
fifth, patience of the virtuous person.
Sixth is patience toward all conditioned phenomena;
seventh is patience that eliminates affliction;
eighth is patience for the sake of happiness in this world and the next.
Ninth is pure patience (*viśuddha-kṣānti*).
What is patience by nature (*svabhāva-kṣānti*)?

When a bodhisattva, relying on the power of reflection, is naturally able to endure the harmful actions of others, and when all forms of patience are based upon a mind free from greed and a single-minded heart of compassion—this is called, in brief, patience by nature.
What is the patience of all bodhisattvas?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds: first, that which relies on the householder; [second, that which relies on the renunciant].
The second is based on renunciation.
Each of these two has three types:
first, patience toward harm inflicted by others;
Second is the patience of enduring suffering;
third is the patience of resolving through reflection on the Dharma.
Regarding the patience of enduring harm from others: since time immemorial, one has been subjected to uninterrupted great suffering, and now such harm from others manifests with immediate urgency.
The bodhisattva trains in this way:
"This is brought about by the faults of my own past karma; having previously committed sinful deeds, I have obtained this suffering today.

If I do not endure it now, it will again become the cause and condition for great suffering in the future. Thus, I would now be creating heavy suffering for myself once more, not through the agency of another."
Furthermore, both my own body and theirs are equally subject to the suffering inherent in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Because they lack wisdom, they increase their own suffering upon that which is already suffering by its very nature.
Since I now possess wisdom, how could I wish to further add to their suffering?
"Furthermore, even a Śrāvaka, who seeks his own benefit, does not inflict suffering upon others; how much more so a Bodhisattva, who extensively benefits all sentient beings.

Having reflected thus, one cultivates five kinds of perceptions regarding enemies, friends, and neutral persons—whether of inferior, middling, or superior quality, whether experiencing suffering or happiness, and whether possessing virtue or lacking it—and is able to endure all such sentient beings.
What are the five kinds of perception?
First, the perception of original kinship;
second, the perception of numerical categories of phenomena.
Third is the perception of impermanence;
fourth is the perception of suffering;
fifth is the perception of grasping.
Regarding the thought of kinship, a bodhisattva trains in this way:

"Among sentient beings, there has been none who has not been a relative since time immemorial—whether as father or mother, brother or sister, preceptor or ācārya, teacher or one equal to a teacher, or any other object of veneration."
When one correctly reflects in this way toward those who are hostile and hateful, one abandons the perception of hostility and harm, and dwells in the perception of them as original kin.
Having relied upon the perception of them as original kin, one is able to endure all harms inflicted by others.
Regarding the conceptualization of numerical categories of phenomena (*dharmagaṇanāsaṃjñā*), a bodhisattva trains as follows:

"The causal conditions, the formations, and the numerical categories of phenomena are devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a soul, one who is born, one who reviles, one who strikes, or one who quarrels."
When one reflects correctly in this manner, one leaves behind the perception of sentient beings and abides in the perception of phenomena (dharmasaṃjñā).
Having relied upon the perception of phenomena, one is able to endure all harms inflicted by others.
Regarding the perception of impermanence, the bodhisattva trains in this way:
"All that arises for sentient beings is entirely subject to the law of impermanent death; furthermore, there are harmful matters above this that seek to terminate their lives."

Thus, since the nature of sentient beings is impermanent and subject to death, a wise person does not give rise to an impure mind, much less desire to end their life with hands, stones, swords, or clubs.
When one reflects correctly in this way, one abandons the notion of permanence and solidity, and dwells in the notion of impermanence and lack of solidity.
Based upon the notion of impermanence, one is able to endure all harms inflicted by others.

Regarding the perception of suffering: even those endowed with great power, when observed by a bodhisattva, do not escape the three characteristics—namely, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*)—let alone those who lack such power.

When a bodhisattva trains in this way, wishing to cause sentient beings who are constantly suffering to be free from suffering, how could he inflict retribution that further increases their suffering?
When reflecting correctly in this manner, he abandons the perception of pleasure and dwells in the perception of suffering.
Having formed the perception of enduring suffering, one is able to fully endure all that others do not benefit one.
Regarding the perception of gathering [beings], the Bodhisattva trains as follows:

"I have resolved upon bodhicitta for the sake of all sentient beings; I regard all sentient beings as my own kin. I should gather them in and bring them universal peace and happiness; I must not inflict further harm upon those who are my kin when there is an opportunity to benefit them."
When one reflects correctly in this way, the notion of "other" is eliminated and one dwells with the notion of "appropriation.
Based on the notion of appropriation, one is able to endure all harms inflicted by others.
What is patience? If one does not become angry, does not retaliate, and harbors no resentment in the mind, this is called patience.
Regarding the patience of enduring suffering, the bodhisattva trains in this way:

"From the distant past, I have constantly sought after sensual pleasures, which serve as the cause of all sufferings and give rise to immeasurable great suffering—namely, managing worldly livelihoods, engaging in commerce and agriculture, and serving royal households."
Thus, there is no such suffering that one has not fully experienced; all this is due to the fault of ignorance and the darkness of delusion.
Now, one should cultivate the causes of happiness and fulfill wholesome dharmas, enduring all immeasurable sufferings with equanimity, let alone minor ones.
When one reflects correctly in this manner, being endowed with awakened wisdom, one is able to endure all matters of suffering.
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds of such matters of suffering:
first, the basis;...
Second is the sphere of worldly dharmas;
third is the sphere of dignified deportment;
fourth is the sphere of gathering the Dharma.
Fifth, the stage of following the precepts;
sixth, the stage of skillful means;
seventh, the stage of benefiting sentient beings.
Eighth, regarding the various spheres of activity:
"reliance" refers to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
By relying on the True Dharma (*saddharma*) one leaves the household life and attains the status of a bhikṣu.
If a bodhisattva receives offerings that are coarse, harsh, inferior, disrespectful, obstructed, or untimely, their mind remains free from sorrow and affliction.
The bodhisattva does not abandon diligence in the face of such manifold sufferings; this is called patience based on suffering.
There are nine kinds of worldly dharmas: first, disadvantage;
second, disrepute; [and so forth].
Third is disparagement;
fourth is suffering;
fifth is the destruction of the Dharma.
Sixth, that which is subject to exhaustion is exhausted;
seventh, that which is subject to aging ages;
eighth, that which is subject to illness falls ill.
Ninth is death according to the nature of death.
These worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), whether separated from or joined together, can give rise to manifold sufferings; this is called the locus of worldly phenomena.
When a bodhisattva does not abandon their diligence in the face of those manifold sufferings, this is called the patient endurance of the suffering of worldly phenomena.
Regarding dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), there are four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

Whether walking or sitting, this bodhisattva, during the two periods of day and night, removes the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*) so that the mind attains purity, and does not lie down at improper times.
Whether lying on a bed, sitting on a seat, or resting on a mat of grass or leaves, he is able to endure all the various sufferings born of such extreme exhaustion.
The Bodhisattva does not abandon his diligent effort amidst those manifold sufferings; this is called the endurance of the suffering of deportment.
The encompassing of the Dharma consists of seven kinds of jewel-like offerings and offerings of virtue:

receiving and studying the true Dharma, extensively expounding it for others, praising it with sublime sounds, reflecting in solitary stillness, weighing and examining it, recollecting and internalizing it, and practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

When a bodhisattva practices by encompassing these seven kinds of skillful means, they are able to endure all the various sufferings that arise, and never, on account of them, abandon their correct skillful means.
There are seven ways in which a bhikṣu conforms to the precepts:
first, by altering one’s physical appearance through the removal of hair and beard to abandon worldly characteristics;
second, by wearing robes of dyed color.
Third, abandoning improper worldly conduct and dwelling with the mind established in right mindfulness;
fourth, relying on others for one's livelihood and relinquishing worldly occupations;
fifth, seeking clothing from others for as long as life lasts, without hoarding it.
Sixth, for as long as life lasts, one shall restrain oneself from the five desires that obstruct people, guard the doors of the sense faculties, and renounce unchaste conduct;
seventh, for as long as life lasts, one shall abandon singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and all manner of amusements.
Regarding such difficult practices as those performed in accordance with the bhikṣu precepts, which give rise to suffering, the bodhisattva remains patient and does not abandon diligence.

As for diligent application, the bodhisattva diligently makes offerings to the Triple Gem, upholds, recites, and studies the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, copies and explains it, contemplates its meaning, and exerts great effort to cultivate and accumulate the Noble Path; although these things give rise to suffering, the bodhisattva remains patient and does not, because of them, abandon sentient beings.
Regarding the matters that benefit sentient beings, there are briefly eleven points, as previously explained.
Although suffering arises because of these, the bodhisattva practices patient endurance; he does not, on account of this, abandon his diligent effort.

Regarding all conditioned activities—such as the tasks concerning robes and alms bowls for those who have left the household life, or the occupations for maintaining a livelihood for those who remain at home—these give rise to suffering; yet the bodhisattva practices patient endurance and does not, because of this, abandon their diligent effort.
Although a bodhisattva undergoes manifold sufferings, they must practice patience and cultivate unexcelled bodhi; it is not that they do not practice.
Having completed their cultivation, they never regress; their minds are always joyful and free from defilement. This is called the dharma of the patience of enduring suffering.

Regarding the patience of contemplative understanding (*cintāmayī kṣānti*): it is when a bodhisattva correctly discriminates and skillfully contemplates the Dharma to achieve awakening; they deeply apply focused mindfulness to the eight bases of understanding, namely: the true meaning of the merits of the Three Jewels; the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the meanings that ought to be attained regarding causes and fruits; the skillful means for attaining those meanings; and the spheres of objects to be known.
Furthermore, there are two causes and conditions for this understanding:
first, long-term cultivation and practice;
second, attaining swift and pure wisdom. This is called the "all-encompassing patience" of a bodhisattva.
Based on three kinds of conceptualization, these are explained in detail as being difficult to endure and so forth.
What is meant by "difficult to endure"?
Briefly stated, there are three types.
If a bodhisattva is able to endure all those who do not benefit inferior sentient beings, this is called the first difficult endurance.
If one is able to endure even one's own servants and attendants, this is called the second difficult endurance.
When a person of inferior lineage gives rise to excessive transgressions yet is able to endure them, this is called the third "difficult-to-endure" patience.
What is the bodhisattva’s patience through all gates?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds:
first, enduring harm inflicted by one's own relatives;
second, enduring harm inflicted by enemies.
Third, being able to endure harm from neutral persons;
fourth, being able to endure harm from inferior, neutral, or superior persons.
What is the patience of virtuous persons?
Briefly stated, there are five kinds.

This bodhisattva first perceives that practicing patience brings great benefit and merit: namely, that one who practices patience will harbor little resentment and experience little discord in future lives; their mind will be filled with joy and happiness; they will have no regrets at the time of death; and upon the dissolution of the body after life ends, they will be reborn by transformation in the heavens of the happy realms.

Seeing such merits and benefits as these, one is able to endure oneself and teach others to practice patience; one constantly praises the merit of patience for others and rejoices in their hearts when seeing others practicing patience.
What is the patience of all practices of a bodhisattva?
It consists of six kinds and seven kinds, briefly stated as thirteen kinds.
A bodhisattva practices patience because they see that one who lacks patience will receive the retribution of great suffering, and thus they endure out of fear.
One endures out of affection, possessing a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, and intimacy toward all sentient beings.
One endures as a cause, being earnestly desirous of unsurpassed bodhi and wishing to fulfill the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience).

One leaves the household life by the power of patience; as the World-Honored One has taught, one should always fully and correctly uphold the precepts. This patience of leaving the household life is called the patience of receiving the Dharma.
The full possession of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and its cultivation in the past, abiding in the present—this is called "patience by nature" (*prakṛti-kṣānti*).

Knowing that all phenomena are devoid of the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*) and are beyond the categories of verbal expression—this is called "right mindfulness patience regarding phenomena" (*dharmānusmṛti-dharma-kṣānti*).
Patience toward all that is non-beneficial, patience toward all things, and patience in all circumstances—referring to a single individual as well as a great assembly.
Patience at all times—referring to dawn, midday, sunset, and night, as well as the past, future, and present.
Whether ill or healthy, whether lying down or rising, one should always practice patience of body, refraining from causing affliction or distress to others;
always practice patience of speech, avoiding unkind words;
and always practice patience of mind, not giving rise to anger, nor conceiving impure desires.
What is the bodhisattva’s patience in removing affliction?
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds:
first, when a seeker comes with suffering, the bodhisattva endures it without causing further distress.
Second, toward those who are violent and exceedingly wicked, one endures them without causing provocation by relying on great compassion.
Third, toward those who have left the household life but violate the precepts, one endures them without causing provocation by relying on great compassion.

There are five kinds of diligence: being patient and not vexing sentient beings who are suffering; seeking the Dharma and the practice leading to the Dharma in order to eliminate their suffering; extensively proclaiming such teachings; and being capable of diligent assistance in all that sentient beings undertake.
These are called the eight kinds of patience for removing affliction.
One endures the sufferings of sentient beings in order to eliminate them, and one endures their deficiencies in order to provide for them.
What is the bodhisattva’s patience for the happiness of this world and other worlds?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds.

These bodhisattvas abide in the wholesome dharma of heedfulness and are able to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, the touch of mosquitoes and gadflies, and the touch of wind, sun, and various poisons; they endure all such things.
They are able to endure all physical and mental exhaustion and suffering.
Out of compassion for sentient beings who have fallen into the ocean of birth and death and are beset by the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, they exercise such forbearance.

A bodhisattva abides in happiness within the present life, remaining far removed from all evils; furthermore, they create the causes and conditions for happiness in future lives, and likewise lead others toward peace and joy in both this world and the next. Therefore, this is called the patience that brings happiness in this world and the next.
What is the pure patience of a bodhisattva?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds:
first, the mind that harbors no resentment toward those who cause harm.
Second, not giving rise to anger or resentment;
third, being free from thoughts of enmity or aversion;

fourth, constantly acting for the benefit of others with a mind directed toward them as one would toward oneself, and having thus rendered such benefit, subsequently relinquishing any non-beneficial conduct.
Fifth, toward those who cause one harm, one should respond with gentle words and an apology;
sixth, if they repent and apologize, one should be able to accept it quickly and patiently;
seventh, seeing their inability to endure [the offense], one should increase one's heart of compassion.
Eighth, seeing others practice patience, one’s reverence for the Buddha increases manifold;
ninth, when sentient beings are terrified, one gives rise to profound compassion;
tenth, one eliminates all faults such as impatience, becoming free from desire and pure.
These ten kinds are called the pure patience of a bodhisattva.

Thus, from the patience of nature up to the pure patience, the vast and immeasurable fruit of great enlightenment depends upon this patience as its cause; by means of it, one will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter 12: The Chapter on Diligence. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya-viniścaya*, the twelfth chapter, the Chapter on Diligence: What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*)?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, diligence of essential nature;
second, all-encompassing diligence; [and so forth].
Third, difficult diligence;
fourth, all-gate diligence;
fifth, the diligence of virtuous persons.
Sixth is the diligence of all practices;
seventh is the diligence of removing afflictions;
eighth is the diligence for the happiness of this world and other worlds.
Ninth is pure diligence. What is the essential nature of diligence?

It is the bodhisattva’s mental capacity to embrace immeasurable wholesome dharmas, acting with fervor and without interruption for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and doing so without error.
The physical, verbal, and mental actions arising from that are called the bodhisattva’s essential diligence (*svabhāva-vīrya*).
What is all-encompassing diligence?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
First, based on the laity;
second, based on those who have gone forth.
Each of these two has three types:
First is the vigor of the great vow;
second is the gathering of all wholesome dharmas;
third is the benefiting of sentient beings.
Regarding "vigor of the great vow," the Bodhisattva first initiates the skillful means of vigor; his mental faculties become capable of donning the armor of the great vow, thinking to himself:

"For the sake of liberating even a single sentient being from suffering, I shall take hundreds of thousands of great kalpas as a single day and night. Even if I must remain in hell for hundreds of thousands of millions of such great kalpas until the attainment of Buddhahood, I vow not to regress. I shall never abandon my vigor until I have attained unsurpassed bodhi, let alone endure minor suffering for a short time."
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of the great vow.

When such a bodhisattva’s diligence of the great vow gives rise to even a slight understanding and slight faith, it is able to nurture immeasurable qualities of awakening, diligent application, and skillful means; how much more so when one has fully accomplished such diligence of the great vow.
For the sake of unsurpassed *bodhi*, the bodhisattva benefits sentient beings without regarding it as difficult, nor does he give rise to thoughts of retreat or despondency.

Regarding the diligence of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-vīrya*), because the bodhisattva’s diligence serves as the skillful means for the accomplishment of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), and as the skillful means for the accomplishment of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom, it is briefly explained as being of seven kinds:
first, immovability, because he is not shaken by any discursive thoughts, afflictions, heterodox doctrines, or immeasurable sufferings.
Second is firmness, because of the sudden application of skillful means.
Third is attaining the sphere of immeasurable illumination, because of abiding securely in right mindfulness.
Fourth is the perfection of skillful means, because one attains in accordance with the non-perverted path the meaning that ought to be realized.
Fifth is the meaning of right diligence being beneficial, because it accomplishes the aspirations for the goals that ought to be attained.
Sixth is its intensity, because one constantly exerts skillful means.
Seventh is freedom from pride, because through the application of diligence, the mind does not become self-exalting.

When a bodhisattva cultivates these seven kinds of practices that encompass all wholesome dharmas, they swiftly fulfill the various pāramitās through diligent skillful means and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
All bodhisattva practices and wholesome dharmas are accomplished through this diligence; therefore, this diligence is the supreme and most excellent cause, peerless and unsurpassed.
Therefore, in the sūtras, the World-Honored One has praised various forms of diligence as the cause for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are eleven kinds of diligence through which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings, as explained in the "Chapter on Precepts."
That refers to the precepts, while this refers to diligence.
What constitutes the difficult diligence of a bodhisattva?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds.

This Bodhisattva practices diligence without interruption, free from thoughts of clothing and food, thoughts of bedding and furniture, and thoughts of his own body; he constantly cultivates wholesome dharmas. This is called the first difficult diligence.

When a bodhisattva practices such diligence, continuing from the relinquishing of one body to the taking up of another, constantly cultivating wholesome dharmas without abandoning diligence, this is called the second difficult diligence.

This bodhisattva is fully endowed with the merit of impartial discernment; with a mind that is neither lax nor hasty and free from inversion, they achieve diligence through the benefit of meaning. This is called the third difficult-to-practice diligence.
Furthermore, one should know that this bodhisattva’s power of difficult-to-perform diligence is the cause for embracing great compassion and wisdom.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence of all gateways?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds:
first, abandoning defiled phenomena;
second, giving rise to pure phenomena.
Third, purifying the three karmas;
fourth, augmenting wisdom.

Regarding the relinquishing of defiled phenomena, the bodhisattva exerts diligence to distance themselves from all afflictions, ensuring that those not yet arisen do not arise, and causing those already arisen to be extinguished.

Regarding the production of pure and white dharmas: one employs skillful means to cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise, and employs skillful means to increase and expand those wholesome dharmas that have already arisen.
Regarding the purification of the three karmas: through the bodhisattva’s diligence, the three karmas become pure, and they are able to fully embrace wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the increase of wisdom: through the bodhisattva’s diligence, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are attained, increased, and brought to fulfillment.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence of virtuous persons?
Briefly stated, there are five kinds:
first, never failing to employ skillful means for all desires, because one does not rest;
second, not falling into inferiority, because one cultivates and increases diligence whether the [arising] state is middling or superior.

Third is non-laxity: because one is courageous, ardent, and persistent for a long duration without interruption, applying skillful means with diligence such that the mind does not retreat, desist, or become impaired.
Fourth is the benefit of non-perverted meaning, because it is embraced through skillful means.
Fifth is earnestness, because one exerts oneself with skillful means to swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence in all practices? It consists of six kinds and seven kinds, briefly stated as thirteen kinds.
As for the six kinds: they are constant diligence, because of constant application of skillful means;
and sudden diligence, because of reaching the goal through skillful means.
It relies on diligence because it is based on the power of original diligence;
it is the diligence of skillful means because it involves contemplating and calculating skillful methods;
it is unshakable diligence because it is not swayed by any contact with suffering, nor does it turn toward any other objective.
Because one who lacks the diligence of non-contentment does not rejoice in superior progress that is limited.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these six kinds of all-encompassing diligence, their earnest diligence becomes capable and firm, and they cannot be undermined in regard to any wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
first, diligence accompanied by aspiration, because one earnestly desires and vows to nurture unexcelled bodhi;

second, balanced and complete diligence, because while other afflictions cause the mind to dwell in defilement, the bodhisattva’s diligence causes the mind to dwell with equanimity toward all dharmas of goodness.

Third is the diligence of superior progress (*viśeṣa-vīrya*), because one dwells with a mind focused on overcoming all other afflictions and secondary afflictions, severing them as if putting out a fire on one's head.
Fourth is the diligence of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-vīrya*), because one seeks after all fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*).
Fifth is the diligence of training, because one gives rise to the successive stages of the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti) in accordance with those various dharmas as appropriate.
Sixth is the diligence for the benefit of sentient beings, which consists of eleven matters as previously explained.
Seventh is the diligence of protecting one's own correct application, because one repents according to the Dharma for any deficiencies or lapses.
These are called the seven kinds.
Thus, these thirteen kinds are called the bodhisattva’s diligence of all practices.
The bodhisattva’s diligence in removing afflictions and the diligence for the happiness of this world and other worlds are as explained in the section on patience.
What is the bodhisattva’s pure diligence?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds:
First is compliance;
second is cultivation;
third is single-minded devotion.
Fourth, excellence in gathering;
fifth, excellence in timing;
sixth, excellence in the discernment of characteristics.
Seventh, non-retrogression;
eighth, indestructibility;
ninth, equanimity.
Tenth is dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This bodhisattva, in order to eradicate the afflictions (*kleśa*), cultivates their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) as appropriate:

for those bound by craving, they cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); for anger, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); for delusion, the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); for those distracted by discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*); and for pride, the skillful contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātuvibhāga-upāya-bhāvanā*). Such practices as these are called "conformable diligence" (*anuloma-vīrya*).

This bodhisattva does not merely achieve the diligence of a beginner; rather, with the mind already established in instruction and admonition, they cultivate skillful means and the means of subduing. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of diligence.
This bodhisattva does not abide in a mind that has cultivated diligence, nor in instructions and admonitions, nor in skillful means; rather, they are at the stage of a beginner.
Regarding these skillful means, this bodhisattva applies themselves with exclusive diligence, constant application, and immediate application; this is called "exclusive attachment to diligence."

Because this bodhisattva relies on those worthy of veneration, receives teachings without error through the power of extensive learning, and his mind abides in the skillful means of diligence, this is called "skillfully gathering diligence."

When this bodhisattva thus receives [the teachings] without inversion—practicing tranquility (*śamatha*) when it is time for tranquility, practicing exertion (*pragraha*) when it is time for exertion, and practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*) when it is time for equanimity—this is called "diligence endowed with the proper timing."

When a bodhisattva constantly and skillfully observes, without false discrimination, the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity, as well as the signs of entering and emerging from samādhi, this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence in discerning signs.

When this bodhisattva hears it said that there is a supreme and most excellent, foremost, profound, inconceivable, and immeasurable bodhisattva diligence and skillful means, his mind does not disparage itself nor does it become timid; he does not settle for minor progress by conceiving a sense of contentment, but seeks higher advancement. This is called the bodhisattva’s non-retrogressive and undaunted diligence.

This bodhisattva constantly guards the sense doors, knows moderation in eating, and remains without sleep during the first and last watches of the night; with diligence, skillful means, and a mind abiding in right wisdom, they thus possess such meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that they achieve right meaning and great benefit through diligent application. This is called the bodhisattva’s indestructible diligence.

This bodhisattva’s skillful means of diligence are neither lax nor hurried, but are cultivated with equanimity; all skillful means are cultivated simultaneously and equally. This is called the bodhisattva’s equal diligence.
All the exertions performed by this bodhisattva through skillful means are dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment; this is called the bodhisattva’s right dedication of diligence.
Thus, from essential-nature diligence up to pure diligence, one shall attain the fruit of great enlightenment.
By relying on this diligence, the bodhisattva fulfills the *vīryapāramitā* and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Chapter 13:
Dhyāna. In the "Chapter on Dhyāna" within the "Section on Skillful Means" of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the thirteenth chapter, it is asked: What is the bodhisattva’s *dhyānapāramitā*?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, dhyāna of intrinsic nature;
second, universal dhyāna.
Third, the meditation that is difficult;
fourth, the meditation of all gates;
fifth, the meditation of virtuous persons.
Sixth is the meditation on all formations;
seventh is the meditation that removes affliction;
eighth is the meditation for happiness in this world and the next.
Ninth is the pure dhyāna. What is intrinsic dhyāna?

It refers to the mundane and supramundane virtues preceded by hearing and reflection upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, wherein one dwells with a single mind—whether in the portion of calm abiding (*śamatha*), the portion of insight (*vipaśyanā*), that which is concordant with these two, or both portions combined. This is called intrinsic dhyāna.
What is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing dhyāna?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, the mundane; [second, the supramundane].
The second is the supramundane.
Furthermore, according to their respective applications, each has three types:
first, dhyāna for dwelling in happiness in the present life;
Second is the dhyāna that gives rise to the merit of samādhi;
third is the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva’s meditative concentration leaves behind the delusions of this world, the body and mind come to rest in supreme quiescence; with the mind naturally uplifted and stilled, they abandon attachment to flavors and all signs—this is called the dhyāna of dwelling in happiness in the present life.

The bodhisattva’s meditative concentration gives rise to various inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless samādhis subsumed within the lineage of the ten powers; the names of all these samādhis are unknown even to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone their ability to enter them or the liberation produced therein—except for those who have entered the unimpeded wisdom of all entries, the merit of the wishless knowledge of non-contention, and other such supreme and wondrous qualities. This is called the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration of the merit of producing samādhis.
Regarding the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings, there are eleven types as previously described.

Based on the acts performed by Bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings through generosity, they benefit them with righteousness and engage in shared activities (*sabhāgacarita*) with all. To eliminate their various sufferings, they act as appropriate—recognizing kindness and repaying it, protecting them from terrors, providing consolation and resolution for hardships, anxieties, and sorrows, supplying necessary provisions when resources are lacking, properly maintaining their followers in accordance with the Dharma, joyfully praising those who possess genuine merit, impartially subduing those with faults and evils, and using spiritual powers to inspire awe or bring joy. This is a brief explanation of all dhyāna, exhaustive and unsurpassed.
What is the bodhisattva’s difficult meditation?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds.

A bodhisattva has long practiced superior and wondrous meditative concentrations and has attained mastery over the mind in all samādhis; yet, out of compassion for sentient beings and desiring to bring them to maturity, he relinquishes the bliss of the first dhyāna and is born into the desire realm—this is called the bodhisattva’s first difficult meditation.

The Bodhisattva, relying on dhyāna, gives birth to immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable profound samādhis that surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the second difficult dhyāna.
When a bodhisattva attains unsurpassed enlightenment by relying on dhyāna, this is called the third difficult dhyāna.
What is the bodhisattva’s dhyāna of all gates?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds:
First, dhyāna with applied thought and sustained thought;
second, dhyāna accompanied by joy;
third, dhyāna accompanied by bliss.
Fourth is the dhyāna associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s dhyāna of virtuous persons?
Briefly stated, there are five kinds:
First, non-attachment;
second, being accompanied by loving-kindness;
third, being accompanied by compassion.
Fourth, accompanied by a mind of joy;
fifth, accompanied by a mind of equanimity.
What is the bodhisattva’s dhyāna of all-encompassing practice?
That is to say, there are six kinds and seven kinds; briefly stated, there are thirteen kinds:

wholesome dhyāna, indeterminate transformative dhyāna, dhyāna of the factors of tranquility and insight, dhyāna for the benefit of oneself and others, dhyāna of right mindfulness, dhyāna that produces the merit of supernormal powers; and those termed dhyāna of the object, dhyāna of the meaning of the object, dhyāna of the sign of tranquility, dhyāna of the sign of exertion, dhyāna of the sign of equanimity, and dhyāna of the ultimate truth of dwelling in happiness in the present life—these are called the thirteen kinds of bodhisattva dhyāna comprising all practices.
What is the bodhisattva’s meditation for removing affliction?
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds:

first, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they eliminate all suffering, calamities, toxic harms, frost, hail, feverish diseases, and demonic illnesses; this is called the meditation that serves as the basis for incantations.
Second, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, he is able to eliminate the various ailments arising from the four great elements; this is called the meditation for removing affliction.

Third, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, he brings forth sweet rain, capable of dispelling calamitous droughts and rescuing those suffering from famine; this is called the cloud-and-rain meditation.

Fourth, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they rescue all those in peril and fear, whether humans or non-humans, from all dangers on water or land; this is called the dhyāna of equal deliverance.

Fifth, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they are able to benefit sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst in the wilderness with food and drink; this is called the dhyāna of benefiting others.
Sixth, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they are able to subdue sentient beings through material gifts; this is called the dhyāna of subduing.

Seventh, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they awaken those who are deluded and intoxicated; they bring equal awakening to those who are lost throughout the ten directions; this is called the dhyāna of awakening.
Eighth, when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they cause all the undertakings of sentient beings to be fully accomplished; this is called "equanimous action dhyāna.
What is the bodhisattva’s "dhyāna for happiness in this world and other worlds"?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, the dhyāna that subdues sentient beings through the manifestation of supernormal powers;
second, the dhyāna that subdues sentient beings by manifesting in accordance with their speech.
Third is the dhyāna of manifesting instructions to discipline sentient beings;
fourth is the dhyāna of manifesting evil destinies for evil sentient beings;
fifth is the dhyāna of benefiting those who have lost their eloquence by providing them with eloquence.
Sixth is the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings who have lost mindfulness by means of mindfulness;
seventh is the dhyāna for the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide long in the world by composing non-erroneous treatises, subtle and exquisite hymns of praise, and *mātṛkā*s;

eighth is the dhyāna of various requisites such as writing, arithmetic, calculation, and methods for sustaining life, which benefit sentient beings by gathering them through the meaning of worldly arts and crafts.
Ninth is the dhyāna of emitting light that temporarily brings rest to the evil destinies.
What is the bodhisattva’s pure dhyāna?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds:
First, the dhyāna that is pure through worldly purity, being untainted by relish and undefiled;
second, the dhyāna that is pure through supramundane purity;
third, the dhyāna that is pure through the purity of skillful means.
Fourth is the pure dhyāna of fundamental purity;
fifth is the pure dhyāna of fundamental superior progress;
sixth is the pure dhyāna of the power of entering, abiding, and emerging.
Seventh is the pure meditation purified by the power of returning to relinquishment;
eighth is the pure meditation purified by the power of the activities of supernormal knowledges;
ninth is the pure meditation purified by being free from all views.
Tenth is the pure dhyāna that purifies through the severance of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations.
By means of such immeasurable dhyānas, the bodhisattva attains the fruit of great enlightenment; relying upon these, the bodhisattva has attained, and shall attain, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter 14: The Chapter on Wisdom (*Prajñā-varga*) from the Section on Skillful Means (*Upāya-sthāna*) in the Bodhisattva-bhūmi. What is the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, wisdom by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñā*).
Second is all-encompassing wisdom;
third is difficult-to-attain wisdom;
fourth is wisdom of all gateways.
Fifth, the wisdom of virtuous persons;
sixth, the wisdom of all practices;
seventh, the wisdom that eliminates affliction.
Eighth is the wisdom of happiness in this world and other worlds;
ninth is pure wisdom. What is the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva’s wisdom?

Entering the sphere of all that is to be known, and having entered it accordingly, one discriminates and contemplates the objects of the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) in accordance with the Dharma—namely, inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), logic (*hetu-vidyā*), grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), and the worldly arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*). This is called intrinsic wisdom (*svabhāva-prajñā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing wisdom?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, worldly; [second, supramundane].
The second is the supramundane.
Briefly stated, each of these two has three types:
first, the analytical discernment that accords with the realization of the reality of the knowable;

Second, skillfully encompassing the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and the three aggregates of dharma (*triskandha*); third, performing deeds that benefit sentient beings. The bodhisattva, through the ineffable and selfless dharma, awakens to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Having awakened, he fixes his mindfulness and dwells securely in the supreme state of *prajñā*, which is ultimate quiescence; he leaves behind all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), eliminates all falsehoods, and enters into the contemplation of the great universal characteristic (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of equality. He remains free from both affirmation and denial, entering the Middle Way. This is called the wisdom of discernment that accords with awakening (*anubodhavikalpanā-prajñā*).
He is skilled in the five fields of knowledge, as explained at length in the "Chapter on the Lineage of Powers.

Regarding the three categories (*tri-rāśi*): the category of teachings that provide benefit, the category of teachings that do not provide benefit, and the category of teachings that neither provide benefit nor fail to provide benefit.
These eight bases are well-sustained by prajñā; when the requisites for great, unsurpassed wisdom are fully perfected, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

There are eleven matters regarding the deeds performed for the benefit of sentient beings, as previously explained; in each of these instances, one tames sentient beings through wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
What is difficult wisdom?
Briefly stated, there are three kinds.
To know the profound dharma of non-self is called the first difficult wisdom.
The skillful means for taming sentient beings is called the second difficult wisdom.
To have no obstruction regarding all that is to be known is called the third wisdom of difficulty.
What is the wisdom of all gateways?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds.

It refers to the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from reflection regarding the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; the wisdom encompassed by the power of reflection that contemplates the deeds of a bodhisattva in accordance with the state of being free from all obstacles; and the immeasurable wisdom of the stage of right concentration encompassed by the power of cultivation.
What is the wisdom of a bodhisattva as a virtuous person?
Briefly stated, there are five kinds:
first, the wisdom of having heard the true Dharma;
Second, wisdom accompanied by internal right reflection;
third, wisdom accompanied by skillful means for the benefit of oneself and others;
fourth, decisive wisdom that is non-erroneous regarding the characteristics and the abiding nature of all phenomena.
Fifth is the wisdom that is free from afflictions.
This, in turn, has five aspects:
first, entering the sphere of objects according to their subtle nature.
Second, entering the sphere of reality in its entirety according to its nature;
third, the simultaneous arising of the original attainment of wisdom and all its requisites;
fourth, being able to receive and uphold all the meanings of the Dharma taught by the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and the Bodhisattvas of the great stages.
Fifth is the wisdom encompassed by the stages from the Ground of Pure Mind up to the Ultimate Ground.
What is the bodhisattva’s wisdom of all practices?
It consists of six kinds and seven kinds; briefly stated, there are thirteen kinds.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths, there are the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of ultimate exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising; these are called the six kinds.

The seven kinds are: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), knowledge of supernormal powers (abhijñājñāna), knowledge of marks (lakṣaṇajñāna), knowledge of the skillful means of the ten powers (daśabalopāyajñāna), and the knowledge of the fourfold accomplishment (catuḥpratisaraṇasaṃpannajñāna).
What is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that eliminates affliction?
Briefly stated, there are eight kinds:
first, knowing the sūtras and dharmas is called the unimpeded knowledge of dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Second is the unimpededness regarding meanings (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), because one knows the characteristics of phenomena;
third is the unimpededness regarding expressions (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because one knows the names of all phenomena;
fourth is the unimpededness regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), because one knows the various phrases and meanings of all phenomena.
Fifth, the wisdom that subdues all heterodox arguments;
sixth, the wisdom that establishes all correct doctrines;
seventh, the wisdom that is able to manage industries and increase wealth.
Eighth is the wisdom of skillfully knowing the king’s discernment and decision-making regarding worldly affairs.
What is the bodhisattva’s wisdom of happiness in this world and future worlds?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds.

He possesses well-purified established knowledge in the field of inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), and well-purified established knowledge in the fields of logic (*hetuvidyā*), grammar (*śabdavidyā*), medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and the worldly arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*).

Thus, relying upon the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) that are well-purified, the bodhisattva tames the ignorance, negligence, and indolence of sentient beings, causing them to correctly follow the sequence [of the teachings], and thereby manifesting, bestowing, illuminating, and gladdening them.
What is the pure wisdom of a bodhisattva?
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds.
There are two types of the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), up to the meaning of reality as the nature of things (*dharmatā-tattvārtha*).
There are two types of meanings for "appropriating the process of transmigration":
the causal factor and the result.
There are two types of meanings for "appropriating grasping":
There are two kinds of meanings regarding the skillful means of knowing reality as it is: that which is inverted and that which is non-inverted;
namely, all that should be done and all that should not be done.
There are two kinds of ultimate meaning known as they truly are:
defilement and purification.
One should know that among these five kinds and ten kinds of analytical pure wisdom, the first is the most purified.
In this way, the bodhisattva, through well-determined unsurpassed wisdom, attains the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
By relying upon this, the bodhisattva fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, these six pāramitās have been explained by the World-Honored One in various sūtras; I shall now provide a brief exposition, which should be understood as follows.

Within the Tathāgata’s sūtras, the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā are explained as being subsumed under their respective categories, from the dānapāramitā of intrinsic nature up to the dānapāramitā of purity, according to what is appropriate. Likewise, they should be understood as being subsumed under the śīlapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā, according to what is appropriate.

When the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, he engaged in ascetic practices throughout immeasurable lifetimes; it should be understood that he was engaged in all the *dānapāramitās*, up to and including engagement with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Either it subsumes one, or two, or three, or four, or five, or all six pāramitās.

One should know that these six pāramitās give rise to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they are the great, pure Dharma and the great, pure ocean of the bodhisattva, and the most precious jewel that serves as the cause for all kinds of the true Dharma for all sentient beings.
Thus, through these immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom, one attains the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is without remainder and unsurpassed.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, Fascicle Six.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, Fascicle Seven.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty. Chapter Fifteen:

The Four Means of Integration (*Catur-saṃgraha-vastu*). Section on Skillful Means (*Upāya-kauśalya*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya-viniścaya*. Chapter Fifteen: The Four Means of Integration. What is the bodhisattva’s pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*)?
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds:
first, speech of endearment by its own nature;
second, all-encompassing speech of endearment.
Third, difficult loving speech;
fourth, all-encompassing loving speech;
fifth, the loving speech of virtuous persons.
Sixth, speech of loving-kindness regarding all conditioned phenomena;
seventh, speech of loving-kindness that removes affliction;
eighth, speech of loving-kindness that brings happiness in this world and the next.
