Beyond the realm of verbal expression, all phenomena are equal through wisdom that is free from all conceptual constructions.
This wisdom—whether its basis, object, companion, activity, or equipment, as well as its fruit—these seven aspects are designated as the Mahāyāna.
In the past, future, and present, all bodhisattvas have correctly established, are establishing, and will establish all four kinds [of practices] without exception and in an unsurpassed manner.
Bodhisattvas possess five kinds of immeasurables that give rise to all skillful means of practice.
First, the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable;
second, the realm of worlds is immeasurable;
third, the realm of phenomena is immeasurable.
Fourth is the immeasurability of the realm of those to be disciplined;
fifth is the immeasurability of the skillful means for disciplining them.
The sixty-one types of sentient beings are termed the "sentient-being realm"; according to their mental dispositions, stages, and bodies, when analyzed, they are immeasurable.
In the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable names; for example, as this Sahā world is named "Sahā," its lord is named "Sahāpati.
Furthermore, regarding wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, when analyzed, they are found to be immeasurable.
There is one kind of subduing, namely, the subduing of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
those who are bound by all fetters and those who are not bound by all fetters.
Furthermore, there are three types:
those of weak, middling, and superior faculties.
Furthermore, there are four types:
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and discursive thought.
Furthermore, there are six kinds:
householders, renunciants, those who are immature, those who are mature, those who are not yet liberated, and those who are already liberated.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:

Whether it be evil persons, mediocre persons, those of small wisdom, or those of great wisdom; those to be tamed in the present, those to be tamed in the future, or those to be tamed according to conditions—if such conditions are obtained, one should dedicate [the merit] accordingly.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds:
namely, the eight classes from the Kṣatriyas down to the Brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds:
First, the discipline of the Tathāgata;
second, the discipline of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
third, the discipline of the bodhisattvas.
Fourth, those difficult to subdue;
fifth, those easy to subdue;
sixth, those subdued through gentle speech.
Seventh is subduing through reprimand;
eighth is subduing from afar;
ninth is subduing from nearby.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds:
first, the hells; second, animals;... [and so forth].
Third, hungry ghosts;
fourth, humans and devas of the desire realm;
fifth, those in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Sixth, form; seventh, formlessness;
eighth, perception;
Ninth is the realm of non-perception;
tenth is the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These fifty-five types, when further differentiated, become immeasurable.
What is the difference between the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) and the realm of those to be disciplined (*vinayadhātu*)?
The realm of sentient beings refers to the state where the various lineages (*gotra*) of all sentient beings are not differentiated.

The realm of those to be disciplined refers to the fact that within those very lineages, there are immeasurable skillful means for disciplining them as they manifest in various ways; this is as explained previously in the "Chapter on Maturation" (*paripākapaṭala*), where it is also analyzed in immeasurable ways.
Thus, the five kinds of immeasurables are explained in succession. Why is this?
Because these bodhisattvas practice for the sake of sentient beings, the first immeasurable is therefore taught.
Sentient beings can be found there; therefore, the second immeasurable is taught.
Sentient beings can find the dharmas of affliction and purification in various worlds; therefore, the third immeasurable is taught.
Observing each and every sentient being according to their capacity to be liberated from suffering, one therefore speaks of the fourth immeasurable.
Continuing until one employs skillful means to liberate sentient beings from suffering, one therefore speaks of the fifth immeasurable.
Therefore, it is said that the five kinds of immeasurables give rise to all the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva has four seekings, through which they know all phenomena as they truly are.
First is seeking by name;
second is seeking by object;
third is seeking by the designation of intrinsic nature.
Fourth is the seeking through the designation of distinctions, as explained previously in the "Chapter on Reality.
There are four matters by which a bodhisattva knows all phenomena as they truly are:

knowing as it truly is by seeking according to names; knowing as it truly is by seeking according to things; knowing as it truly is by seeking according to the designation of intrinsic nature; and knowing as it truly is by seeking according to the designation of distinctions, as explained previously in the "Chapter on Reality."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have five ways of preaching the Dharma for sentient beings that result in great fruits and benefits:
first, they preach the Dharma for sentient beings so that they give rise to the stainless Dharma-eye;
second, they preach the Dharma for sentient beings so that they attain the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava).
Third, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings and generating the unsurpassed bodhicitta;
fourth, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings and attaining the foremost bodhisattva-acceptance (kṣānti);
fifth, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings so that, upon hearing it, they receive and recite it, fully practicing and cultivating it to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.
These are called the five kinds of preaching the Dharma that yield great fruits and benefits.
What is meant by "Mahāyāna"?
It is called Mahāyāna because it possesses seven kinds of greatness.
First is the greatness of the Dharma, which refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures; among these, the Bodhisattva Vaipulya Pitaka is the most supreme and greatest.
Second is the greatness of the mind, which refers to the arousal of the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Third is the greatness of understanding, which refers to the understanding of the Bodhisattva’s Vaipulya-piṭaka.
Fourth is the greatness of the pure mind, which refers to transcending the stage of practice through understanding and entering the stage of the pure mind.
Fifth is the greatness of the accumulations, which refers to attaining unsurpassed bodhi through the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom.
Sixth is greatness of time, meaning that one attains unsurpassed bodhi after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Seventh is greatness of attainment, meaning that one attains the body of unsurpassed bodhi, which has no equal, let alone anything superior to it.

Those dharmas are great, the mind is great, the understanding is great, the pure mind is great, the requisites are great, and the time is great; these six greatnesses are called the cause, while the attainment of greatness is called the fruit.

Bodhisattvas possess eight dharmas that encompass all that is taught in the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka. These are: faith in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; revealing the true meaning of all phenomena; revealing the inconceivable, supreme, and wondrous spiritual powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; attaining the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of reflection through contemplation; attaining purity of mind through the skillful means of the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of reflection; entering the practice of the wisdom of cultivation through the skillful means of purity of mind; attaining the fruit of the wisdom of cultivation through the skillful means of entering the practice of the wisdom of cultivation; and the ultimate transcendence resulting from the attainment of such fruits of the wisdom of cultivation. By training in this way, a bodhisattva attains unsurpassed enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they attain unsurpassed enlightenment; briefly stated, there are ten aspects:
first, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
second, the entry (*avatāra*).
Third, the unpurified;
fourth, the purified;
fifth, the unripened.
Sixth, the matured;
seventh, the undetermined;
eighth, the determined.
Ninth is one who has only one more birth;
tenth is one in their final body.
"Spiritual lineage" (gotra) refers to one who has not yet attained the pure mind.
To resolve to cultivate and study is called "entry.
To have entered but not yet attained the Stage of Pure Mind is called "impure";
to have entered the Stage of Pure Mind is called "pure."
Regarding "purity": that which has not yet entered the stage of ultimate reality is called "immature";

that which has entered the stage of ultimate reality is called "mature. Regarding "maturity": that which has not yet entered the stage of meditative concentration is called "unconcentrated"; [that which has entered it is called "concentrated"].
Having entered the stages of meditative concentration is called "concentration.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of ripening:
first, ripening in a single lifetime, whereby one sequentially attains unsurpassed bodhi; [the second is ripening over successive lifetimes].
The second is the final body, which is attained in this very life.

Thus, from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) up to the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment in the final body, these ten types of training are what the bodhisattva studies; beyond these, there is nothing further to be studied.
When a bodhisattva trains exactly as they have been taught, there is no further training for a bodhisattva beyond that.

When a bodhisattva trains exactly as they have been taught, they attain the names of all virtues, namely: Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Unsurpassed Hero, Son of the Buddha, Sustained by the Buddha, Great Teacher, Great Sage, Great Caravan Leader, Great Renown, Great Virtue, and Great Sovereignty.

Thus, throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas and immeasurable causes and conditions, all of which are established through their own conceptual designations.

You should know that if anyone says, "I am a bodhisattva," yet does not skillfully train in what a bodhisattva should learn, you should know that this is a bodhisattva in name only, not a true bodhisattva.
If one says, "I am a bodhisattva who has well studied what is to be studied by a bodhisattva," one should know that such a person is a true bodhisattva.

Chapter One: The Characteristics of Bodhisattvas, Section Two: The Stage of Bodhisattva Practices (*Bodhisattvabhūmi*), Sub-section: The Skillful Means of the Successive Dharmas. In the first part of this section, there are four chapters. A bodhisattva who accomplishes five kinds of true characteristics attains entry into the ranks of the bodhisattvas.
First, compassion;
second, kind speech; third, valor.
Fourth is generous giving;
fifth is expounding the profound meaning of the Dharma.
Regarding these five characteristics, each is analyzed into five aspects:
First, intrinsic nature;
second, objective sphere;
third, retribution.
Fourth is the sequence;
fifth is the inclusion.
There are two kinds of the nature of compassion:
The first is sincerity;
the second is fulfillment.
Sincerity means a settled mind and a joyful mind.
Regarding "endowment," it means that a bodhisattva, with a sincere heart toward all sentient beings, benefits them through body and speech according to their capacity and according to their strength.
Regarding the nature of "loving speech," it consists of first speaking words of consolation, as explained previously in the Chapter on Gathering [Disciples].
The nature of valor is to possess firm resolve and great strength toward all sentient beings.
The nature of generosity is sublime giving and giving free from afflictions.
Regarding the explanation of the self-nature of the profound meaning of the Dharma, it is the wisdom of correct skillful means that arises from the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
There are five types of objects of compassion:
first, sentient beings who undergo suffering;
Second, sentient beings of evil conduct;
third, sentient beings who are heedless;
fourth, sentient beings who have entered wrong paths.
Fifth, there are sentient beings driven by afflictions.
From the hells up to all forms of continuous suffering experience, this is called "suffering.

Although they do not currently experience suffering, they extensively engage in unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind—namely, the twelve types of non-restraint—which is called "unwholesome conduct."

Although one does not undergo suffering and does not commit various evil deeds, yet delights in and is attached to the five desires, singing, dancing, and merriment—this is called negligence (*pramāda*).

Although one does not undergo suffering and does not commit various evil deeds, yet delights in and is attached to the five desires, seeking liberation from suffering by relying on wrong views—this is called a wrong course (*mithyā-gati*).

Having renounced the five desires and gone forth into the Dharma, one does not undergo various sufferings, even those of the evil destinies; yet, whether afflictions are fully present or absent, this is called right application.
Ordinary worldlings and those in training are said to be "impelled by afflictions.
Regarding this state, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion that is unsurpassed and leaves nothing remaining.
There are five kinds of the sphere of loving speech (*priyavāda*):
first, speech that is correct and true;
second, speech that is correct and joyful; [and so forth].
Third, speech that is truly beneficial;
fourth, speech that is in accordance with the Dharma;
fifth, speech that teaches the Dharma through skillful means, as explained previously in the "Chapter on Gathering."
Regarding this sphere of activity, the Bodhisattva’s mind gives rise to loving speech that is unsurpassed and leaves nothing remaining.
There are five kinds of courageous spheres of activity, as previously explained in the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakṣa).
Regarding this sphere of activity, the bodhisattva gives rise to a courageous mind that is unsurpassed and leaves nothing remaining.
There are five kinds of spheres for giving:
first, giving without discrimination; [and so forth].
Second is giving with joy;
third is immediate giving;
fourth is unstained giving.
Fifth is the gift without dependence, as explained previously in the Chapter on Giving.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this sphere, the mind of generosity gives rise to that which is without remainder and unsurpassed.
There are five kinds of spheres regarding the profound meaning of the Dharma:
First, regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, they accord with profound emptiness and dependent origination.
Second, regarding the various codes of discipline, one thoroughly understands what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the methods for emerging from an offense.
Third, establishing the characteristics of phenomena without inversion within the Mātṛkā-piṭaka;
fourth, conceptualizing and discriminating the profound meaning of the Dharma;
fifth, variously discriminating the diverse terminology regarding the phenomena and meanings of all dharmas.
Regarding this sphere, the bodhisattva teaches the profound meaning of the Dharma, giving rise to a mind that is unsurpassed and free from remainder.

Out of compassion for all sentient beings, the bodhisattva cultivates a mind of loving-kindness; they never tire of employing skillful means to benefit and cherish them, dwelling extensively in faultless happiness in the present life to attract and gather sentient beings.
As the Blessed One has said, through the benefit of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one’s body is never harmed by weapons, staves, and the like.
This should be explained in detail herein; it is called the fruit of compassion (*anukampā*).
The bodhisattva’s pleasant speech (priyavāditā) involves, in the present life, abstaining from the four faults of speech:
divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech.

By means of this pleasant speech, he gathers himself and others; in future lives, he achieves right speech (samyagvāc), and his words are always trusted and accepted—this is called the fruit of pleasant speech.

The Bodhisattva is courageous; in this present life, he is free from all indolence and his mind is always joyful. He upholds the Bodhisattva’s vows of discipline without violating or transgressing them, and with a mind of forbearance, he embraces both himself and others. He is able to practice and learn all that is to be done by a Bodhisattva in future lives, and having learned it, he remains steadfast. This is called the fruit of courage.

The fruits of a bodhisattva’s generosity and their exposition of the profound meaning of the Dharma are as explained previously in the *Bala-paṭala*, the *Dāna-pāramitā*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*; these are called the fruits of generosity and the exposition of the profound meaning of the Dharma.

Regarding the sequence: first, the bodhisattva cultivates compassion to gather in sentient beings; in order to cause them to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states, he provides complete instruction and guidance. For this reason, affectionate speech is explained next.
Sentient beings create various evils and are capable of never ceasing their manifold afflictions; for this reason, vigor is explained next.

Furthermore, some sentient beings are gathered through material wealth, some are gathered through the Dharma, and some are gathered by both; for this reason, generosity is explained next, followed by the profound meaning of the Dharma.

There are five aspects by which a bodhisattva encompasses the six pāramitās. By what characteristics are these six pāramitās encompassed? The aspect of compassion (anukampā) encompasses the dhyāna-pāramitā;

the aspect of kind speech (priyavāditā) encompasses the śīla-pāramitā and the prajñā-pāramitā; the aspect of valor (parākrama) encompasses the kṣānti-pāramitā, the vīrya-pāramitā, and the prajñā-pāramitā; the aspect of generous giving (dāna) encompasses the dāna-pāramitā; and the aspect of explaining the profound meaning of the Dharma encompasses the dhyāna-pāramitā and the prajñā-pāramitā.
These are called the five aspects and five types of discrimination of a bodhisattva.

Chapter Two: The Wings (*pakṣa*). In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Skillful Means of the Subsequent Dharmas, this is the second chapter, the Wings. There are four dharmas that constitute the wings for both lay and ordained bodhisattvas; by training in these, a bodhisattva swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
First, the excellent cultivation of karma;
second, skillful means;
third, the gathering of sentient beings.
Fourth is dedication.
What is the skillful cultivation of karma?
A bodhisattva cultivates the six pāramitās with determination, with single-mindedness, constantly, and without fault.
What is the definitive cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)?
It is when this bodhisattva, toward those who come seeking, must give regardless of whether they are beneficial or harmful, or whether they possess virtue or faults.
Regarding all acts of giving, the mind remains unshakable, such that it cannot be disturbed by humans or non-humans, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or those who follow similar worldly paths.
How does one cultivate this with single-minded devotion?
This bodhisattva, toward those who come seeking, gives away all internal and external things without any stinginess.
How does he constantly practice?
This bodhisattva never tires of giving; at all times, with equanimity, he gives whatever he obtains.
What is faultless cultivation?
It is the giving free from afflictions as explained in the Chapter on Giving.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful cultivation of the dānapāramitā.
As it is with generosity, so it is with ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they should be understood accordingly as appropriate to each case.
What is skillful means?

Briefly stated, there are ten kinds: the skillful means for removing affliction and harm for sentient beings who destroy the Dharma; the skillful means for causing those dwelling in the middle way to enter [the path], for maturing those who have entered, and for liberating those who have been matured; the skillful means of worldly discourse; the skillful means of observing whether the Bodhisattva precepts are maintained or violated; the skillful means of right aspiration; the skillful means of the Śrāvaka vehicle; the skillful means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and the skillful means of the Mahāyāna.
All such skillful means should be understood according to their respective distinctions within the various bodhisattva stages.
These ten skillful means serve five purposes:
the first four skillful means are for the benefit of sentient beings.
Skillful means in worldly discourse are for the purpose of subduing opposing arguments.

Skillful means in observing whether one upholds or violates the bodhisattva precepts are for the purpose of ensuring that no transgressions arise, and for causing those who have already committed transgressions to repent according to the Dharma, thereby maintaining pure ethical discipline.
Through skillful means of right aspiration, the bodhisattva obtains everything they desire in all future lives.
Through skillful means of the three vehicles, the bodhisattva provides complete and compliant teaching according to the dispositions, faculties, understandings, and metaphors of beings.
These ten kinds of skillful means serve five purposes.
These five purposes fully encompass all that is to be done, providing the skillful means for benefit in both the present life and future lives.
How does a bodhisattva gather in sentient beings?
This bodhisattva relies upon the four means of attraction:
generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

There may be sentient beings whom one benefits with peace, benefits with happiness, or benefits with both peace and happiness, as explained at length previously in the "Chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others."
What is the dedication of a bodhisattva?
A bodhisattva cultivates roots of goodness through three gateways: namely, skillful means in the cultivation of virtuous actions;
and the gathering of sentient beings.

With a consistently pure mind regarding all things of the past, future, and present, they dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, not seeking any other karmic retribution for their roots of goodness.

If the Blessed One were to speak of the dharmas to be studied by lay and ordained bodhisattvas, one should know that all of them are comprised within the four dharmas of skillful means in the thorough cultivation of practice, gathering, and dedication.
One should know that a Bodhisattva who skillfully cultivates their practice through expedient means, who gathers and accumulates [merit], and who dedicates it, is close to the seat of enlightenment.

For all Bodhisattvas—whether householders or renunciants—in the past, future, and present, who have studied, will study, or are now studying for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these four dharmas are exhaustive and unsurpassed.
These four dharmas are accomplished by both lay and ordained bodhisattvas; however, there is a great distinction between the ordained and the lay.
The ordained bodhisattva is liberated from the attachments to parents, wife, children, relatives, and so forth.
The renunciant bodhisattva is liberated from the sufferings of agriculture, commerce, and royal service.

The renunciant bodhisattva, fully cultivating the holy life and all factors conducive to enlightenment, swiftly attains supernormal powers; if they cultivate wholesome dharmas, they swiftly attain the ultimate goal.
Whatever Dharma the renunciant bodhisattva preaches is received with faith by others.
This is called the great distinction between the householder and the renunciant.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.

Chapter 3: Purification of the Mind. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Skillful Means for Sustaining the Dharma, this is the third chapter, "Purification of the Mind. Regarding all sentient beings, a bodhisattva possesses seven kinds of compassion, which is called the foremost reality.
First, fearlessness;
second, skillful means;
third, lack of weariness.
Fourth is non-seeking;
fifth is non-covetousness;
sixth is vastness.
Seventh is equanimity.

A bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of compassion toward sentient beings out of fear; rather, they cultivate the actions of body, speech, and mind to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings—this is called fearlessness.

When a bodhisattva, through skillful means and wisdom, gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings and does not teach what is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, or contrary to the ultimate truth, nor at an improper time, this is called skillful means.
That a bodhisattva, regarding all sentient beings, never grows weary or fatigued in the use of any skillful means is called "non-weariness.
That a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings and seeks nothing out of fear is called "non-seeking."
When a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings and does not seek any reward for their kindness, this is called non-attachment.

When a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings without limitation, neither abandoning nor neglecting whatever benefit or harm they may receive from those beings, this is called vastness.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, equalizing the realm of sentient beings without any spatial or temporal limitation, this is called equanimity.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these seven kinds of compassion, it is called the first reality.
When a bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha and attains a definitive understanding, this is called the pure mind (*śuddhacitta*).
Briefly stated, there are fifteen kinds:
first, the unsurpassed mind; [and so forth].
Second is the mind of ethical discipline;
third is the mind of the perfections;
fourth is the mind of ultimate reality.
Fifth is the mind of supernormal power;
sixth is the settled mind;
seventh is the joyful mind.
Eighth, the mind of liberation;
ninth, the firm mind;
tenth, the non-empty mind.
Eleventh, the impure mind;
twelfth, the pure mind;
thirteenth, the thoroughly pure mind.
Fourteenth is the mind of subduing;
fifteenth is the co-emergent mind.
A pure mind that is single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels is called unsurpassed.
To purify the mind by receiving the Bodhisattva precepts is called "precept" (śīla).
To purify the mind through the practice of generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is called "perfection" (pāramitā).

The selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, and the mind of profound purity regarding the ultimate truth of the selflessness of both persons and phenomena—this is called the "True Meaning.
The inconceivable supernormal powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, together with the innate power of the pure mind—this is called "Supernatural Power."
To desire to benefit all sentient beings with wholesome dharmas is called peace (*kṣema*).
To desire to benefit all sentient beings through gathering them [into the fold] is called bliss (*sukha*).
To be free from craving for sentient beings and from the retribution of their experiences is called liberation.
To have a mind that is firm and steadfast toward unsurpassed bodhi is called steadfastness.
The skillful means for benefiting sentient beings and the skillful means for awakening them, together with non-perverted wisdom and liberation—this is called "not in vain.
The mind of a Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through understanding is called "impure."
The bodhisattva mind from the Stage of the Pure Ground up to the Stage of Definitive Practice is called "pure.
The bodhisattva mind of the Ultimate Ground is called "thoroughly pure."
That impure mind is called "subdued.
The pure mind and the thoroughly purified mind that engages in contemplation are called "co-emergent.
Because its nature is inherently real and both body and mind are pure, it is therefore called "co-emergent."
These are called the fifteen pure minds.
These fifteen pure minds, according to all stages, are briefly explained as ten matters.
The unsurpassed mind consists of purely cultivating the three jewels, practicing all modes of conduct, cultivating all requisites for enlightenment, and attaining the foremost reality.

The mind of ethical discipline (*śīla-citta*) means that one receives the Bodhisattva precepts and never violates them even at the cost of one's life; should a violation occur, one is immediately able to eliminate it.
The mind of the perfections (*pāramitā-citta*) means that one constantly and diligently cultivates all dharmas of the roots of goodness, abiding in heedfulness.
The mind of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha-citta*) is the unstained mind that, for the sake of sentient beings, undergoes birth and death without abandoning the pure mind of liberation and nirvāṇa.

The mind of supernormal power (*ṛddhi-citta*) consists of awakening through profound and pure faith, as well as cultivating the mental impressions of birth and death, dwelling frequently in hearing and reflection, and knowing the measure of contentment.
A mind of peace, a mind of joy, and a mind of liberation; benefiting sentient beings in every way without weariness.
A firm and steadfast mind, characterized by fervent diligence and vast diligence, employing impartial skillful means, unflagging skillful means, and uninterrupted skillful means.
With an undistracted mind, one swiftly attains various supernormal powers and wholesome dharmas; one does not give rise to a sense of complacency through a limited or inferior mind.
One tames the mind and gives rise to a mind that is co-arisen [with wisdom].
With an innate mind, one swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all devas and people of the world.
One tames the mind and gathers in the impure mind.
The innate mind comprises the pure mind and the thoroughly pure mind.
If the Blessed One speaks of the bodhisattva’s pure mind, everything designated and revealed therein is entirely subsumed within these fifteen types of pure mind.

All bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who have attained, will attain, or are now attaining unsurpassed awakening do so entirely through these fifteen pure minds, which are exhaustive and unsurpassed.
These fifteen pure minds yield great fruits and benefits; by relying upon them, one attains unsurpassed bodhi.

Chapter Four: The Stage of Abiding (*Vihāra*). Following the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya-viniścaya*, in this "Chapter on Abiding," the fourth, the characteristics of a bodhisattva, the wings of a bodhisattva, and the pure minds of a bodhisattva—having already been explained from the bodhisattva lineage up to what a bodhisattva should study—I shall now briefly explain them.
The twelve abodes of a bodhisattva encompass all abodes and all bodhisattva practices; the thirteenth is the Tathāgata-abode, the unsurpassed abode.
What are the twelve abodes of a bodhisattva?
First, the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage;
second, the stage of abiding in practice through understanding;
third, the stage of abiding in joy.
Fourth is the stage of superior ethical discipline;
fifth is the stage of superior intention;
sixth is the stage of superior wisdom.
The dwelling in superior wisdom has three types:
first, that which is associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment;
second, that which is associated with the truths.
Third is the correspondence with dependent origination and arising-and-ceasing.

It is the Bodhisattva’s true contemplation and true wisdom, namely, knowing sentient beings, the arising of suffering, and the cessation of suffering; therefore, the Bodhisattva abides in three gates, three kinds of wisdom, and three modes of dwelling.
Ninth is the signless dwelling with practice and development;
tenth is the signless dwelling without practice or development;
eleventh is the unimpeded dwelling.
The twelfth is the supreme bodhisattva stage (*parama-bodhisattvavihāra*).
These twelve stages encompass all stages and all bodhisattva practices.
As for the Tathāgata stage, it transcends all bodhisattva stages.
The *asaṃbuddha* dwells in the dwelling of a Tathāgata; this will be explained extensively in the subsequent chapter on "Establishment.
Now, the twelve dwellings established by Bodhisattvas shall be explained.
What is the dwelling of the spiritual lineage (*gotrasthiti*)?
This bodhisattva is by nature inherently virtuous and naturally capable of practicing meritorious and wholesome dharmas.
Because of this inherent virtue, through spontaneous skillful means, various wholesome dharmas arise without depending on deliberate reflection before they can be attained.
The bodhisattva of the lineage (*gotra*) is the seed of all Buddha-dharmas; these seeds of all Buddha-dharmas reside within his body, free from coarse afflictions (*kleśa*).

Although a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of the lineage may give rise to the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of superior afflictions, he is ultimately incapable of committing the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*) or severing the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*).
The meaning of *gotra* (spiritual lineage) is as explained in the "Chapter on Lineage"; this is called the stage of abiding in the lineage (*gotravihāra*).
What is the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryāvihāra*)?

It refers to the initial generation of the mind by a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the stage of pure mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*); all the practices possessed by such a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the pure mind are called the stage of practice through understanding.

For a bodhisattva abiding in the lineage, regarding the other bodhisattva abidings and the Tathāgata abiding, they constitute causes for arising and causes for inclusion, but are not skillful means; they are neither attainment nor purification, let alone the Tathāgata abiding.

For a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through understanding, [the stages] of other bodhisattvas and the stage of the Tathāgata are merely skillful means; they are neither attained nor purified, but represent only the attainment of practice through understanding and the orientation toward purification.

The Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) purifies the stage of joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), attaining its preliminary preparations (pūrvaprayoga) and its pure orientation (viśuddhy-ābhimukha).
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of joy purifies the stage of superior ethical discipline (adhiśīla-bhūmi), attaining its preliminary preparations and its pure orientation.
Thus it is explained in detail, up to the point that one should know the supreme bodhisattva dwelling (*bodhisattvavihāra*) in this way.

The supreme bodhisattva dwelling is the gradual purification of the preliminary means (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the Tathāgata dwelling; the Tathāgata dwelling is attained instantaneously and is completely purified. This constitutes the distinction between the bodhisattva dwelling and the Tathāgata dwelling.
What is the Stage of Joy?
The Bodhisattva’s dwelling in a purified mind is called the Stage of Joy.
What is the Stage of Higher Ethics?
The bodhisattva dwells, fully endowed with the morality of the pure mind-nature.
What is the dwelling of the superior intention?
The bodhisattva dwells, based on the purity of superior morality, in worldly dhyāna, samādhi, and meditative attainment (samāpatti).
What is the dwelling in wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment?

It is the dwelling in the observation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, by means of a bodhisattva’s realization of the ultimate truth through the samādhi of true reality and conventional pure knowledge.
What is the dwelling in wisdom associated with the truths?
It is the dwelling in wisdom that observes the true truths by means of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
What is the dwelling in wisdom associated with the arising and ceasing of dependent origination?

Once the Bodhisattva has taken the awakening to ultimate truth as the predominant factor, they observe the abiding nature [of phenomena], wherein suffering arises due to causes and conditions and suffering ceases due to causes and conditions.
What is the signless abiding that involves active practice and development?

When a bodhisattva has made the three types of higher wisdom their supremacy, they practice with cultivation and development, uninterrupted and without interval; they abide together with the wisdom of cultivation, which is the suchness of all phenomena, free from all deluded conceptualizations.
What is the dwelling in signlessness that is without effort, without cultivation, and without development?
It is this very dwelling in signlessness, which, through frequent and intense cultivation without interruption, increases continuously as a dwelling in accordance with the path.
What is unimpeded dwelling?

It is when a bodhisattva, relying on the samādhi of swift, pure, and immovable wisdom, dwells in the analytical observation of the meanings, phrases, and expressions of the vast and extensive discourses spoken by the Buddha.
What is the supreme dwelling of a bodhisattva?
It is when a bodhisattva dwells in the ultimate bodhisattva path, attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and receives the great dharma consecration (*mahā-dharma-abhiṣeka*) in a single continuous life.
If one in their final body dwells in this stage, they will successively attain unsurpassed enlightenment and abide in the performance of all Buddha-activities.

A Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through understanding cultivates minor practices, practices of severance, and indeterminate practices; what they have attained may still involve regression.

From the stage of Abiding in Joy up to the three stages of Abiding in Wisdom, the Bodhisattva practices extensive conduct, uninterrupted conduct, and resolute conduct, thereby attaining non-retrogression.

The bodhisattva who possesses practice and development, abiding in the signless up to the supreme bodhisattva stage, cultivates immeasurable practices, uninterrupted practices, and definitive practices, thereby attaining non-retrogression.
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of practice through understanding cultivate skillful means without signs;
bodhisattvas from the stage of joy up to the stage of superior wisdom attain cultivation without signs;
and bodhisattvas in the first and second stages of signlessness purify cultivation without signs.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the Unimpeded Abode and the Supreme Abode has the fruit of the cultivation of signlessness as their practice.
When a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Stage of Practice through Understanding practices that stage of understanding and conduct, what are its characteristics?

When a Bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) practices the conduct of understanding, they employ the power of reflection to cultivate the skillful means of a Bodhisattva’s activities. However, these cannot yet be inherently true, firm, and irreversible; they do not attain the Bodhisattva’s non-retrogressive cultivation as it truly is. Likewise, they do not yet attain the various fruits of such cultivation—the unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, they have not yet left behind the five fears, namely: the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of the evil realms, and the fear of the great assembly.

While contemplating and practicing for the benefit of sentient beings, they are unable to feel natural compassion; at times they give rise to wrong actions of body, speech, and mind, sometimes becoming attached to the objects of the five desires, and at other times being stingy and begrudging all their possessions.

Due to generating pure faith in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one cannot spontaneously give rise to true wisdom—namely, regarding the true meaning of the merits of the Triple Gem, the supernormal powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whether cause or fruit, whether the meaning of attainment or the means of attainment, or the objective realm. Having heard little and reflected little, their accomplishment of wisdom cannot be immeasurable; at times they forget the path of the Bodhisattva’s gradual and difficult progress, and are unable to practice with single-minded diligence the blazing expedient means for Great Bodhi or take deep delight in pure faith.

Regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—whether pleasant or unpleasant—one may experience them with inverted perception; thus, between two lifetimes, one may at times receive, recite, uphold the Dharma, and practice it for a long time through repeated cultivation.

Regarding these three matters, they lose right mindfulness; at times, though they may be wise enough to receive and uphold the True Dharma and skillfully understand its meaning, at other times they do not understand or do not know how to properly apply it for self-discipline; or again, not knowing how the Buddha-dharma arises within themselves, they preach, instruct, and admonish according to their own whims. Because they act according to their whims, they do not know things as they truly are.
At times they speak falsely, like shooting arrows in the dark—sometimes hitting the mark and sometimes missing it.

At times they abandon the mind of great awakening (*bodhicitta*); at times they receive the bodhisattva precepts and then again violate them; at times they are able to employ skillful means (*upāya*) to benefit sentient beings, yet at times they become weary and disheartened. For this reason, they regress from skillful means and take pleasure in their own comfort, though at other times they contemplate and recognize the joy of sentient beings.

They may be deficient and unable to sever [afflictions], or they may sever them only to fall back into deficiency again and again; at times they may be able to expound the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, yet at other times, upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma, they give rise to fear, agitation, and doubt.
They are devoid of great compassion for all sentient beings; they are able to bring about only slight peace and happiness, but not on a vast scale.

They are unable to train as a bodhisattva should train as described above, nor can they fulfill the marks of a bodhisattva, the wings of a bodhisattva, or the purity of a bodhisattva’s mind. They remain far removed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they cannot purify their minds through a deep delight in *nirvāṇa*, abandon the roots of goodness that are unshakable within *saṃsāra*, and they fail to accomplish any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Such as these are called the characteristics of the bodhisattva practice in the stage of the abode of conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
When the bodhisattva in the abode of conduct through understanding practices at the level of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), the aforementioned characteristics of practice increase.

While practicing middle patience, one is at the middle stage; while practicing superior patience, one is at the lower stage. Thus, while practicing superior patience, one abandons these modes of activity and enters the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-vihāra) in succession. Through skillful means, one attains the Stage of Joy, wherein all phenomena no longer have any further abiding.

The stage of the pure mind (*śuddhacitta-vihāra*) is defined as the accomplishment of all non-defiled factors that are contrary to those taught in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).

While the bodhisattva in the stage of practice through understanding possesses weak, medium, and superior skillful means, resulting in progressively purer liberation, this is not yet the stainless purity [of the pure mind stage].
Why is this? Because that liberation arises from the presence of various afflictions as upper fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
For a Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of Joy (*pramuditā*), liberation arises through the severing and abandoning of afflictions as upper fetters, resulting in pure liberation.
What are the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s stage of Joyful Abiding?

This bodhisattva, having entered the stage of Joyful Abiding from the stage of Abiding in Practice through Understanding, has previously well entered the vow for unsurpassed enlightenment and has well entered the cultivation of certainty regarding the skillful means for enlightenment.
There are six kinds of certainty:
first, being able to personally cultivate and give rise to the vow for enlightenment, which transcends all other pure vows;
second, possessing an incomparable and unshared fruit, which transcends all other worldly realms.
Third, he accords with the deliverance from the suffering of all sentient beings, which is not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Fourth, upon generating a single thought of aspiration, his nature spontaneously delights in immeasurable pure dharmas and tireless practice.
Fifth, they attain inexhaustible vows and never regress.
Sixth, they increase their superior qualities and ultimately realize great bodhi; this is called the true vow.
A Bodhisattva with true vows has four matters:
First, what kind of person generates the resolve?
Second, with what as its object does one generate the resolve?
Third, what are the characteristics of generating the resolve?
Fourth, what are the benefits and merits of generating the mind?

A bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of practice through understanding cultivates all kinds of roots of goodness and generates the mind by giving rise to the correct practice for enlightenment; this is called, in brief, the generation of the mind by a person.

To resolve to swiftly fulfill all the requisites for enlightenment in future lives, to fulfill the bodhisattva’s work of benefiting sentient beings, to fulfill all practices for unsurpassed enlightenment, and to fulfill all buddha-activities—this is called, in brief, the causal arousal of the mind.

When a bodhisattva resolves their mind, they swiftly fulfill all the requisites for enlightenment, the bodhisattva’s activities for benefiting sentient beings, all practices for unsurpassed enlightenment, and all buddha-deeds; transcending the stage of ordinary beings, they enter the rank of bodhisattvas and are born into the family of the Tathāgata, becoming known as a son of the Buddha.

Having attained certainty in ultimate, unsurpassed enlightenment, they obtain indestructible purity and give rise to a heart of joy; free from non-discipline and minds of greed, anger, and the like, they fulfill all modes of benefiting sentient beings, all modes of the requisites for enlightenment, and the spiritual powers of the Buddha-dharma and the Buddha-deeds.

With a purified mind, one focuses on the objects of contemplation through successive stages of mental resolve; seeing those phenomena for oneself, one swiftly accords with them, giving rise to a heart of joy and upholding all roots of goodness. Through renunciation, one benefits others with equanimity and detachment; as body and mind are embraced by this joy, it blazes forth, and wholesome dharmas are perfected.

Approaching unsurpassed enlightenment with a pure and purified mind, one gives rise to a heart of joy toward great bodhi and the resolute mind of a bodhisattva; having become free from the five fears and cultivating the wisdom of non-self, the notion of "I" does not arise. How, then, could there be attachment to a self or attachment to the requisites of life?
Therefore, one is free from the fear of lacking a livelihood;
having no desires or requests for anything from others, one constantly wishes to benefit all sentient beings, and thus is free from the fear of ill repute.
Being free from the view of self and the conception of self, they do not give rise [to such thoughts];

therefore, they are free from the fear of death. Since this body and life, upon their end, will inevitably lead to an encounter with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in future lives, they are free from the fear of the evil realms.
Observing that there is no one in the world equal to him, much less superior, he is therefore free from fear of the great assembly.
Having thus become free from these five fears, he also attains freedom from the fear of hearing the profound Dharma.

They are completely free from arrogance, haughtiness, harming others, resentment, greed, and delight; they practice all wholesome dharmas without defilement or confusion, and through the skillful means of diligence in every way and with pure faith, they practice in the present and give rise to ten great vows regarding future matters.
The ten great vows are as explained previously in the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
This dwelling in joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*) is purified by the cultivation of the following:
first, with a pure mind, one constantly vows to make offerings to all Buddhas;
Second, receiving and upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
third, exhorting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of the unprecedented Dharma;
fourth, practicing the correct conduct of a Bodhisattva in accordance with the teachings.
Fifth, the complete maturation of all requisites;
sixth, the ability to manifest birth in all worlds;
seventh, the purification of one’s own buddha-field;
Eighth, all bodhisattvas employ the same skillful means to transform beings through the Mahāyāna;
ninth, their benefit for sentient beings is entirely non-empty;
tenth, they attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in all worlds and perform all the works of a Buddha.
Such great vows can give rise to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great vows; they do not depart from the realm of sentient beings, nor do they depart from conformity with the world.

Throughout every birth, these great vows are constantly practiced and never forgotten. In the present life, one skillfully applies diligence to cultivate purity, dwelling in the ten dharmas of joyful abiding and purifying their manifestation:
first, indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas; [and so forth].
Second, through skillful means, observing the suffering aggregates of conditioned arising, one gives rise to a mind of great compassion for sentient beings;
third, observing suffering sentient beings and causing them to attain liberation, one gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness;

fourth, desiring to deliver all suffering sentient beings through great loving-kindness and compassion, one personally relinquishes one's own body but does not abandon sentient beings, relinquishing both internal and external things to practice giving.
Fifth, for the sake of delivering sentient beings,
they diligently seek mundane and supramundane dharmas with a mind free from weariness;
sixth, because their minds are free from weariness, they understand all treatises.
Seventh, because of knowing all treatises, one knows the inferior, middling, and superior sentient beings, and understands the world according to what is appropriate for them;
eighth, having acted according to what is appropriate, one knows the proper time and measure, giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse;
ninth, through such skillful means, one attains the power of courage and vigor.
Tenth, receiving worldly wealth, profit, and offerings from the Tathāgata.

These ten dharmas purify the Dwelling of Joyful Delight (*pramuditā-vihāra*); namely: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, generosity, lack of weariness, knowledge of treatises, knowledge of the world, shame and dread of blame, valor, and making offerings to the Tathāgata.

When a bodhisattva cultivates these ten dharmas, within the context of the remaining nine stages—beginning with the stage of superior morality—they examine all aspects of the merits and faults of the path. Seeking the supernormal powers of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they delight in the indestructible path. Skillfully gathering their practice, they attain reliance that transcends all stages. Having attained great enlightenment as a great guide, they deliver sentient beings from the wilderness of birth and death, instructing them to enter the practice; having entered the practice, they attain it, and having attained it, they bring its fruits and benefits to fruition. This is called the stage of reliance (*niśraya-vihāra*).
This dwelling has two causes and conditions: by seeing immeasurable Buddhas and hearing the exposition of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one is then able to understand it.
Knowing the various names of the Buddhas in the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions is called "seeing through coarse pure faith."
Up until one attains the vision of reality, this is called the first causal condition.
Furthermore, one makes this vow: "When that Buddha appears in the world, I shall be born there.
One is then reborn in accordance with this vow.

Thus, through the power of his vows, this coarse yet pure faith and vision perceives all the various articles of worship and means of benefit for all Tathāgatas; according to his capability and according to his strength, he makes offerings to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.

They listen to and receive the true Dharma from the Tathāgata; having heard it, they uphold it and practice in accordance with the Dharma. They bring sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction and dedicate all roots of goodness toward enlightenment.
By means of these three purities, those roots of goodness become even more purified.

Through the Tathāgata’s gathering of offerings to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, maturing sentient beings by means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and dedicating all roots of goodness toward enlightenment.

For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they have purified their body and mind; just as when genuine gold is repeatedly placed in fire and refined by a skilled smith, it becomes increasingly bright and pure.
The Bodhisattva’s roots of goodness likewise become increasingly pure in this way.

If he takes birth again as a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over Jambudvīpa with sovereign ease, he remains far removed from stinginess and greed, and transforms sentient beings so that they too leave behind the defilement of avarice. By means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he gathers in sentient beings, causing them all universally to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

If one wishes to exert diligence by renouncing household wealth and property to leave home and study the Way within the Buddha’s True Dharma, in a single thought-moment one can attain a hundred bodhisattva samādhis; by means of these samādhis one can perceive a hundred buddha-worlds, and through the power of supernormal knowledge one can shake a hundred buddha-worlds.
The body can also surpass radiant light; one can universally transform a single body into a hundred bodies; one can mature sentient beings;
one can abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas;
one can know the events of a hundred past kalpas; and one can know a hundred dharma-gates for each of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana).

He transforms a hundred bodhisattvas to serve as his retinue; yet, through the power of his vows and spiritual transformations, these are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas beyond calculation or knowledge.
This is called a brief explanation of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*).

It consists of four determined matters: the arising of great vows, the arising of skillful means and diligence, the cultivation of the dharmas of pure dwelling and the purification of each respective stage, and the vision of Buddhas, roots of goodness, rebirth, and spiritual powers. A detailed exposition is as taught in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages* regarding the Stage of Joy.
The Sūtras speak of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), while this *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka speaks of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).
It is called "Grounds" because they encompass sentient beings; it is called "Abodes" because they refer to the dwelling place of one's own practice and conduct.
What are the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s practice in the stage of superior morality?
In this stage of joy, the bodhisattva attains ten kinds of pure minds:
first, a mind that honors and reveres all fields of merit with every form of offering, and addresses them with words of greeting.
Second, the mind that delights in associating with fellow bodhisattvas who practice the same Dharma;
third, the mind that transcends all afflictions, entanglements, and the activities of Māra;
fourth, the mind that perceives the faults and evils of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Fifth, the mind that perceives the benefits and merits of nirvāṇa;
sixth, the mind of roots of goodness that constantly cultivates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma);
seventh, the mind that accords with the cultivation of empty and secluded places for enlightenment.
Eighth, the mind that does not dwell on worldly craving, pride, or gain;
ninth, the mind that turns away from the Śrāvaka vehicle toward the Mahāyāna;
tenth, the mind that seeks to benefit all sentient beings in every way.
The arising of these ten kinds of mind is called attaining the pure mind.
When this pure mind is fulfilled, one enters successively into the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).

Having entered the stage of superior ethical discipline, one is fully endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*); all unwholesome conduct subsumed under the traces of perverse karma is no longer practiced, let alone that which is middling or superior.

Thus, he possesses the perfection of natural morality (*śīla*) and knows, as they truly are, defiled and undefiled karma, the karmic tracks leading to happy and miserable destinies, the causal bases and the resultant bases; he knows, as they truly are, the retributive fruits, the dependent fruits, and those karmas themselves. Having himself abandoned the ten unwholesome paths of action and practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, he further teaches this Dharma to sentient beings.

The realms of sentient beings who are undifferentiated by the faults and calamities of poisonous karma, as well as the various hardships and the ultimate suffering arising from wholesome and unwholesome karma—toward these, one attains vast compassion; seeing the roots of goodness of the Buddha, they become pure as previously described.
For example, when genuine gold is treated with *kāśīsa* medicine and placed in fire, it becomes increasingly bright and pure.
The purification of a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness is likewise.

Having attained birth through the accomplishment of a pure mind in this stage, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) ruling over the four continents. By his power of mastery, he causes all sentient beings to abandon evil precepts and practice the traces of wholesome karma; the ten matters of his supernormal powers are as described in the *Sūtra*.
This is called a brief explanation of the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).

It consists of the purity of the nature of mind and the perfection of ethical discipline, being free from all unwholesome precepts and free from all traces of karma; knowing all causes and effects as they truly are; distinguishing the four kinds of karma to instruct sentient beings; and perceiving the suffering and various hardships born of the good and evil karma of the realm of sentient beings. Thus, one attains vast compassion, perceives the roots of goodness of the Buddhas, and gains the power of pure rebirth. A detailed exposition is as described in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the section on the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Because it is free from the stains of immoral conduct, it is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*); that Stainless Stage is itself the dwelling in superior morality (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
What are the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s dwelling in superior intention (*adhicitta-vihāra*)?
This bodhisattva attains ten kinds of reflection while dwelling in the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
Once these ten kinds of reflection are fully perfected, they transcend the stage of superior ethical discipline and enter the stage of superior intention (*adhicitta-vihāra*).
First, purifying the ten kinds of pure minds;
second, abandoning the ten kinds of impure minds;
third, being able to engender weary detachment toward all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Fourth, knowing how to cultivate the remedial dharmas;
fifth, not regressing in the cultivation of the remedial dharmas;
sixth, being firm in the remedies so as to overcome all outflows and all demonic activities.
Seventh, they have no regression or weakness regarding the Buddha-dharmas;
eighth, they do not consider various ascetic practices to be difficult;
ninth, they believe in and understand the Mahāyāna and take no pleasure in the Hīnayāna.
Tenth, regarding the bodhisattva dwelling in the superior intention that benefits sentient beings in every way:

they contemplate the immeasurable faults and evils of all conditioned phenomena and give rise to weary detachment; they contemplate the wisdom, merit, and beneficial rewards of the Buddha and give rise to right mindfulness and pure, profound faith.

Observing the various ascetic practices within the realm of sentient beings, he feels compassion for them and abides in the ultimate meaning; he does not become negligent regarding conditioned activities, and he applies himself with fervent diligence toward great enlightenment.
He gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, causing them to ultimately be liberated from suffering.

He contemplates all afflictions and obstacles to the right wisdom of liberation; he contemplates the wisdom that serves as the remedy arising from all delusions and afflictions within the dharma-realm, thereby accomplishing the meditative observation of wisdom-samādhi and other such states.
Taking the hearing of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as the means, one diligently cultivates vigor by means of that hearing.
Because of hearing the true Dharma, one does not spare body or life, and there is no internal or external thing that is not given in charity.
There is no one who is not respected whom they do not revere; there is no correct teaching that they do not practice and uphold; there is no physical suffering for which they do not seek the Dharma.
To hear a single four-line verse with a heart of loving-kindness and affection surpasses the love and affection for a great mass of precious jewels filling the trichiliocosm.

If one hears a single verse and turns correctly toward the Buddha-way, purifying and cultivating the bodhisattva practices, this is superior to attaining the status of all wheel-turning kings, world-protectors, Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā kings.
If someone were to say:

"I possess this Dharma that leads directly to the path of the Buddha; having purely cultivated the bodhisattva practices, if you can cast yourself into a great pit of fire and undergo great suffering, I shall explain it to you."
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva rejoices and accepts it with gladness, thinking:

"If, by hearing the true Dharma, one correctly advances toward the Buddha-way and purely cultivates the bodhisattva practices, one would enter even into the midst of a great conflagration blazing throughout the trichiliocosm up to the Brahma-heaven, let alone a small fire."
"If one seeks the Buddha-dharma even while undergoing the sufferings of hell, how much more so when facing minor hardships?

Thus, through the skillful means of diligent application and contemplation, he seeks the Dharma; he accords with the Dharma and progresses toward it in accordance with the Buddha-dharma, rather than seeking purity through mere words or sounds.

Having formed this thought, by hearing the characteristics of the true conditions of the Dharma, he became free from desire, evil, and unwholesome states, attaining the four worldly dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurables, and the five supernormal powers. Abandoning those dhyānas, samādhis, and meditative absorptions, he was born again in the realm of desire through the power of his vows, appearing wherever he could observe sentient beings capable of fulfilling the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Because of detachment from desire, the bond of desire is severed;
because of relinquishing the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), the bond of existence (*bhava*) is severed.

Having previously established such a dharma through the practice of liberation, just as the bonds of views are severed upon liberation, greed, anger, and delusion ultimately do not arise; the purity of the roots of goodness for seeing the Buddha is as previously described.
Just as pure gold, when repeatedly refined and purified, becomes free from impurities and radiant, so too do the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva become increasingly pure.

If they take birth again and attain the body of Śakra, they use the wholesome dharmas of detachment to discipline sentient beings; their supernormal powers are hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior to those of the previous stages.

This is called the brief explanation of the dwelling in the superior intention (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*). It consists of ten kinds of contemplations for accomplishing entry into all practices; the great awakening regarding the realm of sentient beings; the correct discernment of reality; the skillful means for liberation from suffering; the correct seeking of great reverence and the seeking of the Dharma; the skillful production of various dhyānas and samādhis through the practice of the Dharma following the Dharma (*dharmānudharma-pratipatti*); the correct reception of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the relinquishing of those dhyānas; being born wherever one desires by the power of vows; and the power of birth through the purification of roots of goodness upon seeing the Buddhas. These are explained in detail as taught in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the "Stage of Radiance" (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

Because one hears and practices the Dharma, and because the practice of the Dharma brings about luminous illumination, and because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) brings about luminous illumination, it is called the "Luminous Stage" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); because the inner mind is pure, it is called the "Abiding in Superior Intention" (*adhyāśaya-vihāra*).
That Luminous Stage is precisely this Abiding in Superior Intention.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment?
Having attained the fulfillment of the ten increases of the light of the Dharma while in the dwelling of superior intention, the bodhisattva enters the first dwelling of superior wisdom.
The ten dharmas of luminosity are as explained in the Sūtra:

namely, the equality of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), whether it be the affliction of defilements or the purity of purification; and the supreme purity within the affliction of being bound by defilements.
This is called the brief explanation of the meaning of the light of the Dharma.
For one who dwells in this abiding, the ten knowledges reach maturity, with the indestructible purities as their foremost, as explained in the sūtras.
When the ten knowledges have matured, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and attains mastery through the observation of the ten knowledges.
Having established these as the dominant influence, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, as described in the Sūtras.
By cultivating and accumulating those dharmas, the subtle attachments to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—such as the view of a self-entity—are ultimately prevented from arising.
The Tathāgata does not praise the non-performance of all actions; rather, he praises that which is entirely in accordance with the truth.

As suchness becomes truly manifest, the mind turns supple and gentle; through practicing various deeds, the mind becomes swiftly pure; one recognizes kindness and repays it, accords with merit, and fully accomplishes all manner of pure dharmas.

By cultivating the practices of the higher stages, one attains great vigor; through that vigor, the pure mind and profound mind reach fulfillment in faith and understanding, such that neither heterodox teachers, Māras, nor adversaries can cause them to waver from the true Dharma.
The purity of the roots of goodness in beholding the Buddha is as previously described.
For example, just as genuine gold used for ornaments cannot be matched by other gold,
so too are the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva superior to the merits of Bodhisattvas on lower stages.
Just as the light of the *yodhaka* jewel is pure and clear, such that other jewels cannot equal it and it cannot be extinguished by any wind or rain;
so too, the light of wisdom of a Bodhisattva cannot be reached by the wisdom-light of Bodhisattvas of lower stages, nor can it be destroyed by Māras, adversaries, or afflictions (*kleśa*).

If he takes birth again as the King of Yama, he teaches and transforms sentient beings through various wholesome dharmas, destroying their view of a self-identity and other errors; his supernormal powers are hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior to those in his previous station.
This is called the brief explanation of the dwelling in superior wisdom regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

It consists of the accomplishment of the ten clarities of the Dharma, entering the ten kinds of maturation, cultivating the body of the factors of enlightenment, severing all attachments such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and exercising restraint over actions—whether through abstaining from them or cultivating them.
Because that mind becomes pliant and supple, all virtues in accordance with it are fully accomplished; by cultivating the practices of the higher stages, one attains great vigor.

Through that vigor, the pure mind and profound mind become purified in their faith and understanding; through that, one is unshakable by the demonic enemies of the True Dharma. One perceives the purity of the Buddha’s roots of goodness and the spiritual power of rebirth, as explained at length in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the description of the Stage of Radiance (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

On that stage, the seeds of the flames of wisdom regarding the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are present; because the light of the wisdom of correctly teaching the Dharma illuminates the world, this stage is called "The Radiant" (Arciṣmatī).
This Radiant Stage is precisely the dwelling in superior wisdom (adhiprajñā-vihāra) associated with these factors of enlightenment.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths?
Having attained ten pure minds of equality in the first dwelling of higher wisdom and having fully perfected them,
the bodhisattva enters the second dwelling of higher wisdom.
The ten kinds of pure minds of equality are as explained in the sūtras.

That is to say, the unequaled awakening that transcends all other sentient beings and is equal to the suchness of phenomena—this is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the pure mind of equality.
For one who dwells in this dwelling, wisdom increases; they possess ten kinds of knowledge of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, as explained in the Sūtras.
Whether through the cognition of another, through self-cognition, or through both, it is as explained in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā.

Present suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of the cause of suffering, and the path that is the means for the cessation of the cause of suffering—these are called the brief exposition of the ten kinds of the Four Noble Truths.
By knowing these truths and their methods, one destroys all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and increases great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all sentient beings.

Regarding the past and future limits, for those who are deluded and erroneously directed concerning the Four Noble Truths, he causes them to enter into the equipment of merit and wisdom for liberation.

He brings to maturity the various genuine virtues such as right aspiration, right mindfulness, right knowledge, and right speech through practice; he increases them without remainder, contemplates all modes, and matures sentient beings through matured skillful means.
In order to gather in sentient beings, they cultivate worldly scripts and treatises as described in the Sūtras.

Through all forms of skillful arts and crafts, they give rise to a heart of compassion, inducing others to advance toward and establish themselves in Bodhi, while providing gifts through worldly expedient means in accordance with the world.

When the four great elements are disordered or one is possessed by non-human spirits, he brings them to rest; he provides benefit through faultless play and articles of enjoyment, and by means of this benefit, he leads them to delight in the Dharma, providing further benefit through the requisites for dwelling in tranquility.

He delivers those afflicted by kings and thieves, establishing them in peace and security; through skillful means regarding what is possible and what is impossible, he grants instruction on what is auspicious and inauspicious, achieves success in generosity, and provides mutual benefit and purification in the present life. To those who are deluded, he teaches the true path.
This is called the conventional meaning of the equality of skillful arts for gathering in sentient beings.
The purity of the Buddha’s roots of goodness is as previously described;
it is like pure gold set with various jewels, its radiance and purity surpassing that of other gold.
In this way, the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva surpass those of other bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
It is like the palaces of the sun and moon, which no wind-circles can cause to fall.
In this way, the wisdom and skillful means of the bodhisattva cannot be destroyed by worldly dharmas.

If he is further reborn as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, he uses all wholesome dharmas to destroy all the heterodox and false teachings of external paths; his supernormal powers are a hundred thousand million times superior to those of his previous dwelling.
This is called, in brief, the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths (*satya-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*).

It is characterized by the accomplishment of a pure mind of equanimity, the entry into the contemplation of the truths, the increase in the destruction of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), the increase in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings, and the maturation of the equipment of merit and wisdom. It involves the complete increase of virtues such as right aspiration, right mindfulness, right knowledge, and right speech. One contemplates all kinds of skillful means for maturation and achieves the mastery of arts for the sake of ripening sentient beings. This includes the vision of the Buddha, the purification of roots of goodness, and the power of intentional rebirth, as explained at length in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the description of the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā bhūmiḥ*).
Because decisive wisdom is difficult to surpass, this stage is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya).
This Difficult to Conquer stage is precisely the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths.
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in superior wisdom associated with dependent origination?
It is when this bodhisattva, in the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the truths, attains ten dharmas of equality.
Having attained superior fulfillment, one enters the sixth stage.
First, the equality of the ultimate nature of all phenomena;
second, the equality of signlessness in conduct beyond verbal expression.
Third is the equality of non-arising;
fourth is the equality of the non-origination of causes and conditions;
fifth is the equality of ultimate quiescence.
Sixth is the equality of being free from all hypocrisy;
seventh is the equality of neither grasping nor rejecting in any practice;
eighth is the equality of all phenomena being detached.
Ninth, the equality of the objects of deluded thought being like illusions and transformations;
tenth, the equality of the non-duality of existence and non-existence regarding the objects of deluded thought.
These are called the ten dharmas of equality explained in brief.

One who dwells in this dwelling increases great compassion for all sentient beings and is single-mindedly devoted to bodhi. They understand the correct practice of dependent origination regarding the conjunction and dispersion, arising and ceasing, of all worlds; they realize the wisdom born of conditions and the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and, by relying on the three samādhis, they transcend the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as the characteristics of a knower, a doer, existence, and non-existence.

In this way, through the skillful means of the ultimate truth, one contemplates how sentient beings are bound by the fetters of affliction; how conditioned phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and are fragile and precarious; and how attachment to self and what belongs to the self gives rise to all manner of faults and evils, thereby becoming detached from the causes and conditions of those afflictive fetters.
Because they are in harmony and protect themselves, they do not extinguish all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
