In accordance with worldly conventions, they certainly employ excellent expedient means to destroy all forms of poverty, provide relief to those suffering from the disorders of the four elements or afflictions by non-human spirits, and provide benefit through blameless amusements and articles of enjoyment.
Therefore, he benefits others by inducing them toward the Dharma through the provision of requisites for dwelling and rest;

he delivers those afflicted by kings or thieves to a state of security; he employs skillful means regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate, whether by permitting or prohibiting matters of fortune and misfortune; and he ensures that those who ought to give do so, thereby enabling them to attain what is suitable for them.
In this present life, they are free from mutual conflict and contention, and even in future lives, they harbor no resentment.
For those who are deluded, they expound the true path.
This is called the mundane craftsmanship and the principle of equality for the gathering and sustaining of sentient beings.
The purity of the roots of goodness from seeing the Buddha is as previously described.
For example, just as refined pure gold polished with mother-of-pearl becomes brilliant and pure, surpassing all other gold;
so too, the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva surpass those of other bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as the palaces of the sun and moon cannot be dislodged by any wind-circle,
so too the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva cannot be overcome by any worldly phenomena.

If he takes birth again, he will become the King of the Tuṣita Heaven; by means of various wholesome dharmas, he will destroy all the heterodox and false teachings of external paths, and his supernormal powers will exceed those of his previous state by a hundred billionfold.
This is called, in brief, the dwelling in higher wisdom associated with the truths (*satya-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*). It is characterized by the accomplishment of the equality of the pure mind;

it involves entering the contemplation of the truths and increasing the destruction of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); it involves the increase of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings; it involves the maturation of the equipment of merit and wisdom; and it involves the increase of virtues such as right aspiration, skillful means, right mindfulness, right knowledge, and right teaching. It is free from further discursive thought, and consists of the maturation in all aspects and the maturation of skillful means. It brings forth the mundane arts and crafts for sentient beings, the purity of roots of goodness, and the power of intentional rebirth (*upapatti-prātihārya*), as explained at length in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* regarding the "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*) stage.
Because the wisdom that is certain regarding the ultimate truth is difficult to surpass, this stage is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).
This Difficult to Conquer stage is, in this sense, termed the "Abiding in Higher Wisdom Corresponding to the Truths."
What is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in superior wisdom associated with dependent origination?
It is when this bodhisattva, having previously dwelt in superior wisdom associated with the truths, attains the ten dharmas of equality as described in the sūtras.

Having attained supreme fulfillment, he enters this dwelling: the equality of the signless intrinsic nature of all phenomena as the ultimate truth; the equality of the illumination of the signless through conduct beyond verbal expression; the equality of non-arising because that very signlessness is itself unarisen; the equality of the non-origination of causes; the equality of ultimate quiescence because causes do not arise by themselves; the equality of being free from the grasping of falsehoods; the equality of being free from practice through neither taking up nor rejecting; the equality of the nature of conceptualization and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) being like illusions and transformations; and the equality of the non-duality of existence and non-existence regarding the intrinsic nature of the realm of wisdom that is free from conceptualization.
This is called a brief explanation of the ten meanings of impartial discernment.

One who dwells in this state increases great compassion for all sentient beings and develops a diligent aspiration for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). They understand the various modes of dependent origination regarding the arising and ceasing of all worlds, correctly perceive and realize the wisdom of causal origination, and enter the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. By relying upon these, they abandon the notions of self and what belongs to self, as well as the conceptions of existence and non-existence.

Thus, through this first-principle reflection, one understands that the conditioned nature of sentient beings—arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions of afflictions and fetters—is inferior; it gives rise to all manner of faults and evils due to the separation from [the realization of] self and what belongs to the self, yet it does not exist apart from the conjunction of the causes and conditions of afflictions.
I shall sever the conjunction of the causes and conditions of those afflictions for the sake of self-protection;
yet I shall not extinguish all conditioned phenomena for the sake of protecting sentient beings.

Thus, practicing with wisdom and compassion, one dwells in this state, which is called the dwelling directed toward unimpeded gnosis (*anāvaraṇajñāna*). Here, the *prajñāpāramitā* dwelling manifests before one, such that one cannot be defiled by anything in the world.

For one who abides thus, if they benefit the seventh stage, their ultimate bodhisattva patience in the practice of skillful means is subsumed within that patience of conformity; this is the perfection of wisdom directed toward unimpeded knowledge.

Having cultivated and perfected the causes and conditions for attaining bodhi, they do not abide in worldly conditioned existence; they manifest quiescence yet do not abide in quiescence. Through such conformity of skillful means and wisdom, they enter the gate of the samādhi of emptiness and proceed toward a million gates of samādhi.
As it is with the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, so it is with the gateways of the *animitta* and *apraṇihita* samādhis.

Having thus directed oneself toward these various samādhis, this is called the "indestructible mind. All aspects of the Buddha-dharma increase and become increasingly sublime; it cannot be destroyed by outsiders, Māras, or enemies. The rest is as previously explained.
Just as genuine gold adorned with lapis lazuli excels all other gold,
so too do the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva excel all others in their purity.
Just as moonlight dispels the afflictions of sentient beings and cannot be obscured by the wind-circles of the four directions;
The light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: it extinguishes the fire of afflictions for all sentient beings, and no demonic adversaries can sever it.

If he takes birth again, he becomes the King of the Heaven of Sovereignty over Others’ Emanations (*Sudharmadevarāja*), constantly using various wholesome dharmas to eliminate all arrogance among sentient beings; his spiritual power is a thousand million times superior to that of his predecessor.
This is called the brief explanation of the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

It is known as the entry into the accomplishment of the equality of phenomena, the awakening to all dependent originations which gives rise to the gate of liberation, the dwelling through the skillful means of embracing [beings] while remaining free from all false conceptions, the orientation toward the *prajñāpāramitā* of unimpeded knowledge, the attainment of direction toward immeasurable samādhis, the acquisition of an indestructible mind, the excellence of the Buddha-dharma, and the purity of roots of goodness, rebirth, and supernormal powers. These are explained in detail as they appear in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the section on the "Manifest Stage" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Because it is directed toward unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna*), that stage is called "Manifest" (*abhimukhī*).
This very meaning is termed the "Abiding in Superior Wisdom Corresponding to Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpādapratisaṃyuktādhiprajñāvihāra*).
What is the bodhisattva’s mode of abiding in the signless (*animitta*) while still possessing practice and development?

This Bodhisattva, in the dwelling of superior wisdom associated with dependent origination, successively gives rise to the wisdom of the ten skillful means; having fully perfected the advancement through the skillful means of the path uncommon to all ordinary beings and all mundane beings, they enter the seventh dwelling.
Those various skillful means and wisdoms are as explained in the sūtras:
namely, because they give rise to worldly wholesome dharmas and embrace meritorious qualities, they establish a mind of peace and a mind of joy toward all sentient beings.

Because the various requisites of merit and the factors of enlightenment gradually increase; because they are not shared with śrāvakas; because they are not shared with pratyekabuddhas; because of knowing the dharma-realm of sentient beings; because of knowing the world-systems; and because of knowing the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata.
One should understand that the path arising from such skillful means and wisdom is explained here in brief for the purpose of ascending through successive stages of skillful means.

Thus, possessing the distinct cognitions of the immeasurable and incalculable realms of the Tathāgatas, one gives rise to a state free from fabrication, free from the perception of signs, and free from conceptualization. One contemplates the source of the immeasurable Buddha-realms as uninterrupted and unfabricated, cultivating all modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and in every situation never departing from the Path. In every moment of thought, one is fully endowed with the ten *pāramitās* and all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), unlike other states of abiding.

In the first stage, the Dwelling of Joy, one cultivates right aspiration; in the second stage, one is free from the defilement of immoral conduct; in the third stage, aspiration increases further and one attains the light of the Dharma; in the fourth stage, one enters the Path; in the fifth stage, one enters worldly activities; and in the sixth stage, one enters the profound gateways of the Dharma.

In this seventh stage, all Buddha-dharmas arise and the factors of enlightenment are fulfilled; the Bodhisattva’s skillful means and practices reach fulfillment and are fully embraced, and through the purity of wisdom and supernormal powers in this dwelling, one enters the eighth stage.
Those who abide in the eighth stage are exclusively pure;
those in this seventh stage are mixedly pure. Because they abide in the preparatory practices, they attain non-defilement, which is called "uncontaminated conduct."
In this seventh stage, because all afflictions such as greed have been severed, it is not called "having afflictions," nor is it called "free from them.
Because afflictions do not manifest, and because one delights in the Buddha-dharma with a mind that is pure according to reality, it is not called "free from afflictions."
In this seventh stage, one accomplishes immeasurable purity of bodily, verbal, and mental karma, as praised by the Buddha; such karma is as previously described.

The mundane knowledge of arts and crafts attained in the fifth stage becomes spontaneously perfected, such that one serves as a great master for the trichiliocosm; except for Bodhisattvas of the higher stages and Tathāgatas, there is no one who can equal them.
All meditative concentrations and factors conducive to enlightenment are cultivated as they manifest before him, yet he does not undergo their karmic retribution.

In this state, the Bodhisattva dwells in the skillful means of contemplation and enters the gateway of the Samādhi of Excellent Discernment, giving rise to a million samādhis that transcend the entire realm of the samādhis of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

They remain far removed from the practices of afflictions and false conceptualizations; they accord with profound physical, verbal, and mental actions; they do not abandon the path of skillful means and superior progress; out of compassion for sentient beings, they fulfill bodhi; their immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions are free from all marks; and they give rise to pure cultivation of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In this dwelling, one transcends the sphere of individual self-realization; in the other six dwellings, one takes the Buddha-dharma as an object of focus.

While a Bodhisattva in the sixth dwelling is able to enter into cessation (*nirodha*), in this present dwelling, one attains moment-to-moment cessation and achieves unprecedented, inconceivable karma of body, speech, and mind. Although one practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not realize that limit of reality.
When such wisdom of skillful means has arisen as the predominant condition, one practices in common with all sentient beings, illuminating the world; the rest is as explained in the Sūtra.

To state the essentials: one should embrace those performing meritorious deeds with the thought of them being one's own kin; through skillful means, one should advance toward and abide in the three liberations.
For those seeking the Lesser Vehicle, one employs skillful means to discipline them;
for those addicted to the five desires, one causes them to seek superior aspirations and turns them away from all false views.
He accords with the minds of others and accords with all great assemblies; the rest is as previously described.

For example, just as refined pure gold adorned with mani-jewels surpasses Jāmbūnada gold, so too do the roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva—purified and stainless—surpass those of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and other stainless Bodhisattvas.
For example, just as the light of the sun illuminates Jambudvīpa and causes all mud and water to dry up and vanish— surpassing all other lights—
so too does the light of this bodhisattva’s wisdom cause the afflictions of sentient beings to dry up and vanish, surpassing the wisdom-light of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and other bodhisattvas.

If he takes birth again, he will become the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, benefiting śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas with his wisdom; all his supernatural powers will exceed those of before by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

This is called a brief explanation of the signless dwelling with practice and development. It refers to the superior progress through the skillful means of the path where wisdom arises; entering the place from which the realm of the Tathāgata’s knowledge originates;

the continuous application of skillful means to accumulate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) in every thought-moment; the fulfillment of practice through skillful means regarding both defiled and undefiled states; and the fulfillment of all worldly arts and crafts due to the generation of the karma of a purified mind. One attains immeasurable samādhis not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, practicing the conduct of universal quiescence in every thought-moment while engaging in all worldly activities common to the world. Through the purity of roots of goodness, one gains the power of intentional rebirth. A detailed explanation is as taught in the Sūtra on the Ten Stages, specifically in the description of the Far-Reaching Stage (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
Because the practice of skillful means is fulfilled, that stage is called "Far-Reaching" (dūraṃgamā).
This very meaning is termed the "signless dwelling with effort and application" (*sābhisaṃskāra-sābhogo nirnimittavihāra*).
What is the characteristic of the bodhisattva’s signless dwelling without effort or application (*anabhisaṃskāro nirnimitto vihāra*)?

This bodhisattva, in the initial stage of the signless dwelling (*animitta-vihāra*), successively attains ten kinds of knowledge that enter into the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena, as taught in the Sūtras.
That is to say: the three times are, as they truly are, originally unarisen and unborn;
because they are signless (*animitta*) and lack any other causal nature, the ultimate reality is a thing whose self-nature is beyond verbal expression.
Regarding the practice of verbal expression, it reveals that the characteristics of intrinsic nature and causal nature do not exist;

because such things are thus unarisen, there is no ignorance or false conceptual attachment toward them. Since those things are non-existent, one is free from verbal expression regarding all times—beginning, middle, and end—and from afflictions and the like.
Thus entering into the correct state of equality free from妄想 (vikalpa), one severs those afflictions.
Because of this freedom from affliction, ten kinds of knowledge increase and reach fulfillment;
having reached fulfillment, one enters the eighth pure dwelling, wherein one attains the supreme patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas and experiences a swift, pure joy.
What are the four kinds of seeking by which one seeks all phenomena?
What are the four kinds of thorough knowledge by which one thoroughly knows all phenomena?

Because of this seeking and knowing, one is free from all conceptual proliferations and attachments; all afflictions do not arise within the present phenomena, and one accordingly contemplates that in future lives, all things will be without remainder and without arising.

One contemplates those phenomena that arise from the causes of false conceptualization and attachment, as previously described; one seeks them through the fourfold search and knows them as they truly are, as explained in the "Chapter on Reality.

From the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of signlessness with effort and development (*sābhisamskāra-animitta-vihāra*), one has not yet attained swift purity;
it is only upon reaching this stage that one attains swift purity, and for this reason it is called the first *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena).

Having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realized the profound Dharma, one becomes free from the four kinds of faults associated with the initial dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*):
first, the presence of volitional effort and mental development;
second, the diligent seeking of higher stages.
Third, one is capable of diligently seeking the benefit of sentient beings in every way;
fourth, because subtle perceptions and activities [are present], this stage is called "Thoroughly Pure" (Suvimalā).

Within the stream of the Dharma of the profound Dharma-gates, the Tathāgata exhorts and inspires the production of immeasurable activities of wisdom and supernormal powers that bring benefit through countless doors.
Because of this exhortation, one produces immeasurable transformations of the honored body and attains wisdom and the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), as described in the sūtras.

Because they have attained mastery, they are able to dwell for as long or as briefly as they desire; they attain all meditative concentrations and liberations according to their wishes; they obtain all necessities of life and worldly crafts and skills according to their wishes; they are born in any dwelling place or mode of birth according to their wishes; they attain all supernatural powers and all vows according to their wishes; they can transform all things into gold and jewels according to their wishes; and when they wish to know the Dharma-realm—its names, phrases, and syllables—they are able to know them by establishing skillful means regarding all phenomena.
Such are the fruits, rewards, and benefits of sovereign power, as described in the sūtras.

In every moment of thought, one constantly perceives the Buddha equally; the purity of one's roots of goodness, the power of taking birth, and the analogy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* are as described in the sūtras.
This is called the brief explanation of the dwelling in signlessness, which is without activity and without cultivation.

It refers to the accomplishment of entering the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), the attainment of entering the non-arising dharma-patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the swift attainment of the pure and serene dwelling that is free from all faults. It is the profound Dharma-gate through which the Buddhas encourage and inspire the production of immeasurable wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and various deeds for the benefit of others; it is the production of immeasurable noble bodies and the production of wisdom. One attains great power and great sovereign power, as well as the spiritual power of birth resulting from the purification of roots of goodness and the fruits of merit. A detailed explanation is as taught in the *Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, specifically in the section on the Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*).
Being free from volitional effort and development, one mounts the superior path of non-movement; therefore, that stage is called "The Immovable.
This very stage is also named "The Abiding in Signlessness, Without Volitional Effort or Development."
What is the characteristic of the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in unimpeded practice?

This Bodhisattva does not consider this profound dwelling to be sufficient; he diligently cultivates the progressive advancement toward the higher stages. He knows the practice of the Dharma and extensively expounds it for others in all its aspects. He knows, exactly as they are, what should be taught according to the needs of others; he knows, exactly as they are, that the Dharma he teaches purifies afflictions, and who is afflicted and who is purified.
One who thus skillfully expounds the Dharma is called a great Dharma-preacher.

Having attained immeasurable dhāraṇīs, they are proficient in all sounds and possess inexhaustible eloquence; through the dharma-dhāraṇī, they master and accomplish the teachings as they have received them.

By means of the unimpeded wisdom of a bodhisattva, one gives rise to verbal expression; seated upon the Dharma throne, one preaches the Dharma as is appropriate, manifesting joy according to that Dharma, as described in the sūtras.
The purification of roots of goodness, the power of taking birth, and the superior progress are as explained in the sūtras.
This is called the brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Unobstructed Abode.

That is to say, it concerns the inconceivable great Dharma-master who delights in profound liberation, expounds the Dharma, and practices wisdom; the purification of roots of goodness, the power of taking birth, and the spiritual transformations are explained in detail as taught in the sūtra on the tenth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*).

Bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, purely cultivating the unimpeded state of a bodhisattva, and extensively expounding the Great Dharma—for these reasons, that stage is named "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī).
This very meaning is also called the "Abode of Non-Obstruction."
What is the characteristic of the dwelling and practice of the supreme Bodhisattva?

This Bodhisattva, abiding in unimpeded dwelling, purely cultivates all kinds of pure dharmas appropriate for the consecration of a Dharma King, and attains immeasurable samādhis such as the Stainless (*vimala*).

Having performed what was to be done, the final samādhi of the supreme empowerment of omniscience manifests before him. He attains a body seated together with all Buddhas, illuminated by the light of the lotus retinue. Having received the empowerment of all-aspect omniscience, he masters the skillful means for taming and liberating beings, understands all Buddha-activities, and attains immeasurable liberations, dhāraṇīs, and supernormal powers.

Because that [faith] increases, great mindfulness and wisdom arise, eloquence is established, and great supernormal powers are produced; with the purification of roots of goodness, one attains the superior progress of authentic spiritual power.

This is called a brief explanation of the supreme Bodhisattva dwelling; a detailed explanation is as taught in the *Sūtra on the Ten Grounds*, specifically in the section on the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

On this Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, the Bodhisattva fulfills the Bodhisattva path and fulfills the requisites for enlightenment; he attains the supreme wisdom of a Bodhisattva and raises a great cloud of Dharma. Through self-awakening by means of perfect enlightenment, he causes all the afflictions and impurities of sentient beings to come to rest, and causes their various roots of goodness to grow and ripen. For this reason, that ground is named the "Cloud of Dharma."
This very meaning is called the "Supreme Bodhisattva Abode.
As explained above, its progressively superior merits are not present in the preceding stages; those with dull faculties are not included in this reckoning.

Regarding those of middling and superior capacity, they fully establish what is attained on the higher stages; each of these abidings lasts for hundreds of thousands of millions of great kalpas, or even for immeasurable time, before being fully perfected.

Abiding in all those stages for three *asaṃkhyeya* great kalpas, he subsequently transcends the stage of "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*) of the first *asaṃkhyeya* great kalpa and attains the stage of "joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*).

Regarding the progressive advancement through the five paths of practice during the second asaṃkhyeya mahākalpa: from the Dwelling of Joy up until the Dwelling of Manifested Signlessness has been passed, one attains the Dwelling of Unmanifested Signlessness.
This very state is "certainty," meaning that the Bodhisattva with a pure mind attains certain and superior progress.

Having passed beyond the unmanifested dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*) and the dwelling in unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna-vihāra*) during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he attains the supreme Bodhisattva dwelling.
There are two types of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*:
first, when a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*)—in terms of its divisions of days, nights, and months—is so vast as to be immeasurable, it is called *asaṃkhyeya*;
second, when the number of those great kalpas reaches a point where the count of a single kalpa exceeds all calculation, it is called *asaṃkhyeya*.
The awakening of the previous asaṃkhyeya kalpa was not attained within a few minor asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
nor was it increased by the three subsequent great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

If one is able to accomplish the transcendence of many intermediate kalpas or even great kalpas through superior and superior skillful means of diligence, there is no transcending of the asaṃkhyeya [kalpa] itself.
Thus, for a bodhisattva in these twelve stages (*vihāra*), the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Among those, during the first three stages, the afflictive obscurations are abandoned: in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), the portion of afflictions leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*) increases, while all higher and middle-grade afflictions do not manifest at all.

Abiding in the unconditioned and signless state, one attains the pure continuity of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); all portions of affliction and all defilements are severed, and no afflictions ever arise again.
In the supreme Bodhisattva stage, all afflictions, habitual tendencies, and hindrances are severed, and one enters the stage of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the defilements that constitute the cognitive hindrance, there are three types:
first, the outer skin;
The second is the skin;
the third is the bone.
In the stage of abiding in joy, the barrier of the skin is severed.
The dwelling in signlessness without development: the hindrance of skin is severed;
the Tathāgata-dwelling:
the hindrance of bone is severed.
All obscurations are purified.
Within these three stages, the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed; in the remaining stages, the true requisites follow their respective order.
Thus, within these thirteen stages, there are eleven kinds of purification:
First, the purity of the spiritual lineage;
second, the purity of practice through understanding;
third, the purity of the pure mind.
The fourth is purity of ethical discipline;
the fifth is purity of mind;
the sixth, seventh, and eighth are purity of the skillful means of right knowledge.
The ninth is the purity of fulfilling the practice of skillful means;
the tenth is the purity of giving birth to the supernormal powers of true wisdom;
the eleventh is the purity of unimpededness in expounding the correct meaning.
The twelfth is the purity of the knowledge that accords with and enters into all aspects of all that is to be known;
the thirteenth is the purity of the knowledge regarding the habitual tendencies of all afflictions and cognitive obstructions within the Tathāgata’s dwelling.
As stated previously in the "Chapter on the Merits of Bodhisattvas," all that is taught in the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka is subsumed within eight dharmas.

These thirteen stages (*vihāra*) encompass the first stage, wherein one generates faith and gives rise to understanding, thereby attaining the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of reflection regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
and the third stage, which consists of the pure mind and the initial practice of the wisdom of cultivation.
From the fourth dwelling up to the ninth—the dwelling of signlessness with effort and development—the wisdom of cultivation is extensive;

the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth dwellings comprise the fruition of the wisdom of cultivation subsumed within the purified practice of wisdom, which constitutes the Tathāgata-dwelling that is ultimately free from all dharmas belonging to the Śrāvaka-dwellings.
These twelve bodhisattva abodes should be understood in their proper sequence.

First, one should understand that the abiding in one's own spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is like the abiding in the skillful means for transcending and departing from the state of ordinary birth (*utpanna-vyutkrānta-nyāma*).
The second dwelling is likewise, like the faith that has transcended and left birth behind.
The third dwelling is likewise, like the attainment of the indestructible purities and the superior dwelling in the precepts beloved by the noble ones, leading to the exhaustion of the outflows.
The fourth dwelling is also like this, just as the dwelling arises from the training in higher ethics and higher mind.
The fifth dwelling is also like this, just as the dwelling in the training in higher wisdom through the attainment of the knowledge of the true truths.
The sixth, seventh, and eighth dwellings are also like this, being similar to the skillful means of the dwelling in the signless samādhi through thorough observation.
The ninth dwelling is also like this, being similar to the ultimate dwelling in the signless.
The tenth dwelling is also like this, being like the dwelling of liberation-awakening arising from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
The eleventh dwelling is also like this, being like the dwelling of an arhat in all its aspects.
The twelfth dwelling is likewise characterized by the arising of liberation and the entry into that dwelling. "Arising" refers to awakening from meditative concentration.
The five liberations and entries are as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Seven;
*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Ten. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.

Translated by Dharmakṣema at Guzang. Section Three: The Ultimate Expedient Means. Chapter One: Birth, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha*. Third Part: There are five types of birth for Bodhisattvas; briefly stated, there are five kinds. All Bodhisattvas dwelling in all practices bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without fault.
First is birth that extinguishes suffering (*duḥkha-praśamana-janma*).
Second, birth according to one's kind;
third, superior birth;
fourth, preeminent birth.
Fifth is the final birth.

By the power of his vows and the power of his mastery, the Bodhisattva assumes the body of a great fish and other such forms during ages of famine, using his flesh to rescue and sustain all sentient beings.
In an age of disease, he becomes a great King of Physicians to treat and heal all ailments.
In an age of weapons, he becomes a powerful king who, through skillful means and words of sincerity and faith, rescues others with an impartial mind and brings an end to conflict and strife.

In places of imprisonment, flogging, and oppression, he is born into a royal family for the sake of quelling suffering, transforming sentient beings of wrong views through the correct governance of the Dharma.

Having served celestial deities and committed various evil deeds, they are born in those heavenly realms through the power of their vows and the power of their mastery; there, they sever those wrong views and all such evil conduct.
Thus, they are reborn in all such immeasurable places of birth; this is called "Birth that Quells Suffering.

By the power of their vows and the power of their mastery, Bodhisattvas are born among various beings—gods, nāgas, spirits, asuras, and others—who mutually afflict one another, as well as among those non-Buddhists who give rise to false views and perform evil, unwholesome deeds. They are born therein as leaders for these beings, guiding them to enter the Path of Rightness.
That which others perform, the bodhisattva does not; that which they do not cultivate, the bodhisattva cultivates; furthermore, he extensively proclaims and explains the wholesome dharmas.
Thus, taking birth according to various types of beings up to an immeasurable extent is called "birth according to type."

The Bodhisattva takes birth by means of their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), which excels the worldly retributions of lifespan, physical form, and so forth, as explained in the "Chapter on the Benefit of Self and Others.
Such births are likewise immeasurable; this is called "superior birth" (*viśiṣṭopapatti*).

From the Bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of pure mind up to the dwelling of the supreme Bodhisattva, regarding the births they undergo—as explained previously in the "Chapter on Dwellings"—they take birth with mastery over Jambudvīpa up to the Great Mastery (Maheśvara). Among all places of birth prior to transcending the ultimate stage, these are extraordinary; this is called "superior birth" (*abhyudaya*).

The supreme Bodhisattva dwells in the stage of taking birth; having brought to full completion the mastery over karmic activities and the requisites for enlightenment, he is born into a family of Kṣatriyas or Brahmins, attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and performs all the works of a Buddha—this is called the final birth.
All bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present are born through these five modes of birth; there are none other and none superior.
By means of these five modes of birth, bodhisattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter Two: The Chapter on Compendium (*Saṃgraha-vastu*) within the Section on Ultimate Expedients (*Upāya-paryanta*) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Regarding how Bodhisattvas, in all their abodes and all their practices, encompass sentient beings, there are briefly six kinds:
first, instantaneous inclusion (*sakṛt-saṃgraha*);
second, superior inclusion (*adhipati-saṃgraha*).
Third, grasping by means of appropriation;
fourth, long-term grasping;
fifth, short-term grasping.
Sixth is subsequent gathering.

When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they regard all sentient beings as their own parents; according to their capacity, they provide them with peace, happiness, and benefit in every way—this is called instantaneous gathering.

Taking the parents as his masters, the bodhisattva honors them with various skillful means, exhorting them to practice wholesome dharmas; he provides them with offerings at the appropriate times, recognizing their kindness and repaying it.
He looks after his wife, children, and kinsmen, instructing them; he endures their transgressions and heals their illnesses, teaching them to practice wholesome dharmas so that they may advance.
Toward servants, laborers, and those who work for him, he treats them with an impartial mind, never conceiving thoughts of contempt.

When a bodhisattva acts as a king, he governs the people by means of righteous transformation rather than inflicting unjust punishments; he benefits them through both material wealth and the Dharma. He maintains his own realm without encroaching upon the lands of others, and according to his capacity, he instructs all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome dharmas.
The Bodhisattva acts as a father; since he harbors no partiality even toward other sentient beings, how much less would he fail to be impartial toward his own kin?
His speech is always gentle, truthful, and not false; he is entirely free from killing, binding, oppression, and harsh treatment. This is called "superior gathering."
There are two causes and conditions for gathering a following:
first, relinquishing a mind of greed and benefiting others with material wealth so they may be freed from poverty;
second, teaching them to practice the right Dharma and benefiting them with the True Teaching so they may uproot evil and false views.

They embrace all with an impartial mind, without following any faction; they do not practice stinginess regarding the Dharma nor do they grow weary of teaching. They do not seek offerings from those who request them.

They do not obstruct those who delight in cultivation, for the sake of increasing their provisions of merit. They cause those who have not yet understood the meaning to awaken to it, and cause those who have already understood it to increase in realization. They resolve the doubts of the uncertain and bring awareness to those who regret. At the appropriate time, they explain the profound and essential meanings, sharing in others' suffering and joy with a mind free of increase or decrease.

For those who have committed offenses, he instructs them with an impartial mind; at times he rebukes them and at times he praises them. He provides medical treatment for their illnesses to eliminate their distress.

Toward those of inferior mindfulness, inferior diligence, and inferior wisdom, he does not give rise to thoughts of contempt, but teaches them the objects of focused attention as appropriate, and instructs them according to the occasion so that they may become patient and free from affliction.

He offers supreme worship to those who are his equals and those who are superior; he cultivates compassion, remaining neither fickle nor wavering; he achieves purity in precepts, views, deportment, and right livelihood; he maintains a serene countenance, looks upon others with equanimity, and is the first to speak words of greeting; he constantly cultivates wholesome deeds and practices no negligence, teaching these dharmas to his disciples while practicing them himself.
A bodhisattva does not gather a retinue at all times, nor does he fail to gather one, nor does he gather one haphazardly; this is called "gathering by means of taking.
Those sentient beings who are weakly matured attain purity only after a long time; this is called "gathering over a long period.
Those sentient beings who are moderately matured attain purity before long; this is called "gathering before long."
Bringing sentient beings to maturity so that they become capable of purification in this very life is called the "subsequent gathering.
These are the six kinds of equal gathering of sentient beings.

The bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present—those who have gathered, will gather, and are currently gathering—all do so through these six kinds; there is nothing beyond them and nothing superior to them.
When Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings through such means as these, there are twelve difficulties:
first, being able to skillfully observe those who violate the precepts and then either instructing them or abandoning them;
second, employing skillful means to discipline sentient beings while protecting oneself from afflictions during difficult practices.
Third, his material wealth is extremely meager while those who seek it are many;
fourth, he possesses only a single body yet is sought after by many who share the same purpose;
fifth, through pure karma he is born among heedless gods and humans, yet within his own mind he is never at all heedless.
Sixth, to compassionately mind sentient beings and engage in beneficial co-operative action;
seventh, whether through teaching or relinquishing, to deal with those who are ignorant, deceitful, and whose limbs and joints are impaired;
eighth, to perceive the faults of birth and death yet not abandon birth and death.
Ninth, even before attaining a pure mind, one does not lose right mindfulness at the time of death;
tenth, even before attaining a pure mind, when sentient beings whom one holds most dear and precious come to beg, one bestows gifts upon them;
eleventh, when those with various different dispositions and various different understandings come to make requests, whether one acts or desists, [one remains steadfast].
Twelfth, while ultimately practicing heedfulness, they do not sever their afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding all sentient beings, Bodhisattvas employ skillful means (*upāya*) without discriminating between their relative importance; they may exercise compassion by observing others, or create causal conditions through courageous skillful means, or cultivate right vows, or purify their faith, or contemplate with focused thought without weariness, or at times act with gentleness, or at times practice equanimity (*upekṣā*), or at times exert diligence, or at times employ clever skillful means. Through such correct antidotes and skillful means, the Bodhisattva is able to resolve these twelve difficulties for themselves, so that their mind does not sink into despair.

Chapter Three: The Stages (Bhūmi). Regarding the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*) previously explained, they are arranged in sequence as seven stages (*bhūmi*): six are the stages of the bodhisattva, and one is the stage shared by both the bodhisattva and the Tathāgata.
First, the stage of the lineage;
second, the stage of practice through understanding;
third, the stage of the pure mind;
Fourth is the stage of practice;
fifth is the stage of certainty;
sixth is the stage of certain practice.

Seventh is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*). The stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*) is called the stage of the spiritual lineage; the stage of abiding in practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) is called the stage of practice through understanding; the stage of abiding in the pure mind (*śuddhādhyāśaya-vihāra*) is called the stage of the pure mind; the stage of abiding in superior morality (*adhiśīla*), the stage of abiding in superior mind (*adhicitta*), the three stages of abiding in superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), and the stage of abiding in the signless with effort (*animitto vyutthitaḥ*) are called the stage of the path (*pratipad-bhūmi*); the stage of abiding in the signless without effort (*animitto ’vyutthitaḥ*) is called the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), which is the first among the three certainties;

the stage of abiding in unimpeded knowledge (*jñāna-pratisaṃvid-vihāra*) is called the stage of certain conduct (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*); and the supreme bodhisattva stage and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-vihāra*) are called the ultimate stage.
The stage of the Tathāgata will be explained extensively in the subsequent chapter on "Establishment.
How does a bodhisattva, upon entering the Stage of Joy from the Stage of Practice through Understanding, escape the retribution of the evil destinies?

This bodhisattva, while on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), relies upon mundane pure dhyāna to gather the requisites for awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). They cultivate a mind of compassion toward one hundred and ten types of suffering sentient beings; regarding those in the evil destinies who have long dwelt in the miserable paths as if they were their own home, they are capable of enduring this because they train in unexcelled awakening. They are able to act as the cause for the removal of suffering for all sentient beings, and with a pure mind, they vow to take upon themselves all the karma of the three evil paths of all sentient beings. Ultimately, they practice all wholesome deeds and cultivate right aspirations.
By the power of the correct vows of mundane pure dhyāna, the defiled bodies received through the afflictions of the evil realms will soon be severed.

The Bodhisattva transforms the body of the evil realms so that all karmic actions leading to the evil realms are no longer performed; this is called the Bodhisattva’s departure from all evil destinies.
The transition from the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) into the stage of pure mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*) is explained in the "Chapter on Prior Abodes.

Regarding the ten qualities, such as faith, which constitute the abode of pure joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), their purification, their respective antidotes, the factors to be countered, and their sequential establishment are set forth in this stage.
What are the remedies?
First, being heedless and not receiving the bodhisattva precepts violates faith in enlightenment; therefore, faith serves as the remedy.
Second, harboring a mind of killing toward sentient beings violates great compassion; therefore, the mind of compassion serves as the remedy.
Third, to harbor a mind of ill will toward sentient beings is to contravene great compassion; therefore, a compassionate mind serves as its antidote.
Fourth, to be preoccupied with one's life and wealth is to contravene the practice of giving; therefore, the practice of giving serves as its antidote.
Fifth, to seek many material requisites from sentient beings violates non-remissness; therefore, non-remissness serves as its antidote.
Sixth, the absence of skillful means wisdom violates knowledge of the treatises; therefore, knowledge of the treatises serves as its antidote.
Seventh, non-virtuous compliance violates proper compliance with others; therefore, it is known that the world serves as its antidote.
Eighth, negligence and indolence regarding the cultivation of wholesome dharmas violate a sense of shame and dread of blame; therefore, shame and dread of blame serve as their antidotes.

Ninth, for those who undergo uninterrupted suffering throughout the long night of birth and death, their minds become timid and inferior, which is contrary to valor; therefore, valor serves as the antidote.
Tenth, regarding those who harbor doubts about the Buddha, this is contrary to making offerings; therefore, making offerings serves as the antidote.
These ten types of remedies for their respective opposites can be summarized into two kinds:
first, purity of mind;
second, purity of skillful means.

The first three types of purity are purity of mind; the remainder are purity of skillful means. What is their sequence? A bodhisattva has faith in enlightenment; toward suffering sentient beings, they give rise to compassion.

Because they give rise to compassion, they desire to deliver sentient beings and thus give rise to loving-kindness. Because they give rise to loving-kindness, they practice generosity. Because they practice generosity, they cultivate the correct meaning without weariness. Because they are without weariness, they come to know the various sūtras and śāstras. Because they know the sūtras and śāstras, they skillfully understand the world and accord with the world. Because they accord with the world, when afflictions arise, they feel shame and remorse. Because of shame and remorse, they do not follow after afflictions and attain the power of valor. Because they have attained the power of valor, they cultivate correct skillful means, whereby wholesome dharmas increase and they gain much benefit by making offerings to the Tathāgata. Thus, these ten dharmas purify all the stages (*bhūmi*).

Chapter Four: On Practice (*Caryā-viniścaya*) In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the ultimate skillful means (*upāya*), this is Chapter Four: On Practice. Briefly stated, from the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) up to the supreme stage of a bodhisattva (*parama-bodhisattva-bhūmi*), there are four types of practice:
first, the perfections (*pāramitā*);
second, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*).
Third is spiritual power;
fourth is the maturation of sentient beings.

As previously explained regarding the six pāramitās, the pāramitā of skillful means, the pāramitā of aspiration, the pāramitā of power, and the pāramitā of wisdom—these are called the practice of the pāramitās.
The twelve skillful means as previously described are called the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
The five kinds of vows as previously described are called the perfection of vows (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
The purification of the skillful means of the ten powers is called the power-pāramitā.
The thorough knowledge of the categories of all phenomena is called the wisdom-pāramitā.
Because of knowing the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
Because it knows conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, immeasurable wisdom is called the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā*); because it seeks the advancement of wisdom, it is called the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*); because all paths of Māra cannot destroy it, it is called the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*); and because wisdom brings about awakening, it is called the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

As previously explained, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness, and the fourfold seeking and fourfold thorough knowledge—these are called the factors of enlightenment.
As previously stated, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are called spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).

As previously stated, the two immeasurables—the immeasurable realm of those to be disciplined (*vineya-dhātu*) and the immeasurable skillful means of disciplining them—are called the maturation of sentient beings.

These four practices encompass all bodhisattva practices; through cultivation over the long night of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, their intrinsic purity surpasses that of other worldly śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they encompass the fruit of great enlightenment.
The ten dharmas beginning with giving consist of the perfection of time, the perfection of intrinsic purity, and the perfection of fruit; for this reason, they are called *pāramitās*.
There are three ways in which these *pāramitās* are established in sequence: first, as antidotes; [second, as causes and effects; third, as the sequence of practice].
Second is the arising of causes;
third is the retribution of results.

Stinginess, covetousness, evil karma, anger, indolence, distracted mind, and ignorance—these six factors obstruct bodhi. The six perfections serve as their respective antidotes; the remaining perfections are subsumed within these six perfections. This is called the establishment of antidotes.

This bodhisattva, from the very beginning, disregards wealth and renounces the world to leave home; having already left home, he receives the bodhisattva precepts. For the sake of guarding the precepts, he cultivates patience, and through the power of patience, he is not afraid of sentient beings, and his patience becomes pure. Because he is not afraid of sentient beings, he cultivates the skillful means of uninterrupted wholesome dharmas to practice diligence. Because he is free from negligence, he brings his mind to a state of singular focus; once the mind is focused, he attains knowledge of reality as it is. This is called "establishment based on causes."

This bodhisattva, having practiced the wholesome dharma of generosity in the present life, will obtain five kinds of karmic fruits in the future: great wealth externally, and internally, longevity, physical beauty, strength, happiness, and eloquence.

One who is fully endowed with the five perfections, such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), is born among the higher realms and possesses extraordinary qualities regarding the lifespan and so forth of all sentient beings; this is called the first endowment.
That innate skillful means is free from weariness; enduring the encroachments of others without troubling sentient beings—this is called the second endowment.
That innate skillful means in all its aspects is firm and capable—this is called the third endowment.
That which is co-nascent, having few defilements, possesses the mental capacity to know all meanings and attain the various supernormal powers; this is called the fourth perfection.
That which is co-nascent, wherein wisdom increases and expands, is called the fifth perfection.
This is called the establishment of the fruit of retribution.
Those four pāramitās, which possess an inexhaustible nature as the equipment and retinue of their own essence, are called the training in higher ethics;
the dhyāna-pāramitā is called the training in higher mind.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
These three trainings constitute the bodhisattva’s path of progressive advancement; these three trainings encompass the six *pāramitās* exhaustively and unsurpassedly.
Briefly stated, there are four types of bodhisattva practices that encompass all activities:
first, the prior cultivation of the roots of virtue for enlightenment;
second, the benefiting of sentient beings.
Third, the increase of wholesome dharmas;
fourth, the maturation of sentient beings.
These four types of practices are established in this sequence, which is called the supreme establishment.
Chapter 53: The Chapter on Establishment, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, Section on Ultimate Expedient Means. The Tathāgata-abode is called the Ultimate Stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), namely: the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, the four kinds of purity in all aspects, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which there is nothing to guard, great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the eradication of all habitual tendencies, and the wondrous wisdom of all modes.
What are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?
First, the soles of the feet are level and firm;
second, there are thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet.
Third, his fingers are slender and long;
fourth, his heels are broad and well-rounded;
fifth, his hands and feet have webbed membranes between the toes and fingers.
Sixth, his hands and feet are soft and supple;
seventh, his calves are rounded like those of the king of the eneya deer;
eighth, his ankle bones do not protrude.
Ninth, standing upright, his hands reach his knees;
tenth, his male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse-king;
eleventh, his body is perfectly symmetrical and well-proportioned like a nyagrodha tree.
Twelfth, the body hairs curl upward;
thirteenth, each hair curls to the right;
fourteenth, the body is golden in color.
Fifteenth, his halo extends one fathom;
sixteenth, his skin is so fine and soft that dust and grime do not adhere to it;
seventeenth, seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the neck—are well-filled.
Eighteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion;
nineteenth, his arms and elbows are well-rounded;
twentieth, the collarbone is full.
Twenty-first: the body is straight and upright;
twenty-second: he has forty teeth;
twenty-third: the teeth are even and closely set.
Twenty-fourth, his teeth are white and pure;
twenty-fifth, his jaw is square like that of a lion;
twenty-sixth, he possesses the faculty of supreme taste in successive order.
Twenty-seventh, the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head;
twenty-eighth, the broad and long tongue;
twenty-ninth, the Brahma-like voice.
Thirty: his eyes are deep blue; thirty-one:
his upper and lower eyelashes are like those of a bull king;
thirty-two: there is a white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.

The eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are as follows: twenty [marks] consisting of the nails and fingers and toes of the hands and feet; and eight locations on the hands and feet—both the palms and soles—which are level and full, as well as the two ankles, the two knees, the two thighs, the two shoulders, and the two elbows.

The marks of concealment on both forearms, both thighs, and both hips; the two rounded [shoulders], the two calves, the two flanks, the two armpits, the two breasts, the waist, the back, the heart, the navel, the throat, and the abdomen—all of which are exquisitely beautiful—these are called the sixty secondary marks below the throat.

The upper and lower teeth, the two lips, the two gums, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyes, the two ears, the two eyebrows, the two nostrils, and the two corners of the forehead—these are called the twenty secondary marks above the throat.

These marks and embellishments are first attained by Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Pure Mind; thereafter, they become progressively more purified across all stages, reaching ultimate, swift purity only upon the seat of enlightenment.

The remaining four uncommon dharmas, such as the purity in all aspects (*sarvākāra-viśuddhi*), are attained when [the qualities] are swiftly purified and fulfilled; those of lower capacity achieve them in the preceding bodhisattva stages.
From the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*) onward, all superior advancements of the bodhisattvas arise, and all the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are produced.

Furthermore, the various constituents of enlightenment have both distant and proximate aspects: those that are distant have not yet attained the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), while those that are proximate have already attained them.
Because sentient beings perform various kinds of karma and thereby obtain various kinds of retribution, the World-Honored One has taught this through his power of transformation.
Why is this? Because sentient beings perform various kinds of evil karma and consequently receive various kinds of evil retribution.

To serve as a true antidote, the Buddha speaks of the karma for the various marks and signs of excellence, so that they may obtain the fruit and retribution of those various marks and signs. Upon hearing this, sentient beings delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas and abandon all evil karma, as described in the *Lakṣaṇavyañjanasūtra*.
Because the Bodhisattva maintains ethical discipline, practices patience, and practices giving, he attains the mark of level soles on his feet.
Because he makes offerings to his parents and acts as a protector for suffering sentient beings, he attains the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet.

By not harming sentient beings and harboring no intent to steal, by first greeting those worthy of respect with words of inquiry, joining his palms in reverence, making offerings of cherished wealth, and destroying all forms of pride, he attains the mark of long, slender fingers.
By having attained the karma for the three aforementioned marks, one obtains the mark of level heels.
Because of gathering sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one obtains the mark of webbed fingers and toes.
Because he bathed and anointed the bodies of those he respected, he obtained the mark of soft hands and feet.
Because he cultivated all wholesome dharmas with tireless progress, he obtained the mark of well-rounded calves.
Because he personally received the True Dharma and extensively expounded it for others, and because he served as a messenger for the Dharma, he attained the mark of non-protruding ankle bones.

Because he practiced the purification of the three karmas in succession, attended to the sick and gave them medicine, and cultivated contentment by abandoning all forms of pride, he attained the mark of standing upright with his hands reaching his knees.

Because he saw those who were separated and brought them together through the Dharma, cultivated a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), and gave clothing to others, he obtained the mark of the horse’s sheath (*aśvakośa*).

Because he purified the three types of action (*trikarma*) himself and taught others to do so, knew moderation in food and drink, gave medicine to the sick, undertook difficult tasks, accumulated hard-earned wealth, and was able to bring the increase and decrease of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) into harmony, he obtained the mark of the perfectly proportioned body (*suparipūrṇakāya*).
By attaining the karma for the mark of well-rounded calves as described above, one obtains the mark of body hairs that curl upward.

By personally cultivating wholesome dharmas with clear and penetrating wisdom, contemplating the subtle meanings of all phenomena, delighting in making offerings to those worthy of respect, and—by means of acting as a virtuous friend to those living together—gathering and instructing them so that they may enter into the meaning of the Dharma, one obtains the mark of each individual hair curling to the right.

By giving excellent clothing, food, vehicles, necklaces, and other ornaments for adorning the body to all beings, and by not giving rise to anger, one attains the two marks of a golden-colored body and a fathom-wide halo.
By attaining the karma for each individual hair to curl to the right, one obtains the mark of soft and supple skin.
Because one practices equal giving to sentient beings and establishes great assemblies of offerings, one obtains the mark of the seven parts of the body being well-filled.

Acting as a leader for those who have already set out and those who have not yet set out, being free from pride and gentle by nature, and teaching through wholesome dharmas to eliminate unwholesome states, he attains the mark of an upper body like that of a lion.

By the very karma through which he attained the mark of long, slender fingers, he also attained the three marks of arms that are rounded and well-proportioned at the elbows, the fullness of the collarbones, and a body that is straight and well-proportioned.
Because he avoided divisive speech and reconciled those who were estranged, he attained the two marks of having forty teeth and teeth that are even and closely set.
Because he cultivated loving-kindness toward the desire realm and contemplated the meaning of the Dharma, he attained the mark of pure white teeth.
Because he joyfully bestowed gifts upon sentient beings according to their requests, he attained the mark of broad and square jaws.
By bestowing the supreme flavor of the Dharma and destroying all [worldly] flavors in order to purify that flavor, one attains the mark of the successive attainment of the supreme flavor.

By upholding the five precepts and transmitting them to others, and by constantly practicing compassion and dedicating [the merit] toward the Great Dharma, one attains the two marks of the uṣṇīṣa and the broad, long tongue.
This mark of the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the mark of the invisible crown of the head are, in fact, one and the same mark.

Because he constantly cultivated truthful speech, pleasant speech, timely speech, and speech in accordance with the Dharma, and because he skillfully taught the Dharma, he attained the mark of the Brahma-voice.

Because he practices a mind of universal compassion toward all sentient beings, just like that of parents, he attains the two marks of having deep blue eyes and the ability to blink both the upper and lower eyelids.
Because he praises and extols those who possess true virtue when he sees them, he attains the mark of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The undifferentiated causes of the thirty-two marks are all the observance of the precepts. Why is this?
If one who violates the precepts cannot even obtain the body of a lowly person, how much less can they obtain the marks of a Great Man?
Thus, each attainment is explained in detail, established separately according to various types of karma.
Furthermore, by cultivating the four kinds of wholesome practices that serve as the wings for both lay and ordained bodhisattvas, one attains all the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
One who practices with determination attains the mark of level soles of the feet.

One who practices with single-minded devotion attains nine marks: the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet, the calves like those of an antelope, webbed fingers and toes, soft and supple hands and feet, fullness at the seven locations, a full collarbone, rounded and well-proportioned arms and elbows, a straight body, and a broad and long tongue.
One who practices constantly attains five marks: long and slender fingers, level heels that stand flat, hands reaching the knees, a well-proportioned body, and teeth that are even and closely set.
One who practices without fault attains the remaining marks.
By being free from anger toward all sentient beings, one attains the two marks of soft hands and feet and fine, delicate skin.
By practicing these in succession, one attains the mark of calves like those of the *eṇeya* deer.

Through the practice of a virtuous mind characterized by joy, radiance, and melodious speech, one attains four marks: a circular halo extending one fathom, a golden-colored body, pure white teeth, and a white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
Not rejoicing in fame and reputation, and concealing one's own merits, one attains the mark of the horse’s sheath.

Dedication of cultivated roots of goodness toward Bodhi results in the four marks of hair curling upward, forty teeth, the successive attainment of the supreme sense of taste, and the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
By diligently cultivating vigor, one attains the two marks of the upper body of a lion and the square jaw.

By dwelling peacefully in the minds of sentient beings as if viewing an only son, one attains the three marks of teeth that are even and closely set, deep blue eyes, and eyelashes like those of a bull king.
Cultivating goodness without weariness results in the attainment of the remaining marks.
These are called the four ways of cultivating wholesome karma to obtain the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

The seeds of the marks and excellences reside in the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*); the Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) cultivates and accumulates skillful means; the Bodhisattva on the stage of the pure mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) attains them; for Bodhisattvas on the subsequent stages, they become progressively more refined and pure; and for the Tathāgata on the ultimate stage, they are supremely and perfectly pure.
This is a brief explanation of the primary marks for the sake of sentient beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacities; all other qualities of a Buddha are secondary marks of greatness.
These and the remaining one hundred and forty marks are called the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) because they constitute the exquisite excellence of the body.

To speak briefly: the accumulation of merit of all sentient beings is equal to one mark of the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); the accumulation of merit of all such marks is equal to one secondary characteristic (*anuvyañjana*); when the accumulation of merit of all secondary characteristics is increased a hundredfold, one obtains one [major] mark—excluding the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) and the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protrusion);

when the merit of all remaining marks is increased a thousandfold, one obtains the *ūrṇā-kośa*; when the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* is increased a hundred-thousandfold, one obtains the *uṣṇīṣa*, the mark of the invisible crown; and when the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* is increased a hundred-thousand times ten millionfold, one obtains the Tathāgata’s mark of the conch-like voice (*brahma-svara*).
The Tathāgata emits a pure Brahma-voice at will, reaching even to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; such is the inconceivable accumulation of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of immeasurability regarding the karma of the marks and signs:
practicing them for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas is called "immeasurable in terms of time";
bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings is called "immeasurable in terms of mind."
Various kinds of wholesome karma are called "immeasurable conduct.
Through the cultivation of these immeasurable requisites of merit, the marks and signs of a Tathāgata emerge.
Regarding the four types of universal purity: first is the purity of the body; [the others follow].
Second is purity of the objective sphere;
third is purity of mind;
fourth is purity of wisdom.
Having abandoned the body of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) without remainder, one attains the supreme body with mastery over arising and ceasing; this is called purity of body.
The various manifested transformations and spoken teachings, wherein all objective spheres are sovereign and unimpeded, are called purity of sphere.
To be entirely free from afflictions and for one's roots of goodness to reach maturity is called purity of mind.
To abandon all defilements of ignorance and to possess unimpeded mastery over all that is knowable is called purity of wisdom.
The ten powers of the Tathāgata are: first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible;
second, the power of knowing the results of one's own karma;
third, the power of knowing the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
Fourth is the power of knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties;
fifth is the power of knowing various inclinations;
sixth is the power of knowing various elements.
Seventh, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to various destinations;
eighth, the power of knowledge regarding past lives;
ninth, the power of knowledge regarding birth and death.
Tenth is the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*). These ten powers are explained in detail in the *Daśabala-sūtra*.
Because his speech does not deviate from suchness (*tathatā*), he is called *Tathāgata*.
That pure and impure fruits depend upon specific causes is called "possible" (*sthāna*).
That pure and impure fruits arise from causes that are contradictory [to their nature] is called "impossible" (*asthāna*).
Knowledge free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
As explained previously in the Chapter on Unsurpassed Bodhi:
all-knowledge, unimpeded knowledge, and pure knowledge—these are called the knowledge free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Being capable of benefiting sentient beings in every way, and having abandoned all Māras and adversaries to attain victory—this is called power (*bala*).
To cultivate and master the power of mastery according to one's will is called "accomplishment.
Unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* is called "sublime.
To attain the Eightfold Noble Path and be free from all affliction, turmoil, and fear is called "peaceful security."
To know for oneself what has been attained is called "self-knowledge.
To extensively expound for others the Dharma one has personally realized with a heart of compassion is called "turning the Brahma-wheel."

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, regarding these various afflictions, disturbances, purity, quiescence, coolness, and reality, first turned [the wheel] so that all sentient beings may attain purity; this is called the Brahma-wheel.

Having attained the supreme teaching and encompassing the discourse of the Unsurpassed Great Master, one destroys heterodox paths through one's own realization and gives rise to no timidity toward any opposing doctrines. Being victorious over all treatises as the most excellent and unsurpassed, one preaches for the fourfold assembly; this is called the lion’s roar.

Briefly stated, this consists of establishing oneself in peace, establishing others in peace, and establishing both self and others in peace; it is the opening, revealing, instructing, and proclaiming [of these].
Furthermore, briefly stated, it consists of attaining the goal and attaining the means.
If gods or humans obtain whatever they seek from me, this is called attaining skillful means (*upāya*).
Just as one who has recovered from an illness is freed from affliction and finds peace, yet further treats others, this is called turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
To enable all false and heterodox teachers to obtain their respective remedies and for all illnesses to be cured is called the lion’s roar.
If the karma that was performed has been accomplished and has already ceased, it is called the past.
If it has not yet been performed and has not yet ceased, but is something that ought to be performed, this is called the future.
If it is an action that has been performed and has not yet ceased, but is something currently being performed, this is called the present.
When distinguished by way of action, there are again three kinds, namely: bodily, vocal, and mental karma.

When distinguished by way of the undertaking of dharmas (*dharmasamādāna*), there are again four kinds: there is the undertaking of a dharma that results in happiness in the present life but suffering as its retribution in future lives, as explained at length previously in the "Chapter on Benefit for Oneself and Others."
To provide the benefit of teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate—whether for peace or unrest in this life or future lives—is called skillful means regarding the locus (*sthāna-upāya*).
If one acts by taking as an object that which is either sentient or non-sentient, this is called a sentient being (*sattva*).
That which is produced by roots of goodness is called the cause.
That the fruits of love and non-love, or misfortune and fortune, are brought to fruition is called the retribution.

Briefly stated, regarding all times, all practices, all skillful means in all places, all sentient beings, all objects, all causes, and all misfortunes and fortunes—such as these, the Tathāgata knows them all completely, without remainder, and unsurpassed.

Regarding the four dhyānas and eight liberations, one attains mastery over the mind within these meditative absorptions and liberations; such that various forms and images are all accomplished according to one's will—this is called the samādhi of correct reception through the dhyānas and liberations.

As it is said, when the World-Honored One enters samādhi and right concentration (*samāpatti*), his radiance illuminates the Brahma heavens; he preaches the Dharma with wondrous sounds, such that one hears only the voice but does not see his form. For this reason, the Tathāgata enters the *samādhis* that resemble those shared with the world and those not shared with the world, and is able to accomplish them swiftly. He attains mastery over the mind regarding dhyāna and liberation, achieving everything according to his will. Therefore, it is called "dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi-right-concentration."
Furthermore, regarding the dhyānas and so forth, there are two kinds of afflictions:
first, those that obstruct the preparatory application (*prayoga*) such that one cannot engage in cultivation;
second, those afflictions and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of one's own stage which, once attained, cause one to deviate from the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

The Tathāgata, by means of various conventional teachings, according to their physical forms and as is appropriate for them, causes them to attain the fulfillment of wisdom cultivated through meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, becoming free from affliction and pure. Whether they have attained it or not yet attained it, whether it is inferior or superior, he knows all as it truly is; therefore, this is called "knowing the meditations, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) as they truly are."
When the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, have reached maturity, they are categorized as weak, middling, or superior; this is called the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*).

Taking the arising of faith through others or through one's own reflection as the means, one gives rise to weak, middling, or superior aspirations; this is called various inclinations (*nānādhimukti*).

The establishment of various lineages refers to the lineages of the three vehicles, the dispositions of sentient beings such as their greed and other afflictions, and even up to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct; these are called the various realms (*dhātu*).

Knowing the various gateways of the perfections and their corresponding remedies—such as contemplating impurity to counteract desire, as explained at length in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*—this is called the path leading to all destinations.
Furthermore, various factions and groups oppose one another, giving rise to divergent views and desires, and constantly engaging in disputes, such as the non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere toward all states in this world and the next is also called the *sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*, as explained at length in the *Kāla-sūtra*.

They know the conventional designations established for sentient beings in the four directions through various names—namely, the eight types of past matters and the six types of common practices—and they are able to fully comprehend all such varieties.
The eight aspects are: such a name, such a birth, such a lineage, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such duration of stay, and such a limit to one's lifespan.
