There are six kinds of commonalities: conventional names, physical forms such as those of the kṣatriya caste and so forth, parents, food and drink, good and evil, and lifespan.
Regarding these eight matters and six kinds of commonalities, others and oneself speak thus: "This is my name."
"I am a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra. These are my parents. I eat such food."
"I performed such wholesome and unwholesome deeds during my youth, middle age, or old age.
In this way, through the knowledge of past lives, he knows these six types of co-residents exactly as they truly are.
All meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are called the celestial abodes (devasthāna).
Because one attains the eye by relying on these absorptions, it is called the purity of the divine eye (divyacakṣurviśuddhi).
Because its fruition is fulfilled, it is called the supreme purity (praṇītaviśuddhi).
Since this does not exist among humans, it is said to "surpass humans.
Although the gods of the desire realm possess the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye) as a karmic retribution, it is likewise absent among humans.
When sentient beings are on the verge of death, it is termed the "time of death."
There are two kinds of darkness:
those born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who possess such characteristics are like the blackness of night or the luster of black wool; therefore, they are called "of evil color.
There are also two kinds of pure white.
Beings born in the intermediate state (antarābhava) who possess such characteristics are like the light of the bright moon or a garment from Varanasi; therefore, they are called "of beautiful color.
To give rise to unwholesome precepts is what is meant by "unwholesome precepts."
Committing evils of body, speech, and mind, practicing various wrong views, and accomplishing such evil conduct, one slanders the noble sages; this is called "slandering through wrong views.
Clinging to wrong views, wrong causes, and wrong effects, one consequently performs all manner of wrong karmas.

Having performed wrong actions, one experiences pleasure in the present life and suffering as retribution in the future, or experiences suffering in the present life and suffering as retribution in the future; this is called the accomplishment of the causes for experiencing wrong dharmas.
The arising of various unwholesome dharmas within the evil realms is called "due to that.
The separation of name-and-form is called "the destruction of the body.
The total exhaustion of the factors of rebirth is called "the end of life."
Unrighteous and evil conduct is called "evil.
To experience the touch of extreme suffering for a long night without interruption is called an "evil destination" (durgati).
To fall into the lowest place and turn one's back on great compassion and the like is called "falling."
That which is increasingly loathsome is called *niraya* (hell).
That which is the opposite of the above is called the pure portion (*śuklabhāga*).
Being born through the power of virtuous conduct is called a happy destination (*sugati*).
That which is spontaneously attained is called "heaven" (deva).

All outflows (āsrava) are abandoned without remainder; all latent tendencies (anuśaya) are counteracted; and there is the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), supreme higher intention (adhiprajñā), and supreme higher wisdom (adhiprajñā).

The exhaustion of outflows is called liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; based on the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, the mind attains liberation and wisdom attains liberation—this is termed "subsequent existence."

Having attained the six supernormal powers, one knows them as they truly are and is able to explain them to others; therefore, it is said that one has personally realized and witnessed for oneself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established," and so forth, as explained at length.
The ten powers of the Tathāgata are of seven kinds:
first, their intrinsic nature;
second, their classification; [and so forth].
Third, non-commonality;
fourth, equality;
fifth, the creation of karma.
Sixth is the sequence;
seventh is the differentiation.
Regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), some say it is the nature of the five sense faculties, while others say it is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the intrinsic nature of wisdom, it is described as the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), rather than the powers of faith and so forth.
As it is with the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, so it is with the remaining powers.
Regarding differentiation (*vibhāga*), there are briefly three kinds:
first, differentiation by time, wherein the past, future, and present enter into all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
second, differentiation by mode (*ākāra*), wherein the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) enter into all modes.
Third is the differentiation of sentient beings, wherein the entire realm of sentient beings enters into all forms of benefit.
These three types of differentiation, when explained in detail, are immeasurable.

Regarding "unshared": the Tathāgata’s ten powers are not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. "Equal" means that the ten powers of all Tathāgatas are equal; there is no distinction of inferior, middling, or superior among those who perform karma. As for the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*): he knows the true nature of cause and effect as it really is, thereby subduing the disputations concerning cause and effect among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

By means of the power of knowledge regarding the results of one’s own karma (*karmasvaka-jñānabala*), he knows as it truly is that whatever karma one has performed will bear its fruit; thus he subdues those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who dispute the merit of giving.

By means of the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (*dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-samāpatti-jñānabala*), he manifests the three modes of demonstration to discipline and instruct, thereby subduing those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold opposing and contradictory views.

The power of knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties: he knows, as they truly are, the soft, medium, and superior faculties of all sentient beings, and he teaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate and by whatever means are effective.

The power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations of beings: it knows, in accordance with reality, the inferior, middling, and superior inclinations of all sentient beings, as well as their pure and impure inclinations; it teaches them to cultivate pure inclinations and to abandon impure ones.

By the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*), he knows, as they truly are, the inferior, middling, and superior elements of all sentient beings; according to their minds, their faculties, their inclinations, and their underlying tendencies, he provides instruction and benefit through whichever gateway of liberation is appropriate for each.

Regarding the power of knowledge concerning the paths leading to various destinations, the Tathāgata provides various gateways for liberation and various instructions for all sentient beings, developing, revealing, instructing, and proclaiming them according to the sequence of the Śrāvaka-bhūmi.
How does the Tathāgata instruct a beginner bodhisattva on how to collect the requisites for samādhi and settle the mind?
For those who are free from deceit and crookedness, the Tathāgata teaches them to practice and train, saying:
"O son of good family!
You should dwell alone, deeply delighting in tranquility, and contemplate the names assigned by your parents and teachers.
Such names do not exist at all within the six internal and external sense bases or in between them; they lack intrinsic nature and are merely conceptual designations.
Reflecting in this way, one finds that phenomena are unattainable; thus, one does not give rise to the notion of "the future" regarding what is yet to come.
Son of good family!

Regarding the present eye, one applies the name "eye," the perception of "eye," and the designation "eye. You should observe for yourself: since even the eye itself is unattainable, how much more so its name, perception, and designation as "this is the eye"?

"In this way, all designations of names and concepts are entirely non-existent; these designations of names and concepts lack any reality whatsoever, and the intrinsic nature of that eye is likewise non-existent. Why is this?"

It is not that the eye gives rise to the cognition of "eye" through the name, the notion, the designation, or the convention of "eye"; rather, the cognition of "eye" arises merely from names and verbal expressions.
The nature of that eye cannot be heard or known; it is only with respect to the name and the object that the cognition of "eye" arises.

Therefore, one should contemplate that what is originally called the "eye" is merely a designation for the eye, a conceptualization of the eye; all future phenomena are likewise entirely unobtainable.

As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and even seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, as well as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—whether seeking or attaining, whether perceiving or examining—all such conceptualizations of phenomena, up to and including conceptualizations of the future.
In this way, one is embraced by the path of skillful means that destroys the notion of a self, up to being embraced by the path of skillful means that destroys the notion of all phenomena.

Thus, having thoroughly examined all that is knowable, one regards the notions of all phenomena and future notions as entirely deceptive—devoid of thought, devoid of volition, and devoid of signs—and without grasping at any objective referent, one shall attain the lineage of the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom-samādhi.

Those bodhisattvas attain the contemplation of impurity, practice loving-kindness, observe dependent origination, discern the elements, and maintain mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, thereby reaching the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The Bodhisattva’s contemplation of immeasurable samādhis and meditative attainments, proceeding gradually until the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is called the Bodhisattva’s path to all destinations.
The Tathāgatas of the past have instructed beginner bodhisattvas in this way; the Buddhas of the future shall instruct them in this way; and the Buddhas of the present also instruct them in this way.
The Śrāvaka-vehicle contemplates in this way, swiftly attaining supernormal powers and unimpeded knowledge.

Through the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations, one knows as it truly is the path that leads out of all suffering; thus, one benefits others by departing from non-leaving paths and establishing them on the path of departure.

With the power of knowledge regarding past lives, he observes past existences; regarding good and evil, whether with a mind of revulsion or a mind of purity, he tames and teaches the Dharma, subduing those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who maintain eternalist views.

By the power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*), he proclaims the births and the places of rebirth for sentient beings, thereby subduing and severing the annihilationist views of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
By the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*), he subdues those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who harbor doubts regarding liberation.
Regarding the sequence: although the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* instantaneously, the ten powers (*daśabala*) manifest sequentially thereafter.

Because the factors of the Dharma of the *avaivartika* Buddha involve the differentiation of causes and effects, he observes these causal and effectual distinctions by means of the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).

Due to the distinctions within the desire realm, he observes their own karma through the power of knowledge of the results of one's actions and teaches the Dharma accordingly, causing them to abandon evil karma and practice virtuous karma.

In order to bring about detachment through the mundane path, he teaches sentient beings by means of his power of knowledge regarding the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments (*dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-samāpatti-jñānabala*).

Furthermore, for the sake of supramundane detachment, he first teaches sentient beings the mundane path to detachment by means of his power of knowledge regarding the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments, so that they subsequently achieve detachment through the supramundane path.

Desiring to enable sentient beings to attain the supramundane state free from desire, he observes their faculties by means of the power of knowledge regarding the sharpness or dullness of those faculties.
Having known their faculties, and desiring to know their inclinations, he observes their inclinations by means of the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of dispositions.

Having observed their aspirations, he employs the power of knowledge regarding the various elements to examine their faculties and latent tendencies, delivering them through the gateways of liberation according to their respective skillful means and spheres of experience.

By means of the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations, he dwells with a mind established in skillful means regarding the gateways of the spheres of experience and dwells with a mind that embraces them; having purified his conduct and abandoned the view of a self-identity along with views of eternalism and nihilism, he teaches the Middle Way for their sake.

Because he is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*), he enters the power of knowledge regarding past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*) and the power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*).

Because he teaches in order to cause those who are bound by cessation and do not sever their afflictions to abandon their overweening pride (*adhimāna*), he enters the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).

Furthermore, as for the sequence: after an *avaivartika* Buddha has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he first uses the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) to observe the ultimate reality of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-paramārtha-dharmasthititā*).

Having established himself in the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena according to the ultimate truth, he observes the various karmas of the householders' sphere by means of the power of knowing the results of one's own actions.

Having observed the various karmas of the householders' sphere, he observes the renunciant's sphere by means of the power of knowing the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
"How can these who have gone forth be liberated from suffering? I shall preach the path for them," he thought, and gave rise to great compassion, observing with the Buddha-eye.
With the power of knowledge regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties, he observed their inferior, middling, and superior capacities and preached the Dharma accordingly.
The remaining powers, such as the power of knowing the various inclinations (*nānādhātujñānabala*), follow the sequence previously explained.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence: by means of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*), the Buddha of the *Avivartya* stage observes the realm of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmadhātu*); by means of the power of knowing one's own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*), he observes the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), [seeing] that such sentient beings perform such karma and receive such results.

Having contemplated the realm of phenomena and the realm of sentient beings, he employs the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and correct meditative attainment to provide instruction for suffering sentient beings through three kinds of manifestations.

The remaining powers, such as the power of knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and so forth, deliver all sentient beings through the Path, causing them to be liberated from all suffering.

The distinction is that knowing wholesome and unwholesome karma and the resulting attainment of pleasant or unpleasant fruits is called the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).

Knowing that wholesome and unwholesome karmas yield pleasant and unpleasant fruits respectively, and that one does not create nor experience [the results of] anything other than those—such as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*)—and understanding that "this karma belongs to this person, and that karma belongs to that person," is called the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*svakarmasvakatājñānabala*).

Knowing the teachings that manifest the three types of dhyāna, liberation, and so forth, up to knowing the minds associated with the innate purity and its concomitants, is called the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, samādhis, and attainments (dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-samāpatti-jñānabala).
To know the inferior, middling, and superior faculties is called the power of knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*).
Furthermore, to know the skillful means by which the faculties give rise to aspiration for those [states] is also called the power of knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties.
To know various aspirations is called the power of knowledge regarding the diverse inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).
There are six kinds of inclinations:
first, non-emergent inclination, which refers to the aspiration for Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, the Brahma-world, and so forth.
Second is the liberation of emergence, which refers to the aspiration for the liberation of the three vehicles.
Third is the liberation of remote purification, which refers to the aspiration for the maturation of the weak and middling levels.
Fourth is the liberation of proximate purification, which refers to the aspiration for the maturation of the superior level.
Fifth is the understanding of attaining nirvāṇa in the present life, which refers to the understanding of attaining nirvāṇa through aspiring to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Sixth is the understanding of attaining nirvāṇa in the future, which refers to the understanding of attaining nirvāṇa through aspiring to the Mahāyāna.
Even the metaphor of the seeds that give rise to various understandings is called the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*).
There are four kinds of distinctions regarding elements (*dhātu*); like seeds according to their nature, this is termed the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of inclinations.
To know the seeds of various conceptual discriminations is called the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
Furthermore, to know the dharmas of nirvāṇa as well as the paths that accord with the elements is also called the power of knowledge regarding the diversity of elements.

To know all types of paths and tracks, as well as their various afflictions and various purifications, is called the power of knowledge regarding the path leading to the respective destinations (*yathāgata-mārga-jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, even knowing the causes for all destinies in past lives is also called the power of knowledge regarding the path leading to the respective destinations.
To know the six kinds of verbal expressions of the past is called the power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*).
Furthermore, to know the births and deaths of sentient beings in the past is also called the power of knowledge of past lives.
To know the future births and deaths is called the power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*jāti-maraṇa-jñāna-bala*).
Even knowing the future births and deaths of sentient beings who have not yet perfected their own welfare is likewise called the power of knowledge regarding birth and death.
To know that one’s own ultimate goal is attained—nirvāṇa in this very life—is called the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
These ten kinds of powers of knowledge each have their respective distinctions.
The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are as explained in the Sūtras.
By means of these four matters, the Tathāgata personally realizes them amidst the great assembly and remains fearless.
Being liberated from the cognitive obscurations and possessing the equal awakening to all phenomena—unshared with the śrāvakas—is the first fearlessness.
Liberation from the hindrance of afflictions in common with the śrāvakas is the second fearlessness.
Proclaiming the path leading out of suffering is the third fearlessness.
The factors that obstruct the path constitute the fourth fearlessness.
The Tathāgata knows these four meanings exactly as they truly are; it is impossible that anyone could revile him by saying he does not know them.

Because this is impossible, he attains fearlessness, being without timidity or doubt, knowing with certainty for himself that he is fit to be a Great Teacher who brings peace to himself and peace to others.
The fulfillment of the first two stages is the path of self-comfort;
the fulfillment of the latter two stages is the path of comforting others.
The awakening to the equality of all phenomena is for the sake of the bodhisattvas who are directed toward the Mahāyāna.
Liberation from the afflictive hindrances is for the sake of those who incline toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
this is because both the path that leads out of suffering and the dharmas that obstruct the path must be addressed.
Thus, for the sake of all Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, the Tathāgata teaches the Sūtras concerning the practice of the path leading out of suffering.

The compilers of the Sūtra-piṭaka established the Bodhisattva-piṭaka by teaching the practices of bodhisattvas, and established the Śrāvaka-piṭaka by teaching the practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The three applications of mindfulness are as explained in the sūtras.
For a long night, the Tathāgata has maintained this thought:
"I am the great Dharma Lord of my well-expounded discipline; regarding those who accept it or do not accept it, I give rise to no mind of vexation.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of assemblies:
First, the right course;
second, the wrong course;
third, that which is neither right nor wrong.
Regarding these three assemblies, he maintains a mind of right mindfulness without increase or decrease.
The three things that need no protection are as explained in the Sūtras.
Briefly stated, all concealment of his actions has been completely severed; therefore, the Tathāgata reveals the three things that need no protection.
Arhats still possess indeterminate *duṣkṛta* offenses, occasionally occurring through forgetfulness or error;
only the Tathāgata is entirely free from these, being wholly true and real.

An Arhat may at times fear falling into a position of defeat during debate, or at times feel displeasure, or at times act out of his intellectual nature; for these reasons, he guards himself so that latent tendencies (vāsanā) do not give rise to impure actions of body, speech, and mind.
All such things are entirely absent in the Tathāgata.
Great compassion is as previously explained in the *Anantavastuka-parivarta* regarding making offerings and cultivating intimacy.

As for "not forgetting the Dharma," it means that the Tathāgata constantly recollects all that he has done: at all times, in all actions, in all teachings, and through all skillful means; he always maintains mindfulness of these matters without ever forgetting them.

"Having eliminated all residual habits" means that in the Tathāgata’s movements, gestures, gazes, speech, walking, and standing, there are no residual habits resembling those arising from afflictions (*kleśa*).
While the movements, gestures, gazes, speech, walking, and standing of Arhats still possess residual habits resembling those arising from afflictions, the Tathāgata has eternally severed them;
therefore, he is said to have "eliminated all residual habits."
Regarding the one with the wondrous knowledge of all modes, the Tathāgata knows three kinds of phenomena:
those that bring benefit in meaning, those that do not bring benefit in meaning, and those that neither bring benefit nor non-benefit in meaning.

The knowledge of all phenomena that knows what is non-beneficial, what is neither beneficial nor non-beneficial, and the knowledge of all phenomena—this is called the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The knowledge of all phenomena that knows what is beneficial—this is called wondrous knowledge (*prajñā*).
The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) are collectively termed the "sublime wisdom of all modes.
This is a brief explanation of the one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) and all the marks and signs of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).

In his final existence, the bodhisattva attains the swift purification of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); beneath the Bodhi tree, he then fulfills the requirements of that final existence. By cultivating the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, he attains the various marks [of a Great Man], which are subsumed by the samādhi free from hindrances and the vajra-samādhi. Subsequently, in the second moment of mind, he suddenly attains the ten powers, up to the swift purification of the supreme knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding all that is knowable, they are unimpeded and unobstructed; being swiftly purified and free from defilement, they attain equal awakening. Transcending all bodhisattva practices, they practice the conduct of the Tathāgata and attain the supreme body and the ultimate stage.
What is the difference between the wisdom of a bodhisattva and the wisdom of a Tathāgata?
The wisdom of a bodhisattva on the ultimate stage is like looking through a fine gauze, whereas the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like looking with the gauze removed.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is like seeing forms from a distance; the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like seeing forms up close.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is like viewing through a slight cataract; the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like seeing with pure eyes.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is like seeing while in the womb; the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like seeing after birth.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is like seeing in a dream; the wisdom of a Tathāgata is like seeing when awake.
This constitutes the distinction between the wisdom of the Tathāgatas and that of Bodhisattvas at the stage of ultimate perfection.
Briefly stated, there are nine ways in which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, perform Buddha-works to benefit sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
What are the nine?
First, because he wishes to cause the faith of sentient beings to be pure, he receives a male body and manifests the various marks and signs of excellence.
Second, because he wishes to benefit all sentient beings and sever all their doubts, he manifests the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

Third, by means of the ten powers of a Buddha, one gives rise to all meanings, develops the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing knowledge and vision, answers all questions, subdues all heterodox arguments, and establishes correct doctrine; thus, one gives rise to the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses.

Fourth, because the Tathāgata’s wisdom—whether abiding or non-abiding—subdues beings accordingly and brings them free from all afflictions, he gives rise to the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Fifth, as previously explained, because he acts in such a manner, he gives rise to the three ways in which he needs no protection (*arakṣya*).
Sixth, because he constantly observes all worlds day and night with the Buddha-eye, he gives rise to great compassion.
Seventh, because he has already accomplished all that is to be done for all sentient beings, he gives rise to the quality of non-forgetfulness.
Eighth, because the conduct of the Tathāgata accords with suchness (tathatā) without exception, he gives rise to the eradication of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Ninth, because he completely distances himself from all dharmas that do not benefit the goal, those that neither benefit nor harm the goal, and because he analytically reveals the dharmas that do benefit the goal, he gives rise to the sublime wisdom of all modes (*sarvākāra-prajñā*).

The Tathāgata performs nine kinds of Buddha-activities based on these one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); if explained extensively, they are immeasurable. This is called the Tathāgata’s dwelling; this is called the establishment.
Why is this? Because based on the training of a bodhisattva, all activities for the benefit of sentient beings are established; therefore, it is called "establishment.
Since its self-benefit and benefit of others is not like that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is termed "unshared" (āveṇika).

The great compassion of all Buddhas is never-forgotten; it eradicates all habitual tendencies and possesses the wondrous knowledge of all modes, which cannot be attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Since all other types [of qualities] are likewise not fully perfected [in them], they are called "unshared" (āveṇika).

In this, the fulfillment of the bodhisattva’s path of training and the fruit of that training is revealed; it is the locus for the teaching of all aspects of the bodhisattva’s path of training and its fruit in their true reality. Therefore, it is called the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Bodhisattvapitaka-mātṛkā*, the Compendium of the Mahāyāna, the Unfailing Revelation, and the Root of Unobstructed Pure Wisdom.

If there are devas, humans, asuras, humans and non-humans, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas who give rise to firm faith and understanding toward the bodhisattva stages, and who listen to, receive, practice, and extensively explain them to others, or transcribe the sūtra scrolls and make various offerings to them, the merit they obtain shall be equal and no different from all the merit that the World-Honored One has revealed, displayed, instructed, and proclaimed for bodhisattvas at the beginning of their practice within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.

Why is this? This Bodhisattva-bhūmi and Bodhisattva-piṭaka reveal the laws and regulations of the bodhisattvas, causing many sentient beings to receive, uphold, and contemplate them, thereby establishing the sequential realization of the Dharma (dharmānudharma-pratipatti). It causes these practices to gradually expand and increase, preventing the appearance of the extinction of the Dharma during the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma) age; it can cause the true meaning of the Semblance Dharma to blaze forth and ensure that the True Dharma (saddharma) never perishes.

Therefore, by conceiving firm faith and resolve regarding the Bodhisattva stages, listening to and receiving them, practicing and cultivating them, explaining them extensively for others, copying them, and making offerings to them, the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless.
The Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra, Scroll Ten.
